topics.ch: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
topics.h: Long before GPS, Indian astronomers were already giving addresses to stars!
p: A coordinate system is a framework that fixes the exact location of a place or point using numbers.
Cities of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation, such as Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira, had streets laid out in a grid, mostly meeting at right angles.
Indian astronomers used Ujjayini (Ujjain) as a reference line for longitude, and Aryabhata described positions of heavenly bodies with angle-like coordinates.
Brahmagupta gave rules for working with zero and negative numbers; Al-Biruni located cities using latitude and longitude; Omar Khayyam solved algebra problems with geometry.
René Descartes showed that any point on a flat surface can be named by just two numbers, joining algebra and geometry. That is why the plane is called Cartesian.

ex.q: Why are negative numbers (made popular in India by Brahmagupta's rules) needed for a coordinate system with the origin in the middle?
st: Places to the left of or below the origin must also get numbers.
Positive numbers alone can only describe one side of each axis.
Negative numbers name the other side.
ex.a: They let us name points on both sides of the origin.

topics.rl: A railway ticket's seat number (coach S4, berth 23) is a simple two-number coordinate system that tells you exactly where to sit.

rv.summary: A coordinate system fixes exact locations using numbers. Ideas behind it came from grid-planned Harappan cities, Indian astronomy, Brahmagupta, Al-Biruni, Omar Khayyam and finally Descartes.
focus: Know the job of a coordinate system.
Match each contributor to their idea.
Explain why negative numbers are needed.
remember: Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira: streets in a grid at right angles.
Ujjayini: reference for longitude. Aryabhata: positions of heavenly bodies.
Brahmagupta: zero and negatives. Al-Biruni: latitude and longitude. Omar Khayyam: algebra with geometry.
Descartes: any point on a plane = two numbers (Cartesian plane).
traps: Don't mix up Brahmagupta (negatives) with Al-Biruni (geography).
One number is not enough to fix a point on a plane.

topics.ch: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
topics.t: Making a floor map to scale
topics.h: How do you fit a whole room onto one sheet of paper? Shrink it with a scale!
p: A floor map shows a room as seen from above, with each object drawn in its place.
A tactile map is one you read by touch: pins can mark corners of objects and threads can show the walls, so a person who cannot see can feel the layout.
A scale links paper and real sizes, for example 1 cm on paper = 1 foot in the room. Multiply paper length by the scale to get the real length.
Only things standing on the floor (bed, table, door) can be marked on a floor map. A window or ceiling fan is above the floor, so it has no spot on the floor plan.

ex.q: A room is 12 feet long and 9 feet wide. Using 1 cm = 1 foot, what size should the map be? Using 1 cm = 3 feet?

topics.rl: School fire-exit plans pasted near classroom doors are floor maps drawn to scale.

rv.summary: A floor map shows a room from above, drawn to a scale such as 1 cm = 1 foot. Only things standing on the floor can be marked; tactile maps let people read the layout by touch.
focus: Convert between map and real lengths using a scale.
Decide what can appear on a floor map.
Know what a tactile map is and how it is made.
remember: Real length = paper length × scale; paper length = real length ÷ scale.
12 ft × 9 ft room: 12 cm × 9 cm at 1 cm = 1 ft; 4 cm × 3 cm at 1 cm = 3 ft.
Tactile map: pins for corners, threads for walls and edges.
traps: Don't multiply by the scale when shrinking to paper.
Windows and ceiling fans are not on a floor map.

topics.ch: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
topics.h: How do you tell a friend exactly where your seat is in a cinema hall? Row and seat number! Two numbers can pin down any spot.
p: Two perpendicular number lines make the Cartesian plane: the horizontal x-axis and the vertical y-axis.
The axes meet at the origin O, whose coordinates are (0, 0).
Every point is named by an ordered pair (x, y). The x-coordinate (abscissa) tells how far left or right; the y-coordinate (ordinate) tells how far up or down.
Order matters: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different points.
A point on the x-axis has y = 0, and a point on the y-axis has x = 0.

ex.q: Point P is 4 units to the right of the y-axis and 3 units below the x-axis. Write its coordinates.
st: Right of the y-axis means x is positive: x = 4
Below the x-axis means y is negative: y = −3

topics.rl: Maps on your phone use latitude and longitude, which is a coordinate system on the Earth. Chess squares like e4 work the same way.

rv.summary: The Cartesian plane is made by two perpendicular number lines, the x-axis and y-axis, meeting at the origin (0, 0). Every point is an ordered pair (x, y).
focus: Write the coordinates of a point from its position.
Know abscissa and ordinate.
Spot points on the axes.
remember: On the x-axis y = 0; on the y-axis x = 0.
4 right of the y-axis and 3 below the x-axis: (4, −3).
traps: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different points: order matters.
A 0 in the y place puts the point on the x-axis, not the y-axis.
x tells the distance from the y-axis, not from the x-axis.

topics.ch: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
topics.h: The two axes cut the plane like a roti cut into four pieces. Each piece has its own sign pattern!
p: The axes divide the plane into four quadrants, numbered I, II, III, IV going anticlockwise from the top right.
Signs of (x, y): Quadrant I (+, +), Quadrant II (−, +), Quadrant III (−, −), Quadrant IV (+, −).
A point on an axis does not belong to any quadrant.
Distance between two points: across distance and up distance form the two shorter sides of a right triangle, so by Pythagoras, distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
Distance of (x, y) from the origin = √(x² + y²).

ex.q: Find the distance between A(1, 2) and B(4, 6).

topics.rl: Delivery apps estimate the straight-line distance between your home and a shop using coordinates and this very formula.

rv.summary: The axes split the plane into four quadrants numbered anticlockwise from the top right. The distance between two points comes from Pythagoras.
focus: Name the quadrant from the signs of x and y.
Know that points on axes are in no quadrant.
Find distances between points and from the origin.
traps: Don't number quadrants clockwise.
A point such as (0, −6) lies on an axis, not in a quadrant.
Don't add the changes; square, add, then take the square root.

topics.ch: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
topics.h: A treasure map says: from the big banyan tree, walk 3 steps east and 4 steps north. Plotting points is exactly that!
p: To plot (a, b), start at the origin. Move a units along the x-axis: right if a is positive, left if a is negative.
From there move b units parallel to the y-axis: up if b is positive, down if b is negative. Mark the point.
Points with the same y-coordinate lie on one horizontal line; points with the same x-coordinate lie on one vertical line.
On graph paper choose a scale, for example 1 cm = 1 unit, and use it on both axes.
Length of a horizontal segment = difference of the x-coordinates; length of a vertical segment = difference of the y-coordinates.

ex.q: Plot A(2, 3), B(−2, 3), C(−2, −1) and D(2, −1). What shape do they make, and what is its perimeter?
st: AB is horizontal (same y): length = 2 − (−2) = 4 units
BC is vertical (same x): length = 3 − (−1) = 4 units
Similarly CD = 4 and DA = 4, and the sides meet at right angles
So ABCD is a square; perimeter = 4 × 4 = 16 units
ex.a: A square of side 4 units, perimeter 16 units

topics.rl: Rangoli artists often mark dots on a grid first. Each dot is really a point with coordinates!

rv.summary: To plot (a, b), start at the origin, move a units along the x-axis, then b units parallel to the y-axis. Same y means a horizontal line; same x means a vertical line.
focus: Plot points with negative coordinates.
Find lengths of horizontal and vertical segments.
Identify shapes from plotted points.
remember: Right if x > 0, left if x < 0; up if y > 0, down if y < 0.
Horizontal length = difference of x's; vertical length = difference of y's.
A(2, 3), B(−2, 3), C(−2, −1), D(2, −1): square of side 4, perimeter 16.
traps: Move along x first, not y.
Same x-coordinate gives a vertical line, not a horizontal one.
Subtracting a negative means adding: 2 − (−2) = 4.

topics.ch: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
topics.h: Will Dadi's wheelchair fit through the door? Coordinates can answer before anyone tries!
p: Put one corner of a room at the origin with the walls along the axes; then every corner of every object gets coordinates.
Width of a door along a wall = difference of the coordinates of its two ends. Compare it with what must pass through, such as a wheelchair.
A hinged door sweeps a quarter circle whose radius is the door's width; furniture inside that sweep will be hit.
To place an object at the centre of a room, its centre is at (half the length, half the breadth); move half the object's sides each way to get its corners.
Plot given corners and look at the sides: four right angles and opposite sides equal means a rectangle; exactly one pair of parallel sides means a trapezium.

ex.q: A room is 12 ft by 10 ft with a corner at O(0, 0). Place a 4 ft × 2 ft table at the centre. Give its corners.
st: Half of 4 is 2 and half of 2 is 1
x from 6 − 2 = 4 to 6 + 2 = 8; y from 5 − 1 = 4 to 5 + 1 = 6

topics.rl: Architects check door widths and furniture positions on coordinate plans before a house is built, so accessibility is planned, not patched.

rv.summary: Put a room corner at the origin with walls on the axes, then every object gets coordinates. Use differences of coordinates for widths and half-lengths to centre objects.
focus: Find door and furniture widths from coordinates.
Place an object at the centre of a room.
Identify rectangles and trapeziums from corners.
remember: Width along a wall = difference of the coordinates of the ends.
Centre of an L × B room = (L/2, B/2).
A door sweeps a quarter circle of radius = door width.
traps: Don't add coordinates to find a width.
Move half the object's side each way, not the full side.
A four-sided shape with a horizontal base is not always a rectangle.

topics.ch: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
topics.t: Triangles, right angles and reflections on the grid
topics.h: Fold your graph paper along the y-axis: every point lands on its mirror twin!
p: To find the sides of a triangle from its corners, apply the distance formula to each pair of vertices.
A side is parallel to the x-axis if its ends share the same y-coordinate, and parallel to the y-axis if they share the same x-coordinate. A horizontal and a vertical side are perpendicular.
A quick right triangle: pick corners like (a, b), (c, b), (a, d). The legs are |c − a| and |d − b|, and the hypotenuse comes from Pythagoras.
Reflecting in the y-axis turns (x, y) into (−x, y); reflecting in the x-axis turns (x, y) into (x, −y).
A reflection is a flip, not a stretch: all side lengths and angles of the figure stay the same.

ex.q: Find the sides of the triangle A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(1, 5). Is it right-angled?
st: AB is horizontal and AC vertical, so angle A = 90°

topics.rl: Rangoli artists use mirror symmetry: a design reflected across a line keeps all its sizes.

rv.summary: Use the distance formula for the sides of a triangle on the grid. A horizontal and a vertical side meet at a right angle. Reflections change signs but not lengths.
focus: Find side lengths from vertices.
Spot the right angle using horizontal and vertical sides.
Reflect points in the axes.
remember: Same y → parallel to the x-axis; same x → parallel to the y-axis.
Reflect in the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y). In the x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y).
A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(1, 5): sides 3, 4, 5, right angle at A.
traps: Don't change the sign of the wrong coordinate.
Reflection never makes a length negative.
The right angle is where the horizontal and vertical sides meet, not always the last vertex.

topics.ch: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
topics.t: Lines parallel to axes and collinear points
topics.h: Three friends standing in a perfectly straight queue: can coordinates prove it?
p: All points on a line parallel to the y-axis share the same x-coordinate, so you can predict the next point's coordinates and quadrant from the sign pattern.
A horizontal line y = 3 passes through Quadrants II and I; a vertical line x = −4 passes through Quadrants II and III.
Three points A, B, C are collinear (on one straight line) when the longest distance equals the sum of the other two: AB + BC = AC.
If the sum is bigger than the longest distance, the points form a triangle instead.
With only positive numbers, the origin must sit at a corner and nothing can be placed to its left or below; negatives let the origin be anywhere, such as the centre.

ex.q: Are A(1, 1), B(4, 5) and C(7, 9) collinear?

topics.rl: Surveyors laying a straight water pipeline check that marker posts are collinear before digging.

rv.summary: Points on a line parallel to an axis share one coordinate. Three points are collinear when the two shorter distances add up exactly to the longest.
focus: Predict points and quadrants on lines parallel to axes.
Say which quadrants a line like y = −4 passes through.
Test collinearity with distances.
remember: Vertical line: x fixed. Horizontal line: y fixed.
Without negatives, the origin must be at a corner.
traps: A vertical line keeps x fixed, not y.
If the shorter two add to more than the longest, the points form a triangle.
Compare all three distances, not just two.

topics.ch: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
topics.t: Circles, squares and grids in action
topics.h: A game designer must know whether two circles on a screen touch. Coordinates make the call!
p: A point (x, y) is inside a circle of radius r centred at the origin if x² + y² < r², on it if x² + y² = r², and outside if x² + y² > r².
Two circles cut each other when the distance between centres is less than the sum of the radii (and more than their difference); they just touch when it equals the sum.
A circle fits inside a screen if its centre is at least r away from every edge.
Four points form a square when all four sides are equal and both diagonals are equal. Area = side².

In a city grid, each street intersection can be named by an ordered pair (street number, avenue number). An isosceles triangle can be planned by placing the apex on the perpendicular bisector of the base.

ex.q: Does A(1, 1), B(4, 2), C(3, 5), D(0, 4) form a square? Find its area.
st: All sides equal and diagonals equal: a square

topics.rl: Mobile games check collisions between round objects by comparing the distance between centres with the sum of the radii.

rv.summary: Coordinates help test points against circles, check squares, fit shapes on screens and name street corners. Compare x² + y² with r² for a circle centred at the origin.
focus: Decide if a point is inside, on or outside a circle.
Test if four points form a square and find its area.
Place an apex for an isosceles triangle.
remember: Inside: x² + y² < r²; on: = r²; outside: > r².
Two circles cut if distance between centres < sum of radii (and > difference).
Square: four equal sides and equal diagonals; area = side².
Apex on the perpendicular bisector of the base gives equal slant sides.
traps: Don't add coordinates; square them.
Area of a square is side², not diagonal².
Checking only the screen width is not enough.

topics.ch: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
topics.h: Two friends live at different corners of the city. Where should they meet so that both walk equally?
p: The midpoint of A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2): average the x's and average the y's.
To check if M is the midpoint, compute the midpoint formula and see if it gives M.
If M is the midpoint and A is one end, the other end is B = (2 × M's x − A's x, 2 × M's y − A's y).
Points of trisection divide AB into three equal parts: each step is one-third of the change in x and y, so the points are A + (1/3)(B − A) and A + (2/3)(B − A).
If the midpoints of the sides of a triangle are known, the vertices can be found by solving: each vertex equals (sum of the two midpoints next to it) minus the opposite midpoint.

ex.q: Find the points of trisection of A(1, 2) and B(7, 11).
st: Change in x = 6, change in y = 9

topics.rl: A delivery app can suggest a fair meeting point halfway between two friends' homes using the midpoint formula.

rv.summary: The midpoint of two points averages their x's and y's. Points of trisection are one-third and two-thirds of the way from A to B.
focus: Find and check midpoints.
Find the other end of a segment from a midpoint.
Find points of trisection.
remember: Other end B = (2 × M's x − A's x, 2 × M's y − A's y).
Trisection: A + (1/3)(B − A) and A + (2/3)(B − A).
traps: Add the coordinates before halving; don't subtract.
Don't stop at the first trisection point.
Check both coordinates when testing a midpoint.

topics.h: x is just a number wearing a disguise. Polynomials are what you build when you play with such letter-numbers!
p: An algebraic expression is made of terms. In 4x² − 3x + 7, the terms are 4x², −3x and 7; x is the variable (a letter-number), 4 and −3 are coefficients, and 7 is the constant.
A polynomial in one variable (univariate) uses only one letter, with whole-number powers 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
The degree of a polynomial is the highest power of its variable that appears with a non-zero coefficient.
By degree: constant (0), linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3).
A constant like 8 can be written 8x⁰ (since x⁰ = 1), so its degree is 0.

ex.q: Find the degree and the type of p(x) = 5 − 2x + x³ − 4x².

topics.rl: A shopkeeper's bill rule like 'price × quantity + delivery charge' is a polynomial in the quantity.

rv.summary: A polynomial in one variable has terms with whole-number powers of one letter. Its degree is the highest power with a non-zero coefficient: constant 0, linear 1, quadratic 2, cubic 3.
focus: Find the degree of a polynomial.
Name polynomials as constant, linear, quadratic or cubic.
Identify terms, coefficients and constants.
traps: Degree is not the number of terms.
The first written term does not decide the degree.
A constant's degree is 0, not its value.

topics.h: A polynomial is a machine: drop in a number, turn the handle, and out pops its value!
p: The coefficient of a power is the number multiplying it. In 3x² − x + 5, the coefficient of x is −1.
If a power is missing, its coefficient is 0. In x³ + 2, the coefficient of x² is 0.
The constant term is the term with no variable (the coefficient of x⁰).
To evaluate p(x) at x = k, replace every x by k, using brackets for negatives: p(−2) for x² gives (−2)² = 4.
You can write a polynomial of any degree you like: 2x² − 1 is one example of degree 2.

ex.q: If p(x) = 2x² − 3x + 1, find p(−2).

topics.rl: An electricity bill formula with a fixed meter charge plus a rate per unit is evaluated each month at a new number of units.

rv.summary: A coefficient is the number multiplying a power; a missing power has coefficient 0. To evaluate p(k), replace every x by k, using brackets for negatives.
focus: Find coefficients, including missing and hidden ones.
Find the constant term with its sign.
Evaluate polynomials at negative values.
remember: In 3x² − x + 5, the coefficient of x is −1.
In x³ + 2, the coefficient of x² is 0.
traps: Keep the sign of the constant term.
A hidden 1 (as in −x) is not 0.

topics.h: An auto fare of ₹30 plus ₹15 for every km grows by the same amount each km. That steady growth is a linear polynomial!
p: A linear polynomial in x has the form ax + b, where a and b are numbers and a ≠ 0.
Its degree is 1: the highest power of x is x¹. Terms like x², 1/x or √x are not allowed.
a is the coefficient of x and b is the constant term.
To evaluate p(x) at x = k, replace x by k: p(k) = ak + b.
Each time x goes up by 1, the value of ax + b changes by exactly a.

ex.q: A taxi charges ₹50 to start plus ₹12 per km. Write the fare for x km as a polynomial and find the fare for 8 km.

topics.rl: Electricity bills, mobile data plans and taxi fares often have a fixed charge plus a charge per unit: a linear polynomial.

rv.summary: A linear polynomial has the form ax + b with a ≠ 0 and degree 1. To evaluate it at x = k, work out ak + b.
focus: Recognise linear polynomials.
Write a linear rule from a real situation.
Evaluate a linear polynomial.
remember: ax + b: a = coefficient of x, b = constant.
Each step of 1 in x changes the value by a.
traps: x², 1/x and √x are not allowed in a linear polynomial.
Attach x to the per-unit charge, not the fixed charge.
x(x + 1) is quadratic, not linear.

topics.h: A lemonade stall makes a loss at first and a profit later. The exact moment it breaks even is a zero of a polynomial!
p: A zero of p(x) is a value of x that makes p(x) = 0.
For p(x) = ax + b with a ≠ 0, solve ax + b = 0 to get the zero x = −b/a.
A linear polynomial has exactly one zero.
On the graph, the zero is where the line crosses the x-axis: the point (−b/a, 0).
To check a zero, substitute it: the answer must come out as 0.

ex.q: Find the zero of p(x) = 3x − 12 and say where its graph meets the x-axis.
st: The line meets the x-axis at (4, 0)
ex.a: x = 4; the graph crosses the x-axis at (4, 0)

topics.rl: Shopkeepers find the break-even number of items, where profit is exactly zero, by finding the zero of a profit polynomial.

rv.summary: A zero of p(x) makes p(x) = 0. A linear polynomial ax + b has exactly one zero, x = −b/a, where its graph crosses the x-axis.
focus: Find the zero of a linear polynomial.
Check a zero by substitution.
Link the zero to the x-axis crossing.
remember: A linear polynomial has exactly one zero.
traps: The constant term is not the zero.
The y-intercept is not the x-axis crossing.
Keep the sign when moving terms across.

topics.t: Solving word problems with linear equations
topics.h: Every puzzle that says 'think of a number' is secretly a linear equation waiting to be solved!
p: Set a linear polynomial equal to a value to get a linear equation, then solve for the unknown.
Steps: name the unknown, translate the words into an equation, solve, and check the answer in the story.
Ages: if Ravi is x now, in 5 years he is x + 5; numbers in a ratio 3 : 5 can be written 3k and 5k.
Coins: if there are x coins of ₹5, they are worth 5x rupees. Rectangle: perimeter = 2(l + b).
A two-digit number with tens digit x and units digit y is 10x + y; swapping the digits gives 10y + x, and the difference is 9(x − y).

ex.q: A rectangular garden has perimeter 46 m and its length is 5 m more than its breadth. Find its dimensions.

topics.rl: Splitting a restaurant bill or planning how many ₹10 and ₹20 notes make ₹500 are everyday linear-equation problems.

rv.summary: Turn a word problem into a linear equation: name the unknown, translate, solve and check in the story.
focus: Solve age, ratio, coin and perimeter problems.
Write two-digit numbers algebraically.
Check answers in the original story.
remember: Perimeter = 2(l + b): 46 m, l = b + 5 gives 14 m by 9 m.
Two-digit number = 10x + y; swapped minus original differ by 9(x − y).
traps: Add years to every person's age.
After finding k, multiply back to get the numbers.
Answer the question asked: length or breadth.

topics.h: Matchsticks, tiles, rickshaw fares: if each step adds the same amount, one short rule predicts them all!
p: In a linear pattern each stage adds the same amount. Tiles 1, 3, 5, 7, ... add 2 each time, so stage n has 2n − 1 tiles.
General rule: if stage 1 has f and each stage adds d, stage n has f + (n − 1)d.
Use the rule forwards (find stage 50) or backwards (which stage has 99 tiles?). If the stage number is not a whole number, that count is impossible.
Real life: an auto fare of ₹30 plus ₹15 per km, pocket money left after spending ₹20 a day, or savings that grow ₹500 a month.
In a row of hexagons made of matchsticks, the first needs 6 and each new one needs 5 more, so n hexagons need 5n + 1 sticks. Area also grows linearly when only one side grows in equal steps.

ex.q: Tiles: stage 1 has 4, stage 2 has 7, stage 3 has 10. Find the rule and the stage with 61 tiles.

topics.rl: Stacked chairs in a school hall: each extra chair adds the same height, so the stack height follows a linear rule.

rv.summary: In a linear pattern each stage adds the same amount d. Stage n has f + (n − 1)d. Use the rule forwards or backwards.
focus: Find the rule for a growing pattern.
Find a stage from a count, or show it is impossible.
Model fares, savings and matchstick patterns.
traps: Don't forget to subtract 1 from n.
Shared sides mean 5 new sticks per hexagon, not 6.
A non-whole stage number means that count is impossible.

topics.h: A plant grows 2 cm a week, a phone loses ₹1500 of value a year: both change by the same amount each step!
p: Linear growth: a quantity increases by a fixed amount in each equal time interval.
Linear decay: a quantity decreases by a fixed amount in each equal time interval.
Make a table of values, spot the fixed change, and write the rule as start + change × time, e.g. cost C(d) = 100 + 60d.
For decay the change is negative: a tank with 3 m of water draining 0.5 m per hour has h(t) = 3 − 0.5t.
Examples: plant height, a town gaining the same number of people every year, a phone's value dropping by a fixed amount, prepaid balance running out.

ex.q: A tank holds water 3 m deep and loses 0.5 m every hour. Write h(t) and find when it is empty.

topics.rl: A metro card that loses ₹40 per daily trip shows linear decay: you can predict the day it needs a recharge.

rv.summary: Linear growth adds a fixed amount each equal time step; linear decay subtracts a fixed amount. The rule is start + change × time.
focus: Spot linear growth or decay in a table.
Write the rule and use it.
Find when a decaying quantity reaches zero.
traps: For decay the change is negative.
Don't forget the starting value.
Linear growth is not doubling.

topics.t: Finding a linear rule from two points
topics.h: Two bills from a tiffin service are enough to crack its secret pricing rule!
p: A linear relationship between x and y has the form y = ax + b.
Given two pairs (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), substitute each to get two equations; subtracting them gives a, and then b.
Meaning: a is the rate per unit (₹ per km, cm per week); b is the fixed amount when x = 0 (a fixed charge or a starting value).
Axis intercepts: the line meets the y-axis at (0, b) and the x-axis where y = 0, at x = −b/a.

ex.q: A tiffin service charges ₹520 for 6 meals and ₹820 for 11 meals. Find the rule.

topics.rl: Water bills, taxi fares and gym fees often hide a fixed charge plus a rate. Two bills reveal both.

rv.summary: A linear rule y = ax + b can be found from two pairs: subtract the equations to get a, then find b. a is the rate and b the fixed amount.
focus: Find a and b from two data points.
Explain what a and b mean in context.
Find axis intercepts.
remember: a = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); then b = y₁ − ax₁.
traps: Don't divide one total by its quantity: that mixes in the fixed charge.
Don't confuse the rate with the fixed charge.
Don't swap the two intercepts.

topics.h: Water freezes at 0 °C and at 32 °F. Two fixed points are all you need to link the scales!
p: Celsius and Fahrenheit are linearly related. Using freezing (0 °C, 32 °F) and boiling (100 °C, 212 °F): F = (9/5)C + 32.
So 100 Celsius degrees cover 180 Fahrenheit degrees: each 1 °C step is 1.8 °F.
Kelvin starts at absolute zero: K = C + 273.15, so F = (9/5)(K − 273.15) + 32.
Work done by a constant force: W = F × d (joules = newtons × metres). For a fixed force, W is a linear function of d whose graph is a straight line through the origin.

ex.q: Convert 35 °C to Fahrenheit.

topics.rl: Weather apps switch between °C and °F using exactly this linear rule, and a fever of 100.4 °F is 38 °C.

rv.summary: Temperature scales are linearly related: F = (9/5)C + 32 and K = C + 273.15. Work by a constant force, W = F × d, is linear in d through the origin.
focus: Convert between Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin.
Find work done by a constant force.
Describe the W–d graph.
remember: W = F × d (joules); 40 N × 25 m = 1000 J.
traps: Don't forget to add 32.
When going F → C, subtract 32 then multiply by 5/9.
The force is the slope of W = Fd, not the intercept.

topics.h: Put a linear polynomial on a graph and something magical happens: every point falls in one perfectly straight line!
p: To graph y = ax + b, make a table: choose some x-values, work out y, plot the points (x, y) and join them.
The graph of a linear polynomial is always a straight line. Two points are enough to draw it; a third point is a good check.
b is where the line cuts the y-axis: the point (0, b).
a is the slope: when x increases by 1, y changes by a. If a > 0 the line rises; if a < 0 it falls.
Lines with the same a (same slope) are parallel.

ex.q: Draw the graph of y = 2x + 1 using x = 0, 1, 2.
st: Plot and join: a rising straight line cutting the y-axis at (0, 1); y goes up by 2 for each step of 1 in x

topics.rl: A plot of distance against time for a train moving at steady speed is a straight line; the steeper the line, the faster the train.

rv.summary: The graph of y = ax + b is a straight line. It cuts the y-axis at (0, b) and its slope is a: it rises if a > 0 and falls if a < 0.
focus: Draw a linear graph from a table.
Read the y-intercept and slope.
Decide if a line rises or falls.
remember: Two points fix a line; a third is a check.
traps: The y-intercept is (0, b), not (b, 0).
Rising or falling depends on a, not on the constant.
Slope = rise ÷ run, not just the rise.

topics.t: Slope: how steep and which way
topics.h: Two roads climb a hill. One rises 1 m in every 10 m, the other 1 m in every 4 m. Slope tells you which one makes your cycle legs ache!
p: Slope from two points: a = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), rise over run.
When b = 0 the line y = ax passes through the origin (0, 0).
A positive slope rises from left to right (growth); a negative slope falls (decay); slope 0 is a horizontal line.
The bigger |a| is, the steeper the line: y = 5x is steeper than y = 2x, and y = −4x is steeper than y = −x.

ex.q: Find the slope of the line through (−1, 7) and (3, −1). Does it rise or fall?

topics.rl: Railway engineers keep tracks at gentle slopes; a ghat road sign showing a steep gradient warns trucks to use low gear.

rv.summary: Slope is rise over run: (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Positive slopes rise, negative slopes fall, slope 0 is horizontal; larger |a| means steeper.
focus: Find slope from two points.
Compare steepness using |a|.
Link rising and falling lines to growth and decay.
remember: y = ax passes through the origin.
traps: Don't divide run by rise.
Keep the minus signs.
A horizontal line has slope 0, not 'no slope'.

topics.h: Change one number in y = ax + b and watch a whole family of lines spin or slide!
p: Lines with the same slope a are parallel: y = 2x, y = 2x + 3 and y = 2x − 4 never meet.
Changing b with a fixed slides the line up (b bigger) or down (b smaller) without turning it.
Changing a with b fixed turns the line about the point (0, b): all of y = ax + 3 pass through (0, 3).
In the family f(x) = ax + a = a(x + 1), every line passes through (−1, 0), because f(−1) = 0 for any a. The slope and the y-intercept are both a.

ex.q: Show that y = 4x + 4 and y = −2x − 2 both pass through (−1, 0).
st: Both are of the form ax + a

topics.rl: A graph of several mobile plans with the same per-GB rate but different fixed fees shows parallel lines: the cheapest is the lowest one.

rv.summary: Lines with the same slope are parallel. Changing b slides a line up or down; changing a turns it about (0, b). Every line y = ax + a passes through (−1, 0).
focus: Spot parallel lines.
Shift a line up or down.
Find the common point of a family of lines.
remember: f(x) = ax + a = a(x + 1): f(−1) = 0; slope and y-intercept both equal a.
traps: Parallel means equal slope, not equal intercept.
Shifting changes b, not a.
Distinct parallel lines meet at 0 points.

topics.h: A herder with no number words could still check that every cow came home: one pebble per cow!
p: Counting began with one-to-one matching: one pebble, knot or notch for each object. This leads to the natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, ...}.
Ancient tally marks survive on bones: the Lebombo bone from southern Africa has notches, and one column of the Ishango bone from central Africa shows 11, 13, 17 and 19, the primes between 10 and 20.

In the Indus Valley, traders used standard cube-shaped weights in a doubling pattern (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...); Vedic texts gave names to large powers of 10, such as shata (100), sahasra (1000), ayuta (10,000) and parardha (10¹²).
N is not closed under subtraction: 3 − 5 is not a natural number. This need pushed people towards zero and negative numbers.
Not every system uses base 10. Counting the 12 finger joints of one hand with the thumb leads to base 12, which is why we still buy bananas by the dozen.

ex.q: Using thumb-on-joints counting (12 per hand), how would you count 30 mangoes in dozens?

topics.rl: Shopkeepers still sell eggs and bananas by the dozen, a trace of base-12 counting.

rv.summary: Counting began with one-to-one matching, giving the natural numbers. Tally bones, Indus doubling weights and Vedic names for powers of 10 show its history; N is not closed under subtraction.
focus: Explain one-to-one matching.
Know key historical counting records.
Show why N is not closed under subtraction.
remember: Ishango bone: 11, 13, 17, 19, the primes between 10 and 20.
Indus weights double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...; 12 finger joints give the dozen.
traps: Base 12 comes from finger joints, not 12 fingers.
Don't mix up the order of the Vedic names.
Indus weights double; they don't go up by a fixed amount.

topics.t: Shunya: when nothing became a number
topics.h: Is 'nothing' a number? Indian thinkers said yes, and maths was never the same again!
p: Zero has two jobs: a placeholder (the 0 in 105 shows there are no tens) and a number in its own right that can be added, subtracted and multiplied.
The idea of shunyata, emptiness, in Indian philosophy made it natural to think of 'nothing' as something real.
The Bakhshali manuscript, an ancient Indian text, uses a dot (bindu) to mark zero.
Brahmagupta stated rules for zero: a − a = 0, a + 0 = a, a − 0 = a and a × 0 = 0.

ex.q: Use Brahmagupta's rules: simplify (17 − 17) + 9 × 0 + (25 − 0).

topics.rl: The 0 on a lift panel for the ground floor and the 0 in your PIN code are both zeros, one as a level and one as a digit placeholder.

rv.summary: Zero works as a placeholder and as a number. Indian thought on shunyata, the Bakhshali dot and Brahmagupta's rules made zero a full number.
focus: Tell placeholder zero from zero as a number.
Use Brahmagupta's rules for zero.
Know the history of zero in India.
remember: Bakhshali manuscript: a dot (bindu) for zero.
traps: Multiplying by 0 gives 0, not the number itself.
Subtracting 0 does not change the sign.
Not every 0 in a numeral is just a placeholder.

topics.h: Brahmagupta thought of numbers as fortunes and debts. A debt of ₹50 is just −50!
p: Integers Z = {..., −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...} include negatives, zero and positives. On the number line negatives are to the left of 0.
Brahmagupta called positives dhana (fortune) and negatives rina (debt).
Adding: two fortunes make a bigger fortune; two debts make a bigger debt; a fortune and a debt partly cancel (subtract and keep the sign of the larger).
Multiplying or dividing: same signs give a positive answer; different signs give a negative answer.
topics.rl: A bank passbook shows deposits as positive and withdrawals as negative; the balance is their integer sum.

rv.summary: Integers include negatives, zero and positives. Brahmagupta called positives dhana (fortune) and negatives rina (debt) and gave rules for adding and multiplying them.
focus: Add integers with the same and different signs.
Multiply and divide integers using sign rules.
Order integers on the number line.
remember: Same signs → positive product; different signs → negative.
traps: −5 is less than −3, not greater.
Two negatives added give a bigger negative, not a positive.
'Strictly between' excludes the end points.

topics.h: Taking away a debt makes you richer. That one idea explains why minus a minus is plus!
p: Subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive: removing a debt of ₹30 leaves you ₹30 better off, so a − (−30) = a + 30.
Negative × negative is positive: −3 × (−4) means removing 3 debts of ₹4 each, which gains ₹12. The pattern −3 × 2 = −6, −3 × 1 = −3, −3 × 0 = 0, −3 × (−1) = 3 also shows it.
Temperatures, loans and profits give integer expressions: 4 °C falling by 9 °C is 4 − 9 = −5 °C.
Sign reasoning: if ab > 0 then a and b have the same sign; if ab < 0, opposite signs. A square is never negative.
Since squares are never negative, x² + y² + z² = 0 forces x = y = z = 0. With (x + y + z)² = x² + y² + z² + 2(xy + yz + zx), if x + y + z = 0 and xy + yz + zx = 0, then x² + y² + z² = 0.

ex.q: At 6 a.m. Leh is at −7 °C. By noon it is 12 °C warmer, then by night it drops 9 °C. What is the night temperature?

topics.rl: Shopkeepers' profit-loss books track gains (+) and losses (−) daily; the total tells whether the week was good.

rv.summary: Subtracting a negative adds; negative times negative is positive, as patterns and debts show. Since squares are never negative, x² + y² + z² = 0 forces all to be 0.
focus: Explain the sign rules with patterns and money.
Solve temperature, depth and profit problems.
Reason about signs of products and squares.
remember: ab > 0: same signs; ab < 0: opposite signs.
traps: A positive product does not need a positive factor.
Don't think squares can cancel out: a square is never negative, so x² + y² + z² = 0 only when x = y = z = 0.

topics.h: Some numbers can be written as a neat fraction. Others, like √2, refuse to be caught by any fraction at all, no matter how hard you try!
p: A rational number can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Examples: 3 = 3/1, −0.5 = −1/2, 0 = 0/1.
Every natural number, whole number and integer is also a rational number.
An irrational number cannot be written as p/q. Examples: √2, √3, √5 and π.
If n is a natural number that is not a perfect square, then √n is irrational. But √16 = 4 is rational.
Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many more rational numbers; their average is always one of them.

ex.q: Find three rational numbers between 1/3 and 1/2.
st: Multiply top and bottom by 2 to make room: 8/24 and 12/24

topics.rl: The diagonal of a square tile of side 1 m is √2 m long. A carpenter can measure it closely, but never as an exact fraction!

rv.summary: A rational number can be written as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0; an irrational number cannot. √n is irrational when n is not a perfect square.
focus: Classify numbers as rational or irrational.
Find rational numbers between two rationals.
Know that rational + irrational is irrational.
traps: Not every number with a root sign is irrational.
A calculator display of √2 is only approximate.
Adding a whole number to an irrational does not make it rational.

topics.h: ½, 2/4 and 50/100 look different, but they are the same slice of pizza!
p: Equivalent fractions name the same rational number: 2/3 = 4/6 = 10/15. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same non-zero number.
Lowest form: divide by the HCF so that p and q are co-prime (no common factor except 1). 18/24 = 3/4.
Add or subtract using a common denominator; multiply tops and bottoms; to divide, multiply by the reciprocal: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c).
Distributive property: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c and a × (b − c) = a × b − a × c also hold for rationals and can make calculations shorter.
topics.rl: Recipes for 4 people scaled to 6 need fraction multiplication: ¾ cup × 6/4 = 9/8 cups.

rv.summary: Equivalent fractions name the same rational number; reduce by the HCF to get lowest form. Add with common denominators, multiply across, divide by multiplying by the reciprocal.
focus: Write equivalent fractions and lowest forms.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide rationals.
Use the distributive property to simplify.
traps: Change top and bottom by the same number.
Don't subtract tops and bottoms separately.
Different-looking fractions can be the same number.

topics.t: Rationals on the number line and absolute value
topics.h: How far is −3 from 0? Exactly as far as 3. Distance never goes negative!
p: To show p/q on the number line, divide each unit into q equal parts and count p parts from 0 (right for positive, left for negative). 7/4 = 1¾: go to 1, then 3 of the 4 parts.
The absolute value |a| is the distance of a from 0: |−5| = 5 and |5| = 5.
The distance between a and b on the line is |a − b|, e.g. between −2 and 3/2 it is |−2 − 3/2| = 7/2.
For a < b, the average (a + b)/2 lies between them: (a + b)/2 − a = (b − a)/2 > 0 and b − (a + b)/2 = (b − a)/2 > 0. It is exactly halfway.

ex.q: Show that (a + b)/2 is between 1/3 and 1/2, and find it.

topics.rl: The lift display at a mall shows −2 for the second basement; how many floors to go up to floor 3 is |3 − (−2)| = 5.

rv.summary: To show p/q on the line, split each unit into q parts and count p. |a| is distance from 0, and the distance between a and b is |a − b|. The average lies exactly halfway.
focus: Mark rationals on the number line.
Find absolute values and distances.
Show the average lies between two numbers.
traps: Divide each unit by the denominator, not the numerator.
Absolute value is never negative.
Subtracting a negative means adding.

topics.h: Between 1/2 and 3/4 there's always another fraction, and between those another... forever!
p: The rational numbers are dense: between any two rationals there are infinitely many more.
Method 1, averages: (a + b)/2 is between a and b; repeat with the new pairs.
Method 2, common denominators: write both with a bigger common denominator, e.g. 3/5 = 30/50 and 4/5 = 40/50, then 31/50, 32/50, ..., 39/50 are between them.
Method 3, extra decimal places: between 0.3 and 0.4 lie 0.31, 0.32, ..., and between 0.31 and 0.32 lie 0.311, 0.312, ...
To find exactly n rationals between two numbers, scale up the denominators until there are at least n numerators in between.

ex.q: Find five rational numbers between 2/3 and 3/4.

topics.rl: Petrol prices like ₹102.345 per litre and ₹102.346 per litre show there is always a finer value in between.

rv.summary: Rational numbers are dense: between any two there are infinitely many more. Use averages, bigger common denominators or extra decimal places to find them.
focus: Find a given number of rationals between two rationals.
Use the average method.
Use decimals to find rationals between.
traps: There is no 'next' rational as there is for integers.
Don't add tops and bottoms to find a fraction between.
Don't include the end points.

topics.h: Mummy has 13½ metres of cloth. How many kurtas of 2¼ metres can the tailor cut?
p: Turn mixed numbers into improper fractions first: 2¼ = 9/4 and 13½ = 27/2.
'How many pieces of size b fit in a?' means a ÷ b. Any leftover is a − (number of pieces × b).
To solve an equation with fractions, multiply both sides by the LCM of the denominators to clear them, then solve as usual.
Always check by putting the answer back into the original equation or story.

ex.q: How many kurtas need 2¼ m each from 13½ m of cloth?

topics.rl: Dividing a 2½ kg box of sweets into ¼ kg packets for Diwali gifts is exactly this kind of problem.

rv.summary: For fraction problems, change mixed numbers to improper fractions, divide to find how many pieces fit, and clear fractions in equations by multiplying by the LCM.
focus: Solve 'how many pieces' problems by division.
Find leftovers.
Solve equations with fractions.
traps: Divide by the piece size; don't multiply.
Multiply every term by the LCM, on both sides.
Scale a recipe by the ratio, don't just add.

topics.h: The diagonal of a 1 m square tile cannot be written as any fraction at all. Here's the proof!
p: The diagonal of a unit square has length √2 (by Pythagoras, 1² + 1² = 2). No fraction p/q has square exactly 2.
Proof by contradiction (linked to Hippasus): suppose √2 = p/q in lowest form. Then p² = 2q², so p² is even, so p is even: p = 2k.
Then 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k², so q is even too. Both even contradicts 'lowest form', so √2 is irrational.
The same idea works for √3, √5 and √p for any prime p: if p divides a², then p divides a.
For √5: assume √5 = a/b in lowest terms; a² = 5b², so 5 divides a; write a = 5c; then 25c² = 5b², b² = 5c², so 5 divides b. Contradiction.

ex.q: In the proof that √3 is irrational, why does a² = 3b² mean 3 divides a?
st: If a prime divides a square, it divides the number itself
ex.a: Because 3 is prime, 3 | a² gives 3 | a

topics.rl: Tile-setters cutting a square tile diagonally use √2 ≈ 1.414 times the side, knowing the exact value never ends.

rv.summary: √2 is irrational: assuming √2 = p/q in lowest form forces p and q to both be even, a contradiction. The same proof works for √p when p is prime.
focus: Write the proof that √2 is irrational.
Adapt it for √3 or √5.
Know why it fails for perfect squares.
remember: p² = 2q² → p even → p = 2k → q² = 2k² → q even: contradiction.
Key fact: if a prime p divides a², then p divides a.
traps: Conclude about p before q.
(2k)² = 4k², not 2k².
The proof does not apply to √9 = 3.

topics.h: √2 is not a fraction, yet you can mark it exactly on a number line with just a ruler and a compass. Here is the trick!
p: Rational and irrational numbers together make up the real numbers.
Every real number is a point on the number line, and every point on the line is a real number. The line has no gaps.
To mark √2: draw a right triangle on the line with legs 1 and 1. Its hypotenuse is √(1 + 1) = √2; swing an arc from 0 with that length.
In the same way, legs 2 and 1 give √5, and legs √2 and 1 give √3.
To compare roots, compare squares: √10 < 3.2 because 10 < 3.2² = 10.24.

ex.q: Show how to mark √5 on the number line.
st: Mark O at 0 and A at 2 on the number line
At A, draw AB = 1 unit perpendicular to the line
With centre O and radius OB, draw an arc to cut the line at P. Then OP = √5 ≈ 2.24
ex.a: P is the point √5, a little to the right of 2.2

topics.rl: A ruler with marks only at whole and half centimetres still contains the point √2 cm: every length you can draw is a real number.

rv.summary: Rationals and irrationals together form the real numbers, which fill the number line with no gaps. √2, √3 and √5 can be marked using right triangles.
focus: Mark √2, √3 and √5 on the number line.
Compare roots by comparing squares.
Know that every point is a real number.
remember: Legs 1 and 1 → √2; legs 2 and 1 → √5; legs √2 and 1 → √3.
traps: Legs 1 and 2 give √5, not √2.
A number does not need a finite decimal to have a place on the line.

topics.t: The square-root spiral, π and the journey of numbers
topics.h: A spiral of right triangles draws √2, √3, √4, √5 ... one after another like a snail shell!
p: Square-root spiral: start with a right triangle with legs 1 and 1 (hypotenuse √2). On that hypotenuse put a new leg of 1 at right angles: the new hypotenuse is √3, then √4 = 2, √5, and so on.
π, the ratio of circumference to diameter, is irrational. Aryabhata gave the approximation 62832/20000 = 3927/1250 = 3.1416.
Madhava of Sangamagrama found the infinite series π = 4(1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + ...).
Number systems grew by need: N (counting) → Z (debts, zero) → Q (sharing) → irrationals (lengths like √2) → R (the whole number line).
A teaser: no real number squared is negative, so mathematicians later invented i = √(−1), the start of complex numbers.

ex.q: In the square-root spiral, what is the hypotenuse of the 7th triangle?

topics.rl: Space agencies use π to many decimal places for orbits, but Aryabhata's 3.1416 is already accurate to 4 decimal places.

rv.summary: The square-root spiral builds √2, √3, √4, ... by adding legs of 1. π is irrational; Aryabhata gave 3.1416 and Madhava an infinite series. Number systems grew by need, from N to R.
focus: Find hypotenuses in the square-root spiral.
Know Aryabhata's and Madhava's work on π.
Trace N → Z → Q → R and why i is not real.
remember: No real number squared is negative, so i = √(−1) is not real.
traps: 22/7 is not the exact value of π.
Madhava's series uses odd denominators, not all whole numbers.

topics.h: Divide 1 by 8 and the division stops. Divide 1 by 7 and the digits 142857 go round and round forever. Why?
p: The decimal expansion of a rational number either terminates (ends), like 3/8 = 0.375, or is non-terminating and recurring (repeats), like 1/3 = 0.333...
A fraction in lowest terms terminates only if its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. So 7/20 terminates, but 5/12 repeats.
An irrational number has a decimal expansion that is non-terminating and non-recurring: it never ends and never settles into a repeating block.
A repeating decimal can be turned back into p/q. For 0.777..., let x = 0.777...; then 10x = 7.777..., so 9x = 7 and x = 7/9.
The repeating block is shown with a bar on top, for example 0.27 with a bar on 27 means 0.272727...

ex.q: Write 0.474747... (47 repeating) in the form p/q.
st: Two digits repeat, so multiply by 100: 100x = 47.474747...

topics.rl: When ₹100 is shared equally among 3 friends, each share is ₹33.333..., so in real life we round it to ₹33.33.

rv.summary: A rational number's decimal either terminates or repeats; an irrational's never ends and never repeats. A fraction in lowest form terminates only if its denominator has only 2s and 5s.
focus: Decide if a fraction terminates or repeats.
Convert repeating decimals to p/q.
Identify irrational decimals.
traps: An even denominator does not guarantee termination: 5/12 repeats.
A decimal that goes on forever but repeats is rational.
Use 99 when two digits repeat, not 90.

topics.t: Decimals to fractions and cyclic numbers
topics.h: 1/7 hides a magic number: 142857. Multiply it by 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 and the same digits just rotate!
p: If p/q in lowest form has q = 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ, the decimal ends after the larger of m and n places: 7/40 = 7/(2³ × 5) has 3 places (0.175).
Terminating decimal to fraction: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8.
Repeating decimal: if x = 0.4545..., 100x = 45.4545..., so 99x = 45 and x = 5/11. For a mixed repeating decimal like 0.1666..., use 10x = 1.666... and 100x = 16.666...; then 90x = 15, x = 1/6.
0.999... = 1: if x = 0.999..., then 10x = 9.999..., so 9x = 9 and x = 1. Some numbers have two decimal forms.
1/7 = 0.142857..., and 2/7, 3/7, ..., 6/7 use the same six digits rotated (2/7 = 0.285714...). The fractions k/13 split into two such rotating families: 076923 and 153846.

ex.q: Write 0.2333... (3 repeating) as a fraction.

topics.rl: Bank interest rates like 7.5% per year are terminating decimals because their denominators are made of 2s and 5s.

rv.summary: If q = 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ, p/q ends after the larger of m and n places. Repeating decimals convert to fractions by multiplying and subtracting; 0.999... = 1; sevenths and thirteenths form cyclic families.
focus: Convert terminating and repeating decimals to fractions.
Handle mixed repeating decimals.
Use cyclic patterns of 1/7 and 1/13.
traps: 0.999... is not less than 1.
A mixed repeating decimal needs 10x and 100x, not just 100x.
Not every k/13 uses the same six digits.

topics.h: 4² − 3² = 7, 5² − 4² = 9, 6² − 5² = 11... odd numbers keep popping out. Why? Draw squares and see!
p: Number patterns hint at identities: (n + 1)² − n² is always 2n + 1, the odd number n + (n + 1).
(a + b)²: a square of side a + b splits into an a × a square, a b × b square and two a × b rectangles, so it equals a² + 2ab + b².
(a − b)²: from the a × a square cut off two a × b strips (they overlap in a b × b square, which gets removed twice), so add b² back: a² − 2ab + b².
(a + b)(a − b): cut a b × b square from an a × a square and rearrange the L-shape into an (a + b) × (a − b) rectangle, so it equals a² − b².
(x + a)(x + b): a rectangle of sides x + a and x + b splits into x², ax, bx and ab, so it equals x² + (a + b)x + ab.

ex.q: A square of side (x + 3) is split into pieces. List their areas and the total.

topics.rl: Tilers covering a square floor with a border find the tile count using exactly these area splits.

rv.summary: Area models show why identities work: a square of side a + b splits into a², b² and two ab rectangles, and cutting and rearranging shapes gives (a − b)² and a² − b².
focus: Explain each identity with an area picture.
Use area models to expand expressions.
Spot identities from number patterns.
traps: Don't forget the two ab rectangles.
In (a − b)², the b² square is removed twice, so add it back.
Consecutive squares differ by 2n + 1, not 1.

topics.h: Can you find 103 × 103 in your head in five seconds? With the right identity, you can!
p: An identity is an equality that is true for every value of the variables, unlike an equation such as x + 2 = 5, which is true for only one value.
(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Picture a square of side a + b split into an a × a square, a b × b square and two a × b rectangles.
(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
(x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab.

ex.q: Find 103² without long multiplication.
st: 103 = 100 + 3, so use (a + b)² with a = 100, b = 3

topics.rl: Shopkeepers who multiply mentally often use these tricks: 49 × 51 = 50² − 1² = 2499.

rv.summary: An identity is true for every value of its variables. The key ones are (a ± b)², (a + b)(a − b) and (x + a)(x + b); they also speed up arithmetic.
focus: Expand using the standard identities.
Use identities for quick calculations.
Tell an identity from an equation.
remember: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
traps: (a + b)² is not a² + b²: don't drop 2ab.
Double the middle term.
An equation true for one value is not an identity.

topics.h: Expanding is like opening a gift box; factorising is packing it back. Identities show you how the box was folded!
p: To factorise means to write an expression as a product of simpler expressions.
Always take out a common factor first: 3x² − 75 = 3(x² − 25).
Look for patterns: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b); a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)²; a² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)².
For x² + px + q, find two numbers with sum p and product q: x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4).
a³ + b³ and a³ − b³ have their own factor forms. Always check by expanding your answer.

ex.q: Factorise 4x² − 12x + 9.
st: Middle term: 2 × 2x × 3 = 12x, with a minus sign
So it matches a² − 2ab + b² with a = 2x, b = 3

topics.rl: If a rectangular rangoli has area x² + 9x + 20, factorising tells you possible side lengths: (x + 4) and (x + 5).

rv.summary: To factorise, write an expression as a product. Take out common factors first, then use identity patterns or find two numbers with the right sum and product.
focus: Factorise using a² − b², (a ± b)² and cube patterns.
Factorise x² + px + q.
Check by expanding.
traps: Don't stop after taking out the common factor.
A difference of squares is not a perfect square.
a³ − b³ has + ab in the second bracket; a³ + b³ has − ab.

topics.t: Fraction squares, three-term squares and reciprocals
topics.h: x + 1/x = 3? Then x² + 1/x² is exactly 7, and you never need to know x!
p: Perfect squares can have fractional coefficients: x² + x + 1/4 = (x + 1/2)² because 2 × x × 1/2 = x.
A six-term expression may be a three-term square: x² + 4y² + 9z² + 4xy + 12yz + 6zx = (x + 2y + 3z)². Find the square roots of the squared terms and check the cross terms.
(x + 1/x)² = x² + 2 + 1/x², so x² + 1/x² = (x + 1/x)² − 2. Similarly x² + 1/x² = (x − 1/x)² + 2.
'A number plus its reciprocal is k' gives x + 1/x = k, which becomes the quadratic x² − kx + 1 = 0 after multiplying by x.

ex.q: A number plus its reciprocal is 10/3. Find the number.

topics.rl: Engineers simplify formulas with fractions by spotting perfect squares, just as you will here.

rv.summary: Perfect squares can have fractions or three terms. (x + 1/x)² = x² + 2 + 1/x² gives x² + 1/x² from x + 1/x.
focus: Factorise squares with fractional coefficients.
Recognise three-term squares.
Use x + 1/x and x − 1/x to find x² + 1/x².
traps: Use square roots of the squared terms, not the coefficients.
Subtract 2 for x + 1/x; add 2 for x − 1/x.
Square the coefficient too: (2b)² = 4b².

topics.h: 11³ = 1331 and 101³ = 1030301. Patterns like these come straight from the cube identities!
p: (a + b)³ = a³ + b³ + 3ab(a + b) = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³.
(a − b)³ = a³ − b³ − 3ab(a − b) = a³ − 3a²b + 3ab² − b³.
a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) and a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).
(a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca.
a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca). So if a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.

ex.q: Find 11³ using (a + b)³.

topics.rl: Volumes of cube-shaped boxes grow as a cube. If each side of a 10 cm box grows by 1 cm, (a + b)³ shows exactly how much extra space you get.

rv.summary: Cube identities: (a ± b)³, a³ ± b³ and a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc. If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.
focus: Expand (a + b)³ and (a − b)³.
Factorise sums and differences of cubes.
Use the a + b + c = 0 shortcut.
traps: x³ + y³ is not (x + y)³.
Use 3ab(a + b), not just 3ab.
Double every cross term in (a + b + c)².

topics.t: More cube identities and testing identities
topics.h: Is (a + b)³ the same as a³ + b³? Try a = b = 1: 8 versus 2. One test is enough to bust a fake identity!
p: Sum of cubes: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²).
x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − yz − zx).
To use it with only x + y + z and xy + yz + zx known, first find x² + y² + z² = (x + y + z)² − 2(xy + yz + zx).
Verify an identity by multiplying out the right side and checking it equals the left side.
To test a claimed identity, try simple values. If even one value fails, it is NOT an identity; passing a few tests suggests (but does not prove) it is one.

ex.q: If a + b + c = 15 and ab + bc + ca = 74, find a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc.

topics.rl: Software testers do the same as you: one failing case proves a program (or an identity) is wrong.

rv.summary: x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz factorises with (x + y + z). Verify identities by expanding; test claims with values, since one failure disproves an identity.
focus: Use the three-cube identity with given sums.
Verify identities by expanding.
Disprove false identities with a counter-example.
remember: x² + y² + z² = (x + y + z)² − 2(xy + yz + zx).
One failing value shows it is not an identity.
traps: One successful test does not prove an identity.
x = 0 can hide an error; try other values.
Double the pairwise sum when finding x² + y² + z².

topics.h: Factorising can be done with your hands: arrange tiles into a perfect rectangle and read off the sides!
p: Algebra tiles: a big square of side x has area x², a long strip x by 1 has area x, and a small unit square has area 1.
To factor x² + 7x + 12, take 1 big square, 7 strips and 12 unit squares, and arrange them into a rectangle.
The rectangle's sides are the factors: x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4). The units form a 3 × 4 block and the strips split 3 and 4.
A path around a square ground of side x and width w covers (x + 2w)² − x² = 4wx + 4w²; tiles show the four strips and four corner squares.

ex.q: Factor x² + 5x + 6 with tiles.
st: Units arranged 2 × 3; strips 2 on one side, 3 on the other

topics.rl: A gardener laying a paved border around a square lawn can count the paving stones the same way.

rv.summary: Algebra tiles (x², x and 1) can be arranged into a rectangle whose sides are the factors of a quadratic.
focus: Match tiles to the terms of a quadratic.
Factorise by arranging tiles into rectangles.
Find path areas with tiles.
remember: Big square = x², strip = x, unit square = 1.
Path of width w around side x: (x + 2w)² − x² = 4wx + 4w².
traps: The number of strips is not a side length.
Not every set of tiles makes a rectangle.
Add the path width on both sides.

topics.h: 6x² + 7x − 3 looks scary, but find two numbers that multiply to −18 and add to 7, and it falls apart!
p: For ax² + bx + c, find two numbers with product a × c and sum b. Split bx using them, then group in pairs.
Example: 6x² + 7x − 3; a × c = −18, the numbers are 9 and −2: 6x² + 9x − 2x − 3 = 3x(2x + 3) − 1(2x + 3) = (3x − 1)(2x + 3).
For x² + px + q (a = 1) just find two numbers with product q and sum p: r² − r − 42 = (r − 7)(r + 6).
If (x − k) is a factor of a polynomial, then putting x = k makes it zero; this links its coefficients.
n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1), a product of three consecutive integers, so it is always divisible by 2 and by 3, hence by 6.

ex.q: Factorise 2x² + 7x + 3.
st: a × c = 6; numbers 6 and 1 add to 7

topics.rl: Splitting things smartly into pairs is how quiz teams split prize money and how this method splits the middle term.

rv.summary: To factorise ax² + bx + c, find two numbers with product ac and sum b, split the middle term, then group.
focus: Split the middle term for a ≠ 1.
Factorise x² + px + q quickly.
Explain why n³ − n is divisible by 6.
traps: Use the product a × c, not just c.
Watch the signs of the two numbers.
Checking one example is not a proof.

topics.h: Just as 12/18 cancels to 2/3, (x² − 9)/(x + 3) cancels to x − 3 — but watch out for x = −3!
p: A rational expression is a ratio of two polynomials, P(x)/Q(x), with Q(x) not the zero polynomial.
To simplify, factorise the numerator and the denominator fully, then cancel common factors (whole factors only, never single terms).
Values that make the denominator zero are not allowed. List them from the original denominator, before cancelling.

ex.q: Simplify (x² − 4x)/(x² − 16) and state the restrictions.

topics.rl: Scientists simplify formulas before plugging in numbers, but they always note the values where the formula breaks down.

rv.summary: A rational expression is a ratio of polynomials. Factorise top and bottom, cancel common factors, and keep the restrictions from the original denominator.
focus: Simplify rational expressions by factorising.
State values that are not allowed.
Avoid cancelling single terms.
remember: Restrictions come from the original denominator.
traps: Cancel whole factors only, never single terms.
Find restrictions before cancelling.
Look at the denominator, not the numerator, for restrictions.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.h: Tie a goat to a peg with a 5 m rope and let it graze: the edge of the grass it eats is a perfect circle!
p: A circle is the set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance (the radius r) from a fixed point (the centre O).
A chord joins two points of the circle. A chord through the centre is a diameter, and diameter = 2 × radius.
A point P is inside the circle if OP < r, on it if OP = r, and outside if OP > r.
No chord is longer than a diameter: for a chord AB, AB ≤ OA + OB = 2r (triangle inequality), with equality only when AB passes through O.

ex.q: A circle has centre O and radius 6 cm. Where are points P, Q, R with OP = 4 cm, OQ = 6 cm, OR = 7.5 cm?
ex.a: P inside, Q on, R outside

topics.rl: A compass used in geometry works exactly by the definition: the needle is the centre and the pencil stays at a fixed distance.

rv.summary: A circle is all points at a fixed distance r from a centre O. A chord joins two points of the circle; the diameter (2r) is the longest chord.
focus: Use diameter = 2 × radius.
Decide if a point is inside, on or outside a circle.
Explain why no chord exceeds the diameter.
remember: Inside: OP < r; on: OP = r; outside: OP > r.
AB ≤ OA + OB = 2r, equal only for a diameter.
r = 6 cm: OP = 4 inside, OQ = 6 on, OR = 7.5 outside.
traps: Compare with the radius, not the diameter.
A radius is not a chord.
Don't double when asked for the radius.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.h: How many different circles can pass through your pencil dot? Infinitely many!
p: Every line through the centre is a line of symmetry of a circle, so a circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry.
A circle also has rotational symmetry about its centre by every angle: turn it by 1°, 37° or 200° and it looks the same.
Through one point, infinitely many circles can be drawn. Through two points A and B, also infinitely many.
The centre of any circle through A and B is equally far from A and B, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
The smallest circle through A and B has AB as its diameter, so its radius is AB/2.

ex.q: A and B are 10 cm apart. What is the radius of the smallest circle through both, and where is its centre?
st: Centre must be on the perpendicular bisector of AB
Closest such point to A is the midpoint M
ex.a: 5 cm, centred at the midpoint of AB

topics.rl: A wheel can be fitted any way round on its axle because of its rotational symmetry.

rv.summary: A circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry for every angle. Infinitely many circles pass through two points; their centres lie on the perpendicular bisector.
focus: Describe the symmetries of a circle.
Locate centres of circles through two points.
Find the smallest circle through two points.
remember: Every line through the centre is a line of symmetry.
Centres of circles through A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
Smallest circle through A, B: diameter AB, radius AB/2.
traps: Not every chord is a line of symmetry.
Two points do not fix a single circle.
Two points on a circle are at most a diameter apart.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.h: Three villages want one water tank equally far from all of them. Where should it go? At the circumcentre!
p: Through three non-collinear points there is exactly one circle: its centre is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet.
Through three collinear points there is no circle: the perpendicular bisectors are parallel and never meet.
This circle is the circumcircle of the triangle, and its centre is the circumcentre.
To construct it, draw the perpendicular bisectors of two sides; their meeting point O is the centre and OA is the radius.
The circumcentre is inside an acute triangle, at the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.

ex.q: A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Where is its circumcentre and what is the circumradius?

topics.rl: Placing a mobile tower equally far from three towns uses the circumcentre of the triangle formed by them.

rv.summary: Exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points; its centre (circumcentre) is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet. No circle passes through three collinear points.
focus: Construct a circumcircle.
Locate the circumcentre for acute, right and obtuse triangles.
Find circumradius of a right triangle.
remember: Circumcentre = meeting point of perpendicular bisectors.
Acute: inside; right: midpoint of hypotenuse; obtuse: outside.
traps: Perpendicular bisectors, not angle bisectors.
Two bisectors are enough to find the centre.
The circumcentre is not always inside.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.h: Cut equal-length chords in a round roti and the slices to the centre all have the same angle!
p: The angle subtended by chord AB at the centre is ∠AOB.
Triangle OAB is isosceles because OA = OB = r, so its base angles are equal.
Theorem: equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre. Proof: if AB = CD, then △OAB ≅ △OCD by SSS (OA = OC, OB = OD, AB = CD), so ∠AOB = ∠COD.
Converse: chords that subtend equal angles at the centre are equal. Proof: △OAB ≅ △OCD by SAS, so AB = CD.

ex.q: Chord AB subtends 70° at centre O. Find ∠OAB.

topics.rl: A bicycle wheel's spokes cut the rim into equal arcs because the central angles are equal.

rv.summary: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre (by SSS), and chords that subtend equal central angles are equal (by SAS).
focus: Use the equal chords–equal angles theorem and its converse.
Use the isosceles triangle OAB.
Find central angles of regular polygons.
remember: Regular pentagon side: 360° ÷ 5 = 72° at the centre.
traps: Use SSS for the theorem; SAS for the converse.
Subtract from 180°, not 90°.
A bigger central angle gives a longer chord, not a shorter one.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.t: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord
topics.h: Fold a paper circle so a chord's ends meet: the fold goes straight through the centre!
p: Theorem: the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord (△OAM ≅ △OBM by SSS, and the two angles at M are equal and add to 180°).
Converse: the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord (△OAM ≅ △OBM by RHS).
So the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre; two such bisectors locate the centre of a circle.
Parallel chords: their perpendiculars from O lie on one line. Find each distance with Pythagoras; the gap between the chords is the difference (same side of O) or the sum (opposite sides).

ex.q: In a circle of radius 5 cm, parallel chords AB = 8 cm and CD = 6 cm lie on opposite sides of the centre. How far apart are they?

topics.rl: Archaeologists find the size of a broken round pot by drawing two chords on a piece and crossing their perpendicular bisectors.

rv.summary: The line from the centre to a chord's midpoint is perpendicular to it, and the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. So perpendicular bisectors of chords pass through the centre.
focus: Use the perpendicular–bisector theorems.
Find the centre of a given circle.
Find gaps between parallel chords.
remember: OM ⊥ AB when M is the midpoint (SSS); perpendicular bisects (RHS).
r = 5, chords 8 and 6 on opposite sides: 3 + 4 = 7 cm.
traps: Add distances for opposite sides; subtract for the same side.
Use half the chord in Pythagoras.
The midpoints of parallel chords and the centre are collinear.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.t: How far is a chord from the centre?
topics.h: Chords near the edge of a circle are short; chords near the centre are long. Distance decides length!
p: The distance of a chord from the centre is the length of the perpendicular from O to the chord.
Theorem: equal chords are equidistant from the centre. Converse: chords equidistant from the centre are equal.
A longer chord is closer to the centre; a shorter chord is farther. The diameter (distance 0) is the longest.
The midpoints of all chords of a fixed length are the same distance from O, so they lie on a smaller circle with the same centre (a concentric circle).

ex.q: In a circle of radius 10 cm, where do the midpoints of all 12 cm chords lie?
st: Every midpoint is 8 cm from O
ex.a: On a concentric circle of radius 8 cm

topics.rl: Cut a round roti with a straight knife: a cut through the middle is the longest, and cuts closer to the edge get shorter and shorter.

rv.summary: Equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and chords equidistant from the centre are equal. Longer chords are closer to the centre.
focus: Compare chords by their distances from the centre.
Find the distance or length of a chord.
Locate midpoints of equal chords.
remember: Distance = perpendicular from O to the chord.
r = 10, chords of 12 cm: midpoints on a concentric circle of radius 8 cm.
traps: A larger distance means a shorter chord.
Distance is not measured to an end point.
Double the half-chord at the end.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.h: Radius, chord, distance: know any two and Baudhayana's theorem gives the third!
p: The radius, the half-chord and the distance d form a right triangle, so r² = (half-chord)² + d².
Chord length = 2√(r² − d²).
Distance d = √(r² − (chord/2)²) and radius r = √((chord/2)² + d²).
Through a point P inside a circle, the shortest chord is the one perpendicular to OP; its length is 2√(r² − OP²). The longest chord through P is the diameter.

ex.q: A circle has radius 17 cm. Find the length of a chord 8 cm from the centre.

topics.rl: A well-digger measuring the width of a round well at a fixed distance from the centre is using this formula.

rv.summary: The radius, half-chord and distance from the centre form a right triangle: r² = (half-chord)² + d². The shortest chord through an interior point P is perpendicular to OP.
focus: Find chord length, distance or radius.
Find the shortest and longest chords through a point.
Use Pythagoras with half-chords.
remember: Shortest chord through P: 2√(r² − OP²); longest: the diameter.
traps: Use half the chord, not the whole chord, in Pythagoras.
Don't stop at the half-length.
The perpendicular chord is the shortest, not the longest.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.t: Arcs and the angle at the centre
topics.h: Two goalposts stand on the edge of a round ground. Seen from the centre, the angle between them is exactly twice the angle seen from any point on the far edge!
p: Two points on a circle split it into two arcs: the smaller is the minor arc, the larger the major arc. If the points are ends of a diameter, both arcs are semicircles.
An arc AB subtends ∠AOB at the centre and ∠APB at a point P on the remaining part of the circle (an inscribed angle).
Theorem: the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining part of the circle: ∠AOB = 2∠APB.
Proof idea: join PO and extend it. Triangles OAP and OBP are isosceles, so each outer angle at O equals twice the matching base angle; adding gives ∠AOB = 2∠APB.

ex.q: Arc AB subtends 130° at the centre. Find the angle it subtends at a point P on the major arc.

topics.rl: Architects designing arched gates use the doubling rule to set angles of the arch from its centre.

rv.summary: Two points split a circle into a minor and a major arc. The angle an arc subtends at the centre is double the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining part of the circle.
focus: Use ∠AOB = 2∠APB.
Find major and minor arcs.
Follow the isosceles-triangle proof.
remember: 130° at the centre → 65° at the circumference.
Ends of a diameter make two semicircles.
traps: Halve for the circumference angle; don't double.
A large arc is not automatically a semicircle.
Don't subtract from 180° by mistake.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.t: Same segment, semicircle and concyclic points
topics.h: Two lamps stand on the edge of a round pond. Walk along the far side of the edge and the angle between the lamps, as you see them, never changes!
p: Angles in the same segment are equal: all angles subtended by arc AB at points on the same arc are equal (each is half of ∠AOB).
The angle in a semicircle is a right angle: if AB is a diameter, ∠AOB = 180°, so ∠APB = 90° for any point P on the circle.
Points are concyclic if they all lie on one circle.
If a segment AB subtends equal angles at two points C and D on the same side of AB, then A, B, C, D are concyclic.

ex.q: AB is a diameter of a circle and C is on the circle with ∠CAB = 35°. Find ∠CBA.

topics.rl: A photographer standing anywhere on a circle through two ends of a stage sees the stage at the same angle.

rv.summary: Angles in the same segment are equal, and the angle in a semicircle is 90°. If a segment subtends equal angles at two points on the same side, the four points are concyclic.
focus: Use angles in the same segment.
Use the angle in a semicircle.
Test four points for concyclicity.
traps: Angles in the same segment are equal, not doubled.
Nearly equal angles do not prove concyclicity.
Concyclic is not collinear.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.h: Put the four corners of any four-sided figure on a circle, and its opposite angles always team up to make 180°!
p: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on a circle.
Theorem: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°. (The two angles stand on arcs that together make the whole circle, so their centre angles add to 360°.)
Converse: if a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral add to 180°, the quadrilateral is cyclic.
An exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle.
With algebra: if opposite angles are (2x + 10)° and (3x − 5)°, then 5x + 5 = 180, so x = 35.

ex.q: ABCD is cyclic with ∠A = 75° and ∠B = 110°. Find ∠C and ∠D.

topics.rl: Window frames built in round arches often form cyclic quadrilaterals, so carpenters use the 180° rule.

rv.summary: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°, and the converse is true. An exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.
focus: Find missing angles of cyclic quadrilaterals.
Test if a quadrilateral is cyclic.
Solve angle equations with algebra.
traps: Opposite angles are supplementary, not equal.
Pair opposite angles, not adjacent ones.
Use 180°, not 360°, for one pair.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.h: Brahmagupta found the area of any four-sided figure on a circle using only its sides, 1400 years ago!
p: A parallelogram is cyclic only if it is a rectangle: opposite angles are equal and must add to 180°, so each is 90°.
The diagonals of a rectangle inscribed in a circle are diameters, so they meet at the centre.
Brahmagupta's formula: a cyclic quadrilateral with sides a, b, c, d and semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c + d)/2 has area √((s − a)(s − b)(s − c)(s − d)).
A regular hexagon in a circle of radius r splits into 6 equilateral triangles, so each side equals r.
The apothem (distance from the centre to a side) of that hexagon is (√3/2)r, the height of an equilateral triangle of side r.

ex.q: A cyclic quadrilateral has sides 7, 15, 20 and 24 cm. Find its area.

topics.rl: Honeycomb cells and many nut-bolt heads are regular hexagons whose side equals the radius of the circle around them.

rv.summary: A cyclic parallelogram must be a rectangle, whose diagonals are diameters. Brahmagupta's formula gives the area of a cyclic quadrilateral; a regular hexagon in a circle has side equal to the radius.
focus: Use Brahmagupta's formula.
Explain why a cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle.
Find side and apothem of an inscribed hexagon.
remember: Area = √((s − a)(s − b)(s − c)(s − d)), s = semi-perimeter.
Hexagon in radius r: side r, apothem (√3/2)r.
traps: Use the semi-perimeter, not the perimeter.
Don't forget the square root.
Not every parallelogram is cyclic.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.h: A giant wheel at the Dussehra mela lifts you up, brings you down, and does it again and again. Things that repeat like this are called periodic!
p: A motion is periodic if it repeats itself exactly after a fixed interval of time.
The time for one complete cycle is the period. The number of cycles in one unit of time is the frequency: frequency = 1 ÷ period.
Examples: the swing of a pendulum, the hands of a clock, a giant wheel, days of the week, phases of the Moon.
To find where a periodic motion is after a long time, divide the time by the period and look at the remainder.
The graph of height against time for a seat on a giant wheel is a smooth wave that rises and falls again and again.

ex.q: A giant wheel takes 4 minutes for one full turn. Riya's seat is at the bottom at time 0. Where is it after 22 minutes?
st: After 5 full turns the seat is back at the bottom
2 minutes is half of a turn, so the seat goes from the bottom to the top
ex.a: At the very top of the wheel
