topics.rl: Your heartbeat, the seasons and the tides all follow repeating cycles. Doctors even count heartbeats per minute, which is a frequency!

rv.summary: A periodic motion repeats exactly after a fixed time, the period; frequency = 1 ÷ period. Use the remainder after dividing by the period to find the position later.
focus: Identify periodic motions.
Find period and frequency.
Find the position after a long time using remainders.
remember: Wheel: 4 min per turn; 22 min = 5 turns + 2 min → at the top.
Height of a giant-wheel seat vs time: a repeating wave.
traps: A one-time motion is not periodic.
Period and frequency are not the same number.
Don't ignore the remainder.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.h: Every spoke of a cycle wheel sweeps out angles as it turns. One full turn is 360°, but a wheel can keep turning through 720°, 1080° and beyond!
p: A full turn is 360°, a half turn is 180° and a quarter turn is 90°.
Angles are classified as acute (less than 90°), right (90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), straight (180°) and reflex (between 180° and 360°).
An angle at the centre of a circle is called a central angle. Equal slices of a circle have equal central angles: n equal slices have 360° ÷ n each.
Arc length for a central angle θ is (θ/360) × 2πr, the same fraction of the full circumference.
Turning anticlockwise is usually taken as positive. Turning through more than 360° just means extra full turns: 450° = 360° + 90°.

ex.q: A wheel of radius 35 cm turns through 72°. How far does a point on the rim travel? (Use π = 22/7.)

topics.rl: A pizza or a birthday cake cut into 8 equal slices gives each slice a central angle of 45°.

rv.summary: A full turn is 360°. Angles are acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex. Central angles of n equal slices are 360° ÷ n, and arc length is (θ/360) × 2πr.
focus: Classify angles.
Find central angles and reflex angles.
Find arc lengths.
traps: A full turn is 360°, not 100.
Reflex = 360° − angle, not 180° − angle.
Not every angle over 90° is reflex.

topics.ch: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
topics.h: How high is your seat on the giant wheel right now? With an angle and the radius, trigonometry can tell you without a measuring tape!
p: In a right triangle, for an acute angle θ: the hypotenuse is the longest side, the opposite side is across from θ, and the adjacent side is next to θ.
sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent.
For a fixed angle these ratios stay the same however big the triangle is, because all such triangles are similar.
A point on a circle of radius r, at angle θ above the horizontal line through the centre, is r sin θ above the centre and r cos θ across from it. Also sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

ex.q: A giant wheel has radius 10 m and its centre is 12 m above the ground. Riya's seat is at 30° above the horizontal line through the centre. How high is she?
st: Height above the centre = r sin θ = 10 × sin 30°

topics.rl: Engineers use sine and cosine to design ramps, roofs and giant wheels, and to work out heights of towers they cannot climb.

rv.summary: In a right triangle, sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent. These ratios depend only on the angle.
focus: Find sin, cos and tan from a right triangle.
Know standard values.
Find heights on a circle using r sin θ.
remember: Point at angle θ on a circle: r sin θ up, r cos θ across.
traps: Don't divide by the adjacent side for sin.
sin 30° is 1/2, not √3/2.
Don't think sin θ gets smaller as θ grows from 0° to 90°: it increases from 0 to 1.

topics.t: Perimeter and the mystery ratio π
topics.h: Measure round a bangle, a plate and a tyre with a thread, divide by the width each time... and get the same number!
p: Perimeter is the total length of the boundary of a closed shape.
For a composite figure, add the lengths of all the straight parts and curved parts on the outside only, not the lines inside.
For every circle, circumference ÷ diameter is the same constant, called π ≈ 3.14159...

People approximated π over centuries: Mesopotamians used about 3⅛; Archimedes trapped it between 223/71 and 22/7 using 96-sided polygons; Liu Hui got about 3.1416; Zu Chongzhi found 355/113; Aryabhata gave 3.1416; Brahmagupta used √10.

ex.q: A window is a 1.4 m by 1 m rectangle topped by a semicircle on the 1.4 m side. Find its perimeter. (π = 22/7)
st: Straight parts: 1 + 1.4 + 1 = 3.4 m (the top side is replaced by the arc)

topics.rl: Fencing a garden shaped like a rectangle with a round end needs exactly this composite perimeter.

rv.summary: Perimeter is the length of a shape's boundary. For every circle, circumference ÷ diameter is the constant π, which mathematicians approximated over centuries.
focus: Find perimeters of composite shapes.
Define π as C ÷ d.
Match historical approximations to mathematicians.
remember: Archimedes: 223/71 < π < 22/7; Zu Chongzhi: 355/113; Aryabhata: 3.1416; Brahmagupta: √10.
traps: π is C ÷ d, not C ÷ r.
Don't include sides that are covered by a curve.
22/7 is not the most accurate value.

topics.h: A round rangoli, a cricket ground, a bangle: circles are everywhere. Just one number, the radius, decides their size!
p: Circumference (perimeter) of a circle: C = 2πr = πd, where r is the radius and d the diameter.
Area of a circle: A = πr². We often use π = 22/7 or 3.14.
A semicircle has perimeter πr + 2r (the curved part plus the diameter).
Area of a ring (between circles of radii R and r): π(R² − r²).
A sector with central angle θ has area (θ/360) × πr².

ex.q: Meena draws a circular rangoli of radius 21 cm. Find the length of its border and its area. (Use π = 22/7.)

topics.rl: The distance a bicycle moves in one turn of its wheel equals the wheel's circumference. That is how a cycle's odometer counts kilometres.

rv.summary: Circumference C = 2πr = πd and area A = πr². A semicircle's perimeter is πr + 2r; a ring's area is π(R² − r²).
focus: Find circumference and area.
Find perimeters of semicircles.
Find areas of rings and sectors.
traps: Don't confuse 2πr with πr².
A diameter is not the radius.
Ring area is π(R² − r²), not π(R − r)².

topics.h: 22/7 is a great guess, but π never ends and never repeats. Not even a supercomputer can finish writing it!
p: π cannot be written as p/q with integers p and q; its decimals go on forever without repeating.
22/7 = 3.142857... and 3.14 are only approximations; 22/7 is slightly bigger than π, and 3.14 slightly smaller.
Madhava of Sangamagrama (Kerala, about 1400 CE) found π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + 1/9 − ...; the partial sums swing above and below π/4 and slowly settle down.
Pi Day is 14 March (3/14) and Pi Approximation Day is 22 July (22/7).

ex.q: Find 4 × (1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7). Is it above or below π?

topics.rl: Students celebrate Pi Day on 14 March with π-recitation contests and round foods like rotis and pizzas.

rv.summary: π is irrational: its decimals never end or repeat. 22/7 is a little more than π and 3.14 a little less. Madhava's series π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − ... zigzags towards π.
focus: Explain why 22/7 is only an approximation.
Compute partial sums of Madhava's series.
Know Pi Day and Pi Approximation Day.
remember: Pi Day 14 March; Pi Approximation Day 22 July.
traps: 22/7 is not exact.
Madhava's series uses odd denominators only.
Multiply the partial sum by 4 to estimate π.

topics.h: A slice of pizza has two straight edges and one curved crust. How long is the crust?
p: Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr for a central angle θ in degrees.
Perimeter of a sector = arc length + 2r (two radii).
Shapes built from semicircles and quarter circles: add up each curved piece. A flower made of semicircles on the sides of a square has perimeter = 4 × (semicircle arcs).
Circumference is proportional to radius, so if two circles' perimeters are in ratio 3 : 5, their radii are also 3 : 5.

ex.q: Find the perimeter of a sector of radius 21 cm and angle 60°. (π = 22/7)

topics.rl: The crust of a pizza slice is an arc, and decorators trimming fan-shaped cards need the sector perimeter.

rv.summary: Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr, and a sector's perimeter adds two radii. Circumference is proportional to radius.
focus: Find arc lengths and sector perimeters.
Find lengths of curves built from arcs.
Use ratios of perimeters and radii.
traps: Don't forget the two radii.
Use 2πr, not πr², for arcs.
Don't take square roots of perimeter ratios.

topics.h: Two rectangles with the same fence length can hold very different numbers of cows!
p: Same perimeter does not mean same area: 1 × 9 and 5 × 5 rectangles both have perimeter 20, but areas 9 and 25.
Same area does not mean same perimeter: 1 × 16 and 4 × 4 both have area 16, but perimeters 34 and 16.
But two rectangles with the same area AND the same perimeter must be congruent: l + b and l × b fix l and b.
On a running track, outer lanes are longer on the bends, so starting lines are staggered: for one lap the extra is 2π × (lane width) per lane.

Staircase paradox: replace the diagonal of a 3 × 4 rectangle by a staircase. However tiny the steps, the staircase length stays 3 + 4 = 7, never reaching the diagonal's 5. Looking similar does not mean equal length.

ex.q: On a 400 m track, lanes are 1.25 m wide. How much further ahead should a runner in lane 2 start than lane 1 for a one-lap race? (π = 3.14)
st: The two bends make one full circle
Lane 2's circle has radius 1.25 m more

topics.rl: Race officials paint staggered starting lines on school sports tracks using exactly this calculation.

rv.summary: Equal perimeters don't mean equal areas, and equal areas don't mean equal perimeters. Outer lanes on a track are longer on the bends, and the staircase paradox shows looks can mislead.
focus: Compare perimeters and areas of rectangles.
Find track stagger distances.
Explain the staircase paradox.
remember: Same area and same perimeter → congruent rectangles.
Stagger per lane = 2π × lane width; 1.25 m → 7.85 m.
For a fixed perimeter, the square has the largest area.
traps: The staircase length never approaches the diagonal.
Straight sections of a track are equal in all lanes.
A longer rectangle does not enclose more area.

topics.h: A farmer in Punjab wants to sow wheat on an odd-shaped field. Break it into triangles and rectangles, and its area is no longer a mystery!
p: Perimeter is the length of the boundary; area is the amount of surface inside, measured in square units such as cm² or m².
Triangle: area = ½ × base × height, where the height is perpendicular to the base.
Parallelogram: area = base × height. Rectangle: length × breadth. Square: side².
Trapezium: area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × distance between them. Rhombus: area = ½ × d₁ × d₂ (product of diagonals).
Any quadrilateral can be split by a diagonal into two triangles; add their areas.

ex.q: A field is a trapezium with parallel sides 30 m and 20 m, which are 12 m apart. Find its area.

topics.rl: Painters, tile-layers and farmers all estimate costs by area: ₹ per square metre of paint, tiles or seeds.

rv.summary: Area is the surface inside a shape. Triangle ½bh, parallelogram bh, trapezium ½(sum of parallel sides) × height, rhombus ½d₁d₂.
focus: Use area formulas for triangles and quadrilaterals.
Split quadrilaterals into triangles.
Pick the perpendicular height.
traps: Don't forget the ½ for triangles and rhombuses.
Use the perpendicular height, not a slanted side.
Parallelogram area has no ½.

topics.t: Same base, same parallels and medians
topics.h: Push the top of a parallelogram sideways like a deck of cards: its shape changes but its area doesn't!
p: Area pictures prove identities: an a × a square with a b × b corner removed rearranges into an (a + b) × (a − b) rectangle, so a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).
Parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels have equal area, because they have the same base and the same height.
Triangles on the same base and between the same parallels have equal area (½ × base × same height).
A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. It splits the triangle into two triangles with equal bases and the same height, so equal areas.

ex.q: Triangle ABC has area 48 cm² and AD is a median. Find the area of triangle ABD.
st: Triangles ABD and ADC share the height from A

topics.rl: Farmers dividing a triangular plot fairly between two children can draw a median.

rv.summary: Parallelograms (or triangles) on the same base and between the same parallels have equal areas. A median splits a triangle into two equal areas.
focus: Use same base, same parallels results.
Use medians to halve areas.
Prove a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) with areas.
remember: Triangle on the same base and parallels = ½ of the parallelogram.
traps: Slanting does not change the area.
Equal areas don't need congruent triangles.
A median need not be an altitude.

topics.h: Over 1900 years ago, Heron of Alexandria found a way to get a triangle's area from its three sides alone. No height needed!
p: Heron's formula is used when you know all three sides a, b, c of a triangle but not its height.
First find the semi-perimeter: s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2.
Area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)].
For an equilateral triangle of side a, this gives area = (√3/4) × a².
A quadrilateral with a known diagonal can be split into two triangles, and Heron's formula used on each.

ex.q: Find the area of a triangle with sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm.

topics.rl: Surveyors measuring a triangular plot of land can easily measure the three sides with a tape, but not the height across the middle. Heron's formula is perfect for them.

rv.summary: Heron's formula finds a triangle's area from its three sides: area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)], with s the semi-perimeter.
focus: Find the semi-perimeter.
Use Heron's formula.
Split quadrilaterals by a diagonal and use Heron's formula.
traps: Use the semi-perimeter, not the perimeter.
Don't forget the square root.
It works for any triangle, not only special ones.

topics.h: Double the sides of a photo and you need four times the paper. Area grows faster than length!
p: Join the midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral: the inner quadrilateral (a parallelogram) has exactly half the area of the original.
In a parallelogram, any triangle with one side of the parallelogram as base and its third vertex on the opposite side has half the parallelogram's area.
In a square, joining midpoints, diagonals or a vertex to a midpoint creates pieces whose areas are simple fractions of the whole (½, ¼, ⅛ ...).
Scaling: if all lengths are multiplied by k, area is multiplied by k². So doubling lengths makes the area 4 times.

ex.q: A square has side 10 cm. Its side midpoints are joined. Find the area of the new square.
st: Midpoint figure has half the area

topics.rl: Map makers know that a map at half the scale shows each region with only a quarter of the area.

rv.summary: Joining midpoints of a quadrilateral halves the area. A triangle on a side of a parallelogram with its vertex on the opposite side has half its area. Scaling lengths by k scales area by k².
focus: Use midpoint and parallelogram area results.
Find area fractions in a square.
Apply the k² rule for scaling.
remember: Midpoint quadrilateral = ½ of the original.
traps: Midpoint quadrilateral is ½, not ¼.
Use k² for area, not k.
Area ratio 1 : 4 means length ratio 1 : 2.

topics.t: Brahmagupta's formula and squaring a rectangle
topics.h: Ancient altar-builders had to make a square with exactly the area of a rectangle. Baudhayana showed how!
p: Brahmagupta's formula: a cyclic quadrilateral with sides a, b, c, d has area √((s − a)(s − b)(s − c)(s − d)), where s = (a + b + c + d)/2.
If one side shrinks to zero (d = 0), the quadrilateral becomes a triangle and the formula turns into Heron's: √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)).
Identity behind squaring a rectangle: ab = ((a + b)/2)² − ((a − b)/2)².

Baudhayana's method (Sulba Sutras): cut a b × b square from an a × b rectangle, split the leftover strip into two halves and move one half to another side, forming a big square of side (a + b)/2 missing a small square of side (a − b)/2. Then Pythagoras gives a single square with the same area.

ex.q: Find the side of a square with the same area as a 9 m × 4 m rectangle using the identity.

topics.rl: Vedic altar builders (vedi) followed the Sulba Sutras to change shapes while keeping area exactly the same.

rv.summary: Brahmagupta's formula gives the area of a cyclic quadrilateral and becomes Heron's formula when one side is 0. ab = ((a + b)/2)² − ((a − b)/2)² lets Baudhayana turn a rectangle into an equal square.
focus: Use Brahmagupta's formula.
Link it to Heron's formula.
Square a rectangle using the identity.
traps: Use the semi-perimeter.
Don't average the sides to get the square's side.
Squaring a rectangle is Baudhayana's (Sulba Sutras), not Brahmagupta's.

topics.t: Why πr², segments and swept areas
topics.h: Slice a roti into many thin wedges, flip every other one, and the circle turns into a rectangle!
p: Cut a circle into many equal sectors and lay them alternately up and down: they form an almost-rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r, so area = πr². Indian texts such as those of Nilakantha Somayaji describe this rearrangement.
Archimedes showed the circle has the same area as a right triangle with legs r and 2πr: ½ × r × 2πr = πr².
A segment is the region between a chord and its arc. Minor segment area = sector area − area of triangle OAB; major segment = circle area − minor segment.
Area swept by a clock hand or a wiper blade is a sector: (θ/360) × πr²; for a wiper whose blade starts some distance from the pivot, it is the difference of two sectors.

ex.q: Find the area of the minor segment cut off by a chord that subtends 90° at the centre of a circle of radius 14 cm. (π = 22/7)

topics.rl: Car designers calculate the area a wiper clears so drivers can see the road in heavy monsoon rain.

rv.summary: Rearranging sectors into a near-rectangle (πr by r) shows area = πr². A segment's area is sector minus triangle; swept areas are sectors or differences of sectors.
focus: Explain why area = πr².
Find segment areas.
Find areas swept by wipers and clock hands.
remember: Archimedes: triangle with legs r and 2πr.
traps: A segment uses a chord; a sector uses two radii.
Subtract the triangle from the sector.
For a blade starting away from the pivot, subtract the inner sector.

topics.t: Polygons in circles and shaded regions
topics.h: A square inside a circle covers about 64% of it, a hexagon about 83%. More sides, closer to the circle!
p: A square inscribed in a circle of radius r has diagonal 2r, so its area is 2r²; ratio to the circle = 2/π ≈ 0.64.
An inscribed equilateral triangle has area (3√3/4)r²; ratio ≈ 0.41. An inscribed regular hexagon has area (3√3/2)r²; ratio ≈ 0.83.
As the number of sides grows, the inscribed polygon fills more of the circle.
For shaded regions, write shaded area = (big shape) − (pieces removed), or add pieces. Four quarter circles at the corners of a square make one full circle together.

ex.q: A circle is drawn inside a square of side 14 cm, touching all four sides. Find the area outside the circle but inside the square. (π = 22/7)

topics.rl: Tile designs with circles in squares need shaded-area calculations to order the right amount of each colour of marble.

rv.summary: An inscribed square covers 2/π of a circle, a hexagon about 0.83 and a triangle about 0.41. Shaded areas are found by adding or subtracting known shapes.
focus: Find areas of polygons inscribed in circles.
Compare how much of the circle they cover.
Find shaded areas.
remember: Square of side 14 with inscribed circle: 196 − 154 = 42 cm².
traps: The inscribed square's side is not r.
Four corner quarter circles make one circle, not four.
Don't confuse inscribed and circumscribed squares.

topics.ch: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability
topics.h: Will it rain on Sports Day? Will India win the toss? Life is full of 'maybe', and maths can measure it!
p: Probability measures how likely an event is: how confident we can be that it will happen.
Uncertain situations are everywhere: rain tomorrow, the result of a match, whose name is drawn from a box of slips.
In words we say an event is impossible, less likely, equally likely (even chance), more likely or certain.
Subjective probability is a personal judgement. Two fans may give different chances to the same team winning, based on their feelings and knowledge.

ex.q: Describe each in words: (a) the Sun rises tomorrow, (b) a fair coin shows heads, (c) you roll a 7 on an ordinary die.
st: (b) Heads and tails have the same chance: equally likely
(c) A die has only 1 to 6: impossible

topics.rl: Weather reports say '70% chance of rain', turning 'maybe' into a number you can plan with.

rv.summary: Probability measures how likely an event is. In words, events are impossible, less likely, equally likely, more likely or certain. Subjective probability is a personal judgement.
focus: Describe chance in words.
Identify certain and impossible events.
Tell subjective probability from objective.
remember: Sun rises tomorrow: certain. Fair coin heads: equally likely. 7 on a die: impossible.
9 green and 1 yellow: yellow less likely, green more likely.
Subjective = personal judgement, can differ between people.
traps: 'Very likely' is not 'certain'.
'Unlikely' is not 'impossible'.
A percentage given as an opinion is still subjective.

topics.ch: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability
topics.h: Before a cricket match the captains toss a coin. Heads or tails? Nobody knows for sure, but maths can still say how likely each one is!
p: A random experiment is an action whose result cannot be predicted for certain, like tossing a coin or rolling a die.
Each possible result is an outcome. The list of all outcomes is the sample space: rolling a die gives {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
An event is a collection of outcomes, such as 'getting an even number' = {2, 4, 6}.
When all outcomes are equally likely, P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes.
Every probability lies from 0 to 1. A sure event has probability 1; an impossible event has probability 0.

ex.q: A die is rolled once. Find the probability of getting a number greater than 4.

topics.rl: Ludo, snakes and ladders and the cricket toss are all random experiments. Fair dice and coins make the game fair for everyone.

rv.summary: A random experiment has outcomes; all outcomes form the sample space, and an event is a set of outcomes. For equally likely outcomes, P = favourable ÷ total, between 0 and 1.
focus: List sample spaces.
Find probabilities of events.
Know the range of probability.
traps: Probability cannot be more than 1.
1 is not a prime number.
Divide by the total, not by the other outcomes.

topics.ch: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability
topics.h: Every chance in the world fits on one ruler from 0 to 1!
p: Probability is a number from 0 to 1 (or 0% to 100%). 0 means impossible, 1 means certain.
An even chance, like heads on a fair coin, is 0.5 or 50%.
Events can be ranked on the scale: less likely events sit nearer 0, more likely ones nearer 1. Always give a reason.
A fair (unbiased) coin, die or spinner makes every outcome equally likely; a bent coin or loaded die is biased.

ex.q: Place on the 0-1 scale: (a) a fair die shows 6, (b) a fair coin shows heads, (c) it is cold in Delhi in January.

topics.rl: Sports commentators say a team has a '50-50 chance'—that's 0.5 on the probability scale.

rv.summary: Probability runs from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), or 0% to 100%. 0.5 is an even chance. Fair objects make all outcomes equally likely.
focus: Place events on the 0–1 scale.
Convert between fractions, decimals and percentages.
Explain fair and biased.
traps: No number on a fair die is 'luckier'.
A few results cannot prove a coin is biased.

topics.ch: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability
topics.h: Toss a paper cup: does it land on its side, top or bottom? Opinions won't help. Experiments will!
p: Objective probability is based on evidence or reasoning, not opinion.
Two objective ways: from experiments or observations (experimental), and from reasoning about equally likely outcomes (theoretical).
Frequency is how many times an outcome happened; relative frequency is frequency ÷ total trials, which is the experimental probability.
To run trials: fix the experiment, repeat it many times, record each result with tally marks, then count frequencies.
For objects like a paper cup, outcomes are not equally likely, so only experiments can estimate the probabilities.

ex.q: A paper cup is tossed 50 times: side 31, top 12, bottom 7. Find the relative frequencies.

topics.rl: Cricket statisticians use relative frequencies, like a batter's fraction of innings with fifties.

rv.summary: Objective probability comes from experiments or from reasoning about equally likely outcomes. Relative frequency = frequency ÷ total trials.
focus: Tell objective from subjective probability.
Find frequencies and relative frequencies.
Record trials with tally marks.
remember: Cup in 50 tosses: side 0.62, top 0.24, bottom 0.14 (sum 1).
Tally: four lines and a cross line = 5.
traps: Frequency is a count; relative frequency is a proportion.
A paper cup's outcomes are not equally likely.
Strong feelings don't make a probability objective.

topics.ch: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability
topics.h: Toss a coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads. Toss it 1000 times and the share of heads creeps very close to one half. Let's see why!
p: Experimental (empirical) probability is found by actually doing an experiment many times.
P(E) = number of trials in which E happened ÷ total number of trials.
Different runs of the same experiment can give slightly different results.
As the number of trials grows, the experimental probability usually gets closer to the theoretical probability.
The experimental probabilities of all the outcomes add up to 1, so P(not E) = 1 − P(E).

ex.q: Kabir tosses a coin 50 times and gets 28 heads. Find the experimental probability of heads and of tails.

topics.rl: Weather offices say there is a 70% chance of rain because, on past days with similar conditions, it rained on about 70 out of 100 of them.

rv.summary: Experimental probability = trials where E happened ÷ total trials. It varies between runs and usually gets closer to the theoretical probability as trials grow.
focus: Find experimental probabilities from data.
Use P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
Compare with theoretical values.
traps: Use the data, not the theoretical 1/6 or 0.5.
Divide by the total trials.
Experimental and theoretical values are not always equal.

topics.ch: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability
topics.h: A factory cannot test every single pen it makes. So how does it know how many might be faulty? Probability makes the prediction!
p: Expected number of times an event happens = probability × number of trials.
P(not E) = 1 − P(E), because an event either happens or does not.
The probabilities of all the outcomes of an experiment add up to 1.
A prediction is a good estimate, not a promise: the real count may be a little more or less.
A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning.

ex.q: A factory found 3 faulty pens in a sample of 150. About how many faulty pens should it expect in a batch of 2000?

topics.rl: Insurance companies, doctors and weather forecasters all use probability from past data to plan for the future.

rv.summary: Expected number = probability × number of trials. Probabilities of all outcomes add to 1. A game is fair when every player has the same chance.
focus: Predict counts from probabilities.
Find missing probabilities.
Decide if a game is fair.
remember: Expected = P × trials; 3 faulty in 150 → 40 in 2000.
Fair game: equal chances for all players.
traps: P(not E) is not the reciprocal of P(E).
A fair die does not make every game fair.
Short runs prove nothing; coins don't remember.

topics.ch: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability
topics.t: Many trials, fair outcomes and the gambler's fallacy
topics.h: Five heads in a row: is tails 'due' now? Nope! The coin has no memory!
p: Law of large numbers: with more and more trials, the experimental probability tends to get closer to the theoretical one.
Rolling a fair die 60 times may give 6 about 10 times, but maybe 7 or 14; in 6000 rolls the relative frequency is usually very close to 1/6.
Gambler's fallacy: believing that past results change future chances. Each toss of a fair coin is still 1/2 heads, even after 5 heads in a row.
Before using 'favourable ÷ total', check the outcomes are equally likely. 'Win, lose or draw' are three outcomes, but they are usually not equally likely, so P(win) is not automatically 1/3.

ex.q: A fair die is rolled 600 times and shows 6 on 94 rolls. Compare experimental and theoretical probability.
st: Close, and likely to get closer with more rolls

topics.rl: Lottery players sometimes pick 'overdue' numbers, but every draw is a fresh start. That's the gambler's fallacy.

rv.summary: With more trials, experimental probability tends towards the theoretical value. Past results never change the chance of a fair coin or die. Favourable ÷ total needs equally likely outcomes.
focus: Explain the law of large numbers.
Spot the gambler's fallacy.
Check equal likelihood before using the formula.
traps: No outcome is ever 'due'.
Win, lose, draw are not automatically 1/3 each.
Count sector sizes, not colours.

topics.ch: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability
topics.h: A coin and a die together: how many different results? A tree diagram grows the answer branch by branch!
p: List the sample space carefully: one coin {H, T}; one die {1, ..., 6}; two coins {HH, HT, TH, TT}.
A coin with a die gives 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes: H1, H2, ..., T6. Two dice give 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes.
Menus and choices: 3 snacks and 2 drinks give 3 × 2 = 6 combinations.
A tree diagram shows multi-step experiments: each stage branches into its outcomes; the number of end branches is the size of the sample space.

ex.q: Draw a tree for tossing a coin three times. How many outcomes, and what is P(exactly two heads)?

topics.rl: A canteen offering 4 types of paratha and 3 chutneys can advertise 12 different combos!

rv.summary: List sample spaces carefully: a coin and a die give 12 outcomes, two dice give 36. Choices multiply, and tree diagrams show multi-step experiments.
focus: Count outcomes of combined experiments.
Use tree diagrams.
Find probabilities with two dice or three coins.
remember: Two coins: HH, HT, TH, TT.
Three coins: 8 outcomes; exactly two heads 3/8.
traps: HT and TH are different outcomes.
Multiply the choices; don't add them.
The 11 sums of two dice are not equally likely.

topics.ch: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability
topics.h: Put the sweet back or eat it? The answer changes your next chance!
p: With replacement, the object goes back, so the sample space is the same for every draw. Without replacement, it shrinks by one each draw.
Example: a bag of 3 red and 2 blue. Ordered draws of two: with replacement 5 × 5 = 25 outcomes; without replacement 5 × 4 = 20.
From a frequency table, P(outcome) = its frequency ÷ total. For spinners, use the fraction of the circle (angle ÷ 360°). For letter cards, count the letters.
Geometric probability: if a dart lands at a random point of a board, P(region) = area of region ÷ area of board.

ex.q: A dart lands randomly on a square board of side 20 cm with a square target of side 10 cm in the middle. Find P(target).

topics.rl: Lucky-draw organisers at a school fete decide whether to put tickets back after each draw: it changes everyone's chances.

rv.summary: With replacement the sample space stays the same; without replacement it shrinks. Use frequency tables, spinner angles or areas to find probabilities.
focus: Count draws with and without replacement.
Find probabilities from tables, letters and spinners.
Use area for geometric probability.
remember: 3 red, 2 blue: with replacement 25 ordered outcomes; without 20.
Dartboard: P = region area ÷ board area; 400 board, 100 target → 1/4.
traps: Don't reduce the count when the ball is replaced.
Compare areas, not radii.
Count repeated letters each time.

topics.ch: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
topics.h: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... Indian poets studied this pattern of rhythms centuries ago, long before it got the name Fibonacci. Can you guess what comes next?
p: A sequence is a list of numbers in a definite order. Each number is a term: a₁ is the first term, a₂ the second, and aₙ the nth term.
A rule for the nth term lets you jump straight to any term. For aₙ = 3n + 2, the 10th term is 3 × 10 + 2 = 32.
A recursive rule builds each term from earlier ones, like the Virahanka–Fibonacci numbers: each term is the sum of the two before it.
Famous sequences: square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, ...; triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, ...; cube numbers 1, 8, 27, 64, ...
Looking at the differences between terms often reveals the rule.

ex.q: Find the next term of 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ... and a rule for the nth term.
st: Differences: 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12

topics.rl: Seat numbers in a stadium, the rows of dots in a rangoli and the beats in a tabla rhythm all follow sequences.

rv.summary: A sequence is an ordered list of terms a₁, a₂, ..., aₙ. A rule for aₙ gives any term directly; a recursive rule builds terms from earlier ones. Differences often reveal the rule.
focus: Find terms from an nth-term rule.
Use recursive rules.
Find rules from patterns and differences.
remember: Virahanka–Fibonacci: add the last two terms.
traps: Check a rule on every term, not just one.
n² is not 2n.
Differences can change; don't keep the last one fixed.

topics.ch: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
topics.t: Finite, infinite and partial sums; is it a term?
topics.h: Is 100 in the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15, ...? Don't list them all: let algebra check!
p: A finite sequence stops (the days of a week, 1 to 31); an infinite sequence goes on forever (all odd numbers), shown with '...'.
A partial sum Sₙ adds the first n terms: for 1, 3, 5, 7, ..., S₁ = 1, S₂ = 4, S₃ = 9.
To check if a number is a term, set the rule equal to it and solve for n. If n is a natural number, it is a term; otherwise it is not.
The solution n also tells you the position of the term.

ex.q: Is 100 a term of tₙ = 4n − 1? Is 99?
st: 4n − 1 = 100 gives n = 101/4 = 25.25: not a natural number, so no
ex.a: 100 is not a term; 99 is the 25th term

topics.rl: A railway timetable lists a finite sequence of stations; the ticks of a clock form a sequence that goes on and on.

rv.summary: A sequence is finite if it stops and infinite if it goes on. A partial sum Sₙ adds the first n terms. To test if a number is a term, solve the rule for n and check that n is natural.
focus: Tell finite from infinite sequences.
Find partial sums.
Decide whether a number is a term.
remember: Odd numbers: S₁ = 1, S₂ = 4, S₃ = 9; Sₙ = n².
tₙ = 4n − 1: 99 is the 25th term; 100 is not a term.
traps: Don't round n to make it whole.
Sₙ is a sum, not the nth term.
1, 1/2, 1/3, ... is not finite: its terms get closer to 0 but never reach it.

topics.ch: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
topics.t: Recursive rules and the Virahanka numbers
topics.h: How many ways can a drummer fill 5 beats with short (1-beat) and long (2-beat) strokes? Indian poets counted this more than 1200 years ago!
p: A recursive rule can use several previous terms. For example T₁ = T₂ = T₃ = 1 and Tₙ = Tₙ₋₁ + Tₙ₋₂ + Tₙ₋₃ gives 1, 1, 1, 3, 5, 9, 17, ...
Virahanka numbers: V₁ = 1, V₂ = 2 and Vₙ = Vₙ₋₁ + Vₙ₋₂, giving 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ...
Vₙ counts the rhythms of n beats made of short (1 beat) and long (2 beats) syllables: a rhythm of n beats ends in a short (leaving n − 1 beats) or a long (leaving n − 2 beats).

Virahanka (who lived some time between the 6th and 8th centuries CE) found them while studying Sanskrit poetic metres; Gopala (around 1135) and Hemachandra (around 1150) wrote about them before Fibonacci (1202). So they are often called Virahanka–Fibonacci numbers.

ex.q: List all rhythms of 4 beats using S (1 beat) and L (2 beats).

topics.rl: Tabla and mridangam players build rhythms from short and long strokes, the very patterns Virahanka counted.

rv.summary: Recursive rules can use several earlier terms. Virahanka numbers 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... count rhythms of short and long syllables: Vₙ = Vₙ₋₁ + Vₙ₋₂. Indian scholars knew them before Fibonacci.
focus: Generate terms from recursive rules.
Count rhythms with short and long syllables.
Know the Indian history of these numbers.
remember: 4 beats: SSSS, SSL, SLS, LSS, LL = 5.
traps: Add the previous two terms, not a fixed amount.
Subtract in the order the rule says.
These numbers come from poetic metres, not rabbits, in Indian work.

topics.ch: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
topics.h: Saving ₹10 more every week than the week before? Your savings make an arithmetic progression, growing by the same step every time!
p: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a sequence in which each term is got by adding a fixed number d, called the common difference, to the previous term.
d = any term − the term before it. It can be positive, negative or zero.
The nth term of an AP with first term a is aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
To find which term equals a given number, solve a + (n − 1)d = that number for n.
The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d], or n/2 × (first term + last term).

ex.q: Find the 15th term of the AP 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

topics.rl: Auto fares that rise by a fixed amount per km, rows of seats that grow by 2 each row, and monthly EMI schedules are all APs.

rv.summary: An arithmetic progression adds a fixed common difference d each time. aₙ = a + (n − 1)d and Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d].
focus: Find d and the nth term.
Find which term has a given value.
Find sums of APs.
remember: d = term − previous term (can be negative).
traps: Use (n − 1)d, not nd.
A decreasing list can be an AP.
Don't forget to halve in the sum formula.

topics.ch: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
topics.t: More about APs: recursion, two terms, multiples and graphs
topics.h: An AP plotted on graph paper lines up as straight as a cricket pitch!
p: Recursive form of an AP: t₁ = a and tₙ = tₙ₋₁ + d.
From two terms: if t₃ = 11 and t₈ = 26, then 5d = 15, so d = 3 and a = 11 − 2 × 3 = 5.
Counting multiples: the 3-digit multiples of 7 are 105, 112, ..., 994, an AP with d = 7, so n = (994 − 105)/7 + 1 = 128.
Plotting (n, tₙ) for an AP gives points on a straight line, because tₙ = a + (n − 1)d = dn + (a − d) is a linear polynomial in n with slope d.

ex.q: An AP has t₄ = 18 and t₁₀ = 42. Find a, d and t₂₀.

topics.rl: Taxi fares that rise by the same amount each km form an AP, and their graph is a straight line.

rv.summary: An AP can be written recursively (tₙ = tₙ₋₁ + d) or found from two terms. Counting multiples uses the AP formula, and (n, tₙ) points lie on a straight line of slope d.
focus: Find a and d from two terms.
Count multiples in a range.
Write tₙ = dn + c and plot it.
traps: Count = (last − first)/d + 1; don't forget the +1.
The slope is d, not the first term.
Only APs give straight-line graphs.

topics.ch: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
topics.h: Add 1 to 100 in ten seconds? Write the sum forwards and backwards, and every pair makes 101!
p: Write S = 1 + 2 + ... + n and also S = n + (n − 1) + ... + 1. Adding pairs, each pair is n + 1 and there are n pairs: 2S = n(n + 1). This idea appears in Aryabhata's work.
So Sₙ = n(n + 1)/2. Picture: two staircases of dots fit together into an n × (n + 1) rectangle.
The triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, ... are exactly n(n + 1)/2.
A block sum is a difference: 51 + 52 + ... + 100 = S₁₀₀ − S₅₀ = 5050 − 1275 = 3775.
To find the smallest n with Sₙ > target, test n(n + 1)/2 near √(2 × target). Some numbers are sums of consecutive numbers: 15 = 7 + 8 = 4 + 5 + 6 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5.

ex.q: Find the smallest n for which 1 + 2 + ... + n exceeds 300.

topics.rl: Stacks of pipes or cricket balls in a triangle pyramid at a shop have 1, 2, 3, ... per row: the total is a triangular number.

rv.summary: Writing 1 + 2 + ... + n forwards and backwards gives n pairs of n + 1, so the sum is n(n + 1)/2, the nth triangular number.
focus: Find block sums as differences.
Find the smallest n with a sum above a target.
traps: Don't forget to divide by 2.
The staircases make n by n + 1, not a square.
Use n, not n + 1, for the last day.

topics.ch: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
topics.h: A king once promised a wise man 1 grain of rice on the first chessboard square, 2 on the next, 4 on the next... By the last square it was more rice than the whole world had!
p: A geometric progression (GP) is a sequence in which each term is got by multiplying the previous term by a fixed non-zero number r, called the common ratio.
r = any term ÷ the term before it.
The nth term of a GP with first term a is aₙ = a × r^(n − 1).
If r > 1 the terms grow very fast (doubling, tripling). If 0 < r < 1 they shrink, like a bouncing ball.
An AP grows by adding the same amount; a GP grows by multiplying by the same amount.

ex.q: Find the 6th term of the GP 3, 6, 12, 24, ...

topics.rl: Bacteria doubling every hour, a viral video being shared, and money growing with compound interest all follow geometric progressions.

rv.summary: A geometric progression multiplies by a fixed common ratio r each time. aₙ = a × r^(n − 1). GPs grow fast when r > 1 and shrink when 0 < r < 1.
focus: Find the common ratio.
Find the nth term.
Tell a GP from an AP.
remember: AP adds the same amount; GP multiplies by the same amount.
traps: Divide, don't subtract, to find r.
Use r^(n − 1), not rⁿ.
A GP can be decreasing.

topics.ch: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
topics.h: Multiply by −2 each time and the sequence jumps back and forth across zero!
p: Recursive form of a GP: t₁ = a and tₙ = r × tₙ₋₁.
The ratio r can be greater than 1 (growth), between 0 and 1 (shrinking), negative (signs alternate) or even irrational, like √2: 1, √2, 2, 2√2, 4, ...
To test for a GP, check that each term ÷ the previous term gives the same r. To find which term equals k, solve a × rⁿ⁻¹ = k.
Three terms in a GP can be taken as a/r, a, ar. Their product is a³, which quickly gives a; then a sum condition gives r.

ex.q: Three numbers in a GP have product 216 and sum 21. Find them.
st: Take a/r, a, ar: product a³ = 216, so a = 6

topics.rl: A savings scheme that doubles your money every 8 years makes a GP of amounts.

rv.summary: A GP can be written as tₙ = r × tₙ₋₁. Its ratio can be negative or irrational. Three GP terms can be taken as a/r, a, ar, whose product is a³.
focus: Test whether a sequence is a GP.
Find terms with negative or irrational ratios.
Solve three-term GP problems.
traps: Check every ratio, not just the first.
Watch alternating signs.
Middle term from product: a = ∛(product), not product ÷ 3.

topics.ch: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
topics.h: Zoom into a cauliflower floret and you see a tiny cauliflower. That's a fractal!
p: Sierpinski triangle: start with a shaded triangle, join the midpoints and remove the middle one; repeat in each shaded triangle.
After n steps there are 3ⁿ shaded triangles, and the shaded area is (3/4)ⁿ of the original: both are GPs.
Sierpinski carpet: split a square into 9 and remove the centre; repeat. After n steps there are 8ⁿ squares and the area left is (8/9)ⁿ, which gets closer and closer to 0.
Fractals in nature: tree branches, ferns, cauliflower and romanesco, snowflakes, river networks and coastlines repeat similar shapes at smaller scales.

ex.q: After 3 steps of the Sierpinski triangle, how many shaded triangles are there and what fraction of the area is shaded?

topics.rl: Designers use fractal patterns in rangoli, textiles and even mobile phone antennas.

rv.summary: Fractals repeat patterns inside patterns. The Sierpinski triangle has 3ⁿ triangles and (3/4)ⁿ of its area after n steps; the carpet has 8ⁿ squares and (8/9)ⁿ of its area.
focus: Count pieces in fractal steps.
Find remaining area fractions.
Recognise fractals in nature.
remember: Sierpinski triangle after 3 steps: 27 triangles, 27/64 area.
Ferns, trees, cauliflower, coastlines are fractal-like.
traps: 3⁵ is 243, not 3 × 5.
Use 8 for the carpet, not 9.
A fixed fraction kept each step is a GP, not an AP.

topics.ch: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
topics.t: Graphs of GPs and the bouncing ball
topics.h: Drop a ball from 16 m: it bounces to 8, then 4, then 2... Does it ever stop travelling?
p: Plotting (n, tₙ) for a GP gives points on a curve, not a straight line.
With r > 1 the curve shoots up faster and faster; with 0 < r < 1 it drops quickly and then flattens out towards 0.
Bouncing ball: if a ball dropped from height h bounces to r × the height each time, the bounce heights hr, hr², hr³, ... form a GP.

Total distance = first drop + 2 × (sum of bounce heights), because the ball goes up and comes down each bounce. For h = 16, r = 1/2: bounce heights 8 + 4 + 2 + ... approach 16, so the total approaches 16 + 32 = 48 m.

ex.q: A ball is dropped from 16 m and bounces back to half its height each time. How far has it travelled when it hits the ground for the 3rd time?

topics.rl: Sports scientists test cricket and tennis balls by measuring how high they bounce: a fixed bounce ratio gives a GP.

rv.summary: GP graphs are curves: they shoot up when r > 1 and flatten towards 0 when 0 < r < 1. A bouncing ball's heights form a GP; total distance = first drop + 2 × bounce heights.
focus: Describe graphs of GPs.
Find bounce heights.
Find total distance travelled by a bouncing ball.
remember: 16 m, half each bounce: 40 m at the 3rd landing; total approaches 48 m.
10 m, half each bounce: 20 m at the 2nd landing; total approaches 30 m.
traps: Each bounce counts twice: up and down.
Infinitely many bounces can still give a finite distance.
Don't count the first drop twice.

topics.h: 'Mangoes are the best fruit' starts an argument. '7 is a prime number' ends one. Maths loves sentences that are clearly true or clearly false!
p: A proposition (mathematical statement) is a sentence that is either true or false, but not both.
Questions, commands, exclamations and opinions are not propositions: 'Is 5 odd?', 'Shut the door', 'Maths is fun'.
A sentence like x + 3 = 7 is an open sentence: it becomes true or false only once x is known.
Many propositions have the form 'If P, then Q'. P is the hypothesis and Q is the conclusion.
A statement about ALL cases is false if even one counterexample exists. The negation of 'All birds can fly' is 'Some birds cannot fly' (not 'No birds can fly').

ex.q: Is 'Every odd number is prime' a proposition? Is it true?
st: It makes a clear claim that is either true or false, so it is a proposition
Test: 9 is odd, but 9 = 3 × 3 is not prime
One counterexample is enough, so the statement is false
ex.a: It is a proposition, and it is false (counterexample: 9)

topics.rl: Courts, contracts and computer programs all rely on statements that must be clearly true or false. 'If the PIN is correct, then open the account' is a proposition in code!

rv.summary: A proposition is a sentence that is either true or false. Questions, commands and opinions are not propositions; 'If P, then Q' has hypothesis P and conclusion Q. One counterexample disproves an 'all' statement.
focus: Identify propositions.
Find hypothesis and conclusion.
Disprove with a counterexample and negate 'all'.
remember: Negation of 'All birds can fly': 'Some birds cannot fly'.
'Every odd number is prime' is false: 9.
traps: The opposite of 'all' is 'some ... not', not 'none'.
A counterexample must satisfy the 'if' part.
An example that agrees cannot disprove a claim.

topics.h: 'If you are in Jaipur, you are in Rajasthan' is true. But 'If you are in Rajasthan, you are in Jaipur'? Swapping can change everything!
p: The converse of 'If P, then Q' is 'If Q, then P': the hypothesis and conclusion swap places.
A true statement can have a false converse. 'If a number is divisible by 4, it is even' is true, but 6 is even and not divisible by 4.
Some statements and their converses are both true, such as Pythagoras' theorem and its converse.
When a statement and its converse are both true, we can join them with 'if and only if'.
To show a converse is false, give one counterexample: a case where Q is true but P is false.

ex.q: Write the converse of 'If x = 3, then x² = 9' and decide whether it is true.
st: Swap the parts: 'If x² = 9, then x = 3'
Test x = −3: (−3)² = 9, but x is not 3
ex.a: Converse: If x² = 9, then x = 3. It is false (x = −3).

topics.rl: 'If it is a mango, it is a fruit' is true, but 'If it is a fruit, it is a mango' would leave the banana seller very upset!

rv.summary: The converse of 'If P, then Q' is 'If Q, then P'. A true statement can have a false converse; when both are true we say 'if and only if'.
focus: Write converses.
Test converses with counterexamples.
Use 'if and only if' correctly.
remember: 'Divisible by 4 ⇒ even' is true; its converse fails at 6.
'n odd ⇔ n² odd' is true both ways.
traps: Swap the parts; don't add 'not'.
A true statement's converse is not automatically true.
Converses are not always false either.

topics.h: Equal sides give equal angles. Do equal angles give equal sides? Geometry says yes, but it needs a proof!
p: Proposition: if two sides of a triangle are equal, the angles opposite them are equal. Its converse: if two angles are equal, the sides opposite them are equal. Both are true.
Proof idea for the converse: in △ABC with ∠B = ∠C, drop the altitude AD. △ABD ≅ △ACD (AAS: ∠B = ∠C, right angles at D, AD common), so AB = AC.
Congruent triangles always have equal areas, but the converse is false: a triangle with base 6 and height 4 and one with base 8 and height 3 both have area 12 but are not congruent.

Converse of Baudhayana–Pythagoras: if a² + b² = c² in a triangle, the angle opposite c is 90°. Proof: build a right triangle with legs a and b; its hypotenuse is √(a² + b²) = c, so the two triangles are congruent by SSS and the original angle is also 90°.

ex.q: Is a triangle with sides 9, 40 and 41 right-angled? Which angle is 90°?
st: Equal, so by the converse the angle opposite 41 is 90°
ex.a: Yes; the angle opposite the side 41

topics.rl: Carpenters check a right corner with a 3-4-5 rope: that's the converse of Pythagoras in action.

rv.summary: In a triangle, equal sides face equal angles and equal angles face equal sides. Equal area does not imply congruence. The converse of Baudhayana–Pythagoras is true: a² + b² = c² means a right angle opposite c.
focus: Use 'equal angles ⇒ equal sides'.
Prove it with an altitude and AAS.
Test triangles with the Pythagoras converse.
remember: Base 6, height 4 and base 8, height 3: both area 12, not congruent.
traps: Don't use SSS when AB = AC is what you are proving.
Equal area does not mean congruent.
Compare the two smaller squares with the largest.

topics.t: Number converses: both true, both false
topics.h: Count the factors of 16: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Five, an odd number! Only perfect squares do that.
p: A proposition and its converse can both be true: 'If n is a perfect square, it has an odd number of factors' and 'If n has an odd number of factors, it is a perfect square'. Factors pair up as d and n/d, except √n, which pairs with itself.
Both can be false: 'If a number is a multiple of 3, it is even' (3 is a counterexample) and its converse 'If a number is even, it is a multiple of 3' (2 is a counterexample).
The square of a prime p has exactly 3 divisors: 1, p, p². Conversely, a number with exactly 3 divisors is the square of a prime.
A product of two distinct primes pq has exactly 4 divisors: 1, p, q, pq. But the converse fails: 8 has 4 divisors (1, 2, 4, 8) and is not a product of two distinct primes.

ex.q: How many factors does 36 have? Is the count odd?
ex.a: 9, odd, since 36 is a perfect square

topics.rl: Locker puzzles: if students toggle lockers by their factors, only lockers with perfect-square numbers end up open, because they have an odd number of factors.

rv.summary: Some statements and converses are both true (perfect squares ⇔ odd number of factors); some are both false. p² has exactly 3 divisors; pq has 4, but having 4 divisors does not mean pq.
focus: Count factors using pairs.
Test statements and converses about divisors.
Find counterexamples.
remember: 36 has 9 factors (odd) because 6 × 6 pairs with itself.
Exactly 3 divisors ⇔ square of a prime.
8 and 27 have 4 divisors but are not pq.
traps: Count 1 and the number itself as factors.
'Odd number of factors' is not 'odd number'.
Test both directions separately.

topics.h: Two sticks crossing at their midpoints make a parallelogram. Make the sticks equal and you get a rectangle!
p: Parallel lines: if two lines are parallel, corresponding angles made by a transversal are equal; and conversely, equal corresponding angles mean the lines are parallel. Both directions are true.
'If a quadrilateral is a square, all its angles are equal' is true, but the converse fails: a rectangle has all angles equal and need not be a square.

In △ABC let the bisectors of ∠B and ∠C meet at the incentre I and cut AC at E and AB at F. 'If AB = AC, then IE = IF' is true: ∠B = ∠C gives ∠IBC = ∠ICB, so IB = IC, and then △IBF ≅ △ICE (ASA). Its converse 'If IE = IF, then AB = AC' is false: in a triangle with ∠A = 60°, ∠B = 90°, ∠C = 30°, IE = IF but AB ≠ AC.

Two sticks as diagonals joined at their midpoints always give a parallelogram; equal sticks give a rectangle; equal sticks crossing at right angles give a square. But 'equal diagonals ⇒ rectangle' fails if the diagonals do not bisect each other (an isosceles trapezium).

ex.q: Write the converse of 'If a quadrilateral is a rectangle, its diagonals are equal' and test it.
st: Converse: If a quadrilateral has equal diagonals, it is a rectangle
An isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals but is not a rectangle

topics.rl: Kite-makers use two crossing sticks: equal sticks crossing at their middles give a rectangular frame.

rv.summary: Corresponding angles equal ⇔ lines parallel: both directions are true. Other converses fail: equal angles don't make a square, equal diagonals don't make a rectangle, and IE = IF doesn't force AB = AC.
focus: Test converses about lines and quadrilaterals.
Use diagonals to classify quadrilaterals.
Find geometric counterexamples.
remember: Rectangle: all angles equal but not a square.
Equal diagonals bisecting each other → rectangle; plus perpendicular → square.
Isosceles trapezium: equal diagonals, not a rectangle.
traps: Writing the inverse is not writing the converse.
Equal diagonals that bisect each other give a rectangle, not a rhombus.
Nearly equal angles do not make lines parallel.

topics.t: Equations, squares and products: which way works?
topics.h: If x = y, then x² = y². But if x² = y², is x = y? Try x = −4 and y = 4!
p: If a = b, then a + c = b + c (adding the same number keeps equality). The converse, cancellation, is also true: if a + c = b + c, then a = b.
If x = y, then x² = y² is true, but the converse is false: (−3)² = 3² while −3 ≠ 3.
If x = y, then x³ = y³, and the converse is also true for real numbers: cubes keep the sign, so equal cubes mean equal numbers.
The product of two perfect squares is a perfect square: a² × b² = (ab)². The converse fails: 2 × 8 = 16 is a perfect square, but 2 and 8 are not.

ex.q: Is the converse of 'If x = y then x³ = y³' true? Check with x³ = −27.
st: No other real number cubes to −27
So x³ = y³ gives x = y: converse true

topics.rl: Balancing scales: add the same weight to both pans and they stay balanced; that is equality preserved by addition.

rv.summary: Adding the same number keeps equality and cancellation reverses it. x = y ⇒ x² = y² has a false converse, but x = y ⇔ x³ = y³. A product of squares is a square, but not conversely.
focus: Decide which operations work in both directions.
Find counterexamples for squares and products.
Solve x² = k with both roots.
remember: Cubes keep the sign: equal cubes mean equal numbers.
a² × b² = (ab)²; 2 × 8 = 16 shows the converse fails.
traps: Don't forget the negative root.
Squaring does not work both ways.
Product of squares is not about sums.

topics.h: Every number divisible by 24 is divisible by 6. Is every number divisible by 6 divisible by 24? Try 12!
p: 'If n is divisible by 24, then n is divisible by 4 and by 6' is true. Its converse is false: 12 is divisible by 4 and 6 but not by 24 (because LCM(4, 6) = 12, not 24).
'n is divisible by 60 if and only if it is divisible by 5 and by 12' is true both ways, because 5 and 12 share no factor and LCM(5, 12) = 60.
'Divisible by 8 ⇒ divisible by 2 and 4' is true; the converse fails: 4 and 12 are divisible by 2 and 4 but not by 8.
Test for 8: a number is divisible by 8 if and only if the number formed by its last three digits is, because 1000 = 8 × 125.
Test for 3: if the digit sum is divisible by 3 the number is, and conversely; both directions are true.

ex.q: Is 7,35,136 divisible by 8? Use the last three digits.

topics.rl: Shopkeepers packing items in boxes of 8 can check if a big order fits exactly using the last-three-digits test.

rv.summary: Divisible by 24 ⇒ divisible by 4 and 6, but not conversely, since LCM(4, 6) = 12. Divisible by 5 and 12 ⇔ divisible by 60. The tests for 8 (last three digits) and 3 (digit sum) work both ways.
focus: Use LCMs to decide divisibility converses.
Apply the tests for 8 and 3.
Find divisibility counterexamples.
remember: LCM(4, 6) = 12, so 12 or 36 break the converse.
1000 = 8 × 125, so check the last three digits: 7,35,136 → 136 = 8 × 17.
traps: Being divisible by two numbers means divisible by their LCM, not their product.
Use the last three digits for 8, not the last digit.
Not every converse fails.

topics.h: n² + n + 11 gives 13, 17, 23, 31, 41, ... all primes! Keep going and it breaks at n = 10.
p: Any common factor of n and n + 3 must divide their difference 3, so it is 1 or 3.
So: if n and n + 3 have no common factor (other than 1), then n is not a multiple of 3. Conversely, if n is not a multiple of 3, then n and n + 3 share no factor. Both directions are true.
Formulas that seem to give only primes can fail: 4n² + 1 gives 5, 17, 37, then 65 = 5 × 13 at n = 4.
n² + n + 11 fails at n = 10: 121 = 11². 2ⁿ − 1 with n prime fails at n = 11: 2047 = 23 × 89. 2ⁿ + 1 fails at n = 3: 9.
Many examples never prove a statement, but one counterexample disproves it.

ex.q: Does n² + n + 11 always give a prime? Test n = 10.
st: Not prime, so the claim is false

topics.rl: Computer security uses huge primes, so mathematicians must be careful: a formula that 'usually' gives primes is not good enough.

rv.summary: Common factors of n and n + 3 must divide 3. Formulas that seem to give only primes can fail, so examples never prove a pattern but one counterexample disproves it.
focus: Use differences to find common factors.
Test prime-making formulas.
Explain why examples are not proof.
remember: n and n + 3 share no factor ⇔ n not a multiple of 3.
4n² + 1 fails at n = 4 (65); n² + n + 11 fails at n = 10 (121).
traps: Don't stop checking too early.
2ᵖ − 1 is not always prime for prime p.
Many examples are not a proof.

topics.h: Kabir checked 100 examples and says his rule always works. A mathematician smiles: 'Show me a proof that covers ALL numbers, even the ones you didn't try!'
p: A proof is a chain of logical steps that shows a statement is true in every case, starting from facts already accepted.
Axioms are basic facts accepted without proof. Theorems are statements that have been proved. A conjecture is believed true but not yet proved.
Checking examples can suggest a pattern, but it can never prove a statement about all numbers.
Use algebra to cover all cases: an even number is 2m and an odd number is 2m + 1, for some integer m.
To disprove a statement about all cases, one counterexample is enough.

ex.q: Prove that the sum of two odd numbers is always even.
st: Let the odd numbers be 2m + 1 and 2n + 1, where m and n are integers
This is 2 times an integer, so it is even, whatever m and n are
ex.a: The sum is 2(m + n + 1), which is always even.

topics.rl: Online banking is safe because of number facts that mathematicians have proved. Engineers rely on proved results, not lucky guesses, to make bridges stand.

rv.summary: A proof is a chain of logical steps showing a statement is true in every case. Axioms are accepted, theorems are proved and conjectures are unproved. Algebra (2m, 2m + 1) covers all cases.
focus: Prove simple number facts with algebra.
Tell axioms, theorems and conjectures apart.
Know that one counterexample disproves.
remember: Goldbach's conjecture is checked but not proved.
traps: Checking examples is not a proof.
m + 1 is not always odd.
Checking many cases does not make a conjecture a theorem.

topics.h: Your cricket team's scores were 12, 15, 9 and 120. Was the team's 'typical' score really 39? Different averages tell different stories!
p: Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values.
For a frequency table: mean = Σ(f × x) ÷ Σf, where x is each value and f its frequency.
Median: arrange the data in order. For an odd count it is the middle value; for an even count it is the mean of the two middle values.
Mode is the value that occurs most often.
One very large or very small value (an outlier) pulls the mean a lot but hardly changes the median.

ex.q: Find the mean and median of 4, 9, 2, 7, 3, 11.

topics.rl: News reports often give the median house price or median salary, because a few very rich people would push the mean up a lot.

rv.summary: Mean = sum ÷ count; median is the middle value of ordered data; mode is the most frequent value. Outliers pull the mean but barely move the median.
focus: Find mean, median and mode.
Find the mean from a frequency table.
Choose the right average when there are outliers.
remember: Mean from a table = Σ(f × x) ÷ Σf.
Even count: median = mean of the two middle values.
traps: Arrange the data before finding the median.
Don't just average the values; use the frequencies.
The mean is not always the best average.

topics.h: Section A averages 80 and Section B averages 60. Is the whole class average 70? Only if the sections are the same size!
p: Combined average = total of all values ÷ total count. It is NOT simply the mean of the group averages.
For two groups: n values with average a and m values with average b give combined average (na + mb)/(n + m). For three groups add a third term on top and a third count below.
Averaging the averages works only when the groups are the same size.

Uses: class sections of different sizes, rainfall over months of different lengths (weight by days), average price of shares bought in lots, and a cricket team's run rate over spells of different lengths.

ex.q: Section A has 30 students averaging 80; Section B has 20 averaging 60. Find the combined average.

topics.rl: A cricket team's overall run rate weights each spell by the number of overs, which is exactly a combined average.

rv.summary: A combined average is total of all values ÷ total count, not the mean of the group averages, unless the groups are the same size.
focus: Find combined averages of groups.
Find average prices and run rates.
Update a mean when a value is added.
traps: Don't average the averages for unequal groups.
Weight months by days.
The combined average is closer to the larger group's average.

topics.h: Mix a weak sherbet and a strong one: the result is somewhere in between, but where?
p: Concentration of a mixture = total amount of the substance ÷ total quantity of mixture (often as a %).
Mixing two solutions: add up the substance in each and divide by the total volume. The result is a weighted average of the two strengths.
The result lies between the two strengths, closer to the strength of the larger quantity.
Dilution: adding x litres of water keeps the substance the same but increases the volume. Solve substance ÷ (old volume + x) = target.

ex.q: Mix 2 L of 10% sugar syrup with 3 L of 20% syrup. Find the strength of the mixture.

topics.rl: Making nimbu-pani or diluting a juice concentrate at home is exactly this kind of mixture problem.

rv.summary: Concentration = substance ÷ total mixture. Mixing gives a weighted average strength between the two, closer to the larger quantity. Adding water keeps the substance fixed.
focus: Find concentrations.
Find the strength of a mixture.
Solve dilution problems.
remember: Equal volumes: simple average of strengths.
traps: Don't add or average percentages directly for unequal volumes.
The substance amount stays the same when diluting.
Divide by the total mixture, not by the water.

topics.t: Gold purity, mean depth and impossible targets
topics.h: Melt a 22-karat ring and an 18-karat chain together. How pure is the new gold?
p: Gold purity is measured in karats (24 karat = pure) or, in old Indian texts, in varna (16 varna = pure).
Purity of combined gold = Σ(weight × purity) ÷ Σ weights, a weighted mean. Sridharacharya’s Patiganita (about 750 CE) has problems on melting together gold of different varna (16 varna = 24 karat).

Pits and pools dug to different depths appear in Brahmagupta’s Brahmasphutasiddhanta and in Prithudakasvami’s commentary on it (about 864 CE): the mean depth weights each section’s depth by its length, and volume = mean depth × length × width.
If the algebra gives a negative quantity (like −2 L of water), the target is impossible. You cannot reach 25% by mixing 10% and 20%, or make a solution stronger just by adding water.

ex.q: 10 g of 22-karat gold is melted with 5 g of 16-karat gold. Find the purity of the alloy.

topics.rl: Jewellers in India stamp gold with its karat; mixing old jewellery for remaking uses this weighted mean.

rv.summary: Gold purity of an alloy is a weighted mean of purities. Mean depth weights each depth by its length. A negative answer in mixture problems means the target is impossible.
focus: Find the purity of melted gold.
Find mean depth and volume of pits.
Recognise impossible mixture targets.
remember: 10 g of 22 K + 5 g of 16 K → 20 K.
Sridharacharya (Patiganita, c. 750 CE); Brahmagupta and Prithudakasvami on pits.
traps: A mixture cannot be stronger than its strongest part.
Weight depths by length; don't average them simply.
A negative amount of water cannot be added.

topics.h: Your final exam counts more than the class test? That's a weighted average with custom weights!
p: Weights can show importance, not just size: if Term 1, Term 2 and Final are weighted 3 : 2 : 5, the final counts most.
Weighted average = Σ(weight × score) ÷ Σ weights.
If tests have different maximum marks, first convert each to a percentage (marks ÷ maximum × 100), then apply the weights.
Star ratings: from a table of how many people gave 5★, 4★, ..., the average rating = Σ(stars × number) ÷ total people.
To design your own rating scheme (say for choosing a school trip), choose criteria, give each a weight that shows its importance, and compute the weighted score for each option.

ex.q: Term 1: 70%, Term 2: 80%, Final: 90%, weighted 3 : 2 : 5. Find the overall score.

topics.rl: Food-delivery apps show a restaurant's star rating as a weighted average of all customers' ratings.

rv.summary: Weights can show importance. Weighted average = Σ(weight × score) ÷ Σ weights. Convert marks to percentages first when maximums differ.
focus: Compute weighted scores.
Convert marks to percentages before weighting.
Find average star ratings.
traps: Divide by the sum of weights, not the number of scores.
Don't weight raw marks with different maximums.
Count people when averaging star ratings.

topics.t: How weights behave, and overall profit
topics.h: Double every weight and nothing changes! Add the same number to every weight and the scores start to look equal.
p: Multiplying all weights by the same number (like doubling them) leaves the weighted average unchanged: weights 1 : 3 and 2 : 6 give the same result.
Adding the same constant to every weight makes the weights more nearly equal, so the weighted mean moves towards the ordinary (simple) mean.
Overall profit % on several items = total profit ÷ total cost × 100. It is a weighted average of the individual profit rates, weighted by cost.

ex.q: Scores 50 and 90 with weights 1 and 3. Find the weighted mean, then add 10 to each weight.
st: Simple mean is 70; the new mean moved towards it

topics.rl: A shopkeeper selling many items at different profit rates finds the shop's overall profit rate this way.

rv.summary: Multiplying all weights by the same number leaves a weighted average unchanged; adding the same constant to every weight moves it towards the simple mean. Overall profit % = total profit ÷ total cost.
focus: Predict how changing weights affects the average.
Find overall profit percentage.
Explain why it is a weighted average.
remember: Weights 1 : 3 and 2 : 6 give the same result.
traps: Don't take the simple mean of profit rates.
Scaling weights does not scale the answer.
Equal weights give the ordinary mean, not the median.

topics.h: A picture is worth a thousand numbers! But a sneaky graph can also trick your eyes. Let's learn to read graphs like a detective.
p: Bar graphs show separate categories with bars of equal width and equal gaps between them.
A histogram shows grouped (continuous) data. The bars touch each other because the classes have no gaps.
If the classes in a histogram have unequal widths, adjust the heights so that the area of each bar is proportional to its frequency.
A frequency polygon is made by joining the mid-points (class marks) of the tops of the histogram bars with straight lines.
Line graphs show change over time. Always check the scale: an axis that does not start at 0 can make small differences look huge.

ex.q: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–40 have frequencies 6, 9 and 12. What heights should the histogram bars have if a width of 10 is the standard?
st: 0–10 and 10–20 have width 10, so heights stay 6 and 9
20–40 has width 20, twice the standard width

topics.rl: Weather reports use line graphs for temperature, election coverage uses bar graphs, and doctors use histograms of patients' ages.

rv.summary: Bar graphs show categories; histograms show grouped data with touching bars; frequency polygons join class marks; line graphs show change over time. Watch for misleading scales.
focus: Choose the right graph.
Read values and differences from graphs.
Adjust histogram heights for unequal classes.
remember: Histogram bars touch because classes are continuous.
Unequal class: adjusted height = frequency × standard width ÷ class width.
Frequency polygon points at class marks.
traps: An axis not starting at 0 can mislead.
Don't use raw frequency as height for a wider class.
A histogram is not just bars drawn closer.

topics.h: One chart, three questions: which class won, what the total was, and what share each part had. Different charts answer different ones!
p: A clustered column chart puts bars for each group side by side within each category, so you can compare groups category by category.
A stacked bar chart piles the parts on top of each other: the full bar shows the total and each segment shows a part.
A 100% stacked bar chart makes every bar the same height (100%); each segment shows that part's share of its own total.

ex.q: Class 9A: 18 girls, 12 boys. Class 9B: 15 girls, 25 boys. Describe the stacked and 100% stacked bars.
ex.a: Stacked bars show totals 30 and 40; 100% bars show shares 60/40 and 37.5/62.5

topics.rl: News channels show election vote shares and cricket score breakdowns as stacked bars.

rv.summary: Clustered columns compare groups side by side; stacked bars show totals and parts; 100% stacked bars show each part's share of its own total.
focus: Choose clustered, stacked or 100% stacked charts.
Read totals and parts.
Find shares as percentages.
remember: Stacked bar total = sum of segments.
100% bars all reach the same height.
traps: 100% bars do not show actual numbers.
Don't stack quantities that are not parts of one total.
Use the right total when finding a share.

topics.h: Two 100% bars look identical. Does that mean the two classes are the same size? Not at all!
p: Percentage of a part = part ÷ total × 100. Going back: part = percentage × total ÷ 100.
Equal 100% bars do not mean equal totals: 6 of 10 and 60 of 100 both show 60%.
From a stacked chart you can always make a 100% chart (you know the totals), but from a 100% chart alone you cannot get back the actual numbers.
Only draw conclusions the chart supports: a 100% chart tells you shares, not how many. A stacked chart tells you totals and parts, but not the reasons behind them.

ex.q: In a 100% stacked chart, 35% of School P's students and 35% of School Q's students cycle to school. P has 400 students and Q has 1200. How many cycle in each?

topics.rl: Advertisements often show '90% of users prefer...' without saying how many users were asked; always check the total.

rv.summary: Percentage of a part = part ÷ total × 100, and part = % × total ÷ 100. Equal shares can hide very different totals, so only draw conclusions the chart supports.
focus: Convert between parts and percentages.
Find a total from a percentage.
Judge which conclusions a chart supports.
remember: A stacked chart can make a 100% chart, but not the other way round.
traps: Don't read shares as counts.
Divide, don't multiply, to find the total.
Charts don't show reasons or the future.

topics.t: Time-use charts and a better pie
topics.h: Where do your 24 hours go? A 100% bar of your day might surprise you!
p: A time-use chart shows the share of a 24-hour day spent on each activity: 8 hours of sleep is 8/24 = 33⅓%. Smart watches show similar bars for body states like deep sleep, light sleep and active time.
Real data charts (species counts by group, wickets by type of bowler, objects orbiting the Earth by type) are read the same way: find the total, the parts and the shares.
A 100% stacked bar can replace a pie chart: both show parts of a whole.
Comparing shares across several 100% bars side by side is easier than comparing angles in several pie charts.
A family can track monthly spending (food, rent, travel, savings) as 100% bars, one per month, to see how shares change.

ex.q: A student's day: sleep 8 h, school 7 h, study 3 h, play 2 h, other 4 h. Find each share.

topics.rl: Fitness bands use stacked bars to show how your night's sleep splits into deep, light and REM sleep.

rv.summary: Time-use and real-data charts show shares of a whole, like hours of a 24-hour day. A set of 100% stacked bars is often clearer than several pie charts.
focus: Find shares of a day or a total.
Read real-data charts.
Compare shares over time with 100% bars.
traps: Divide by 24 for a day, not 100.
A bigger amount is not always a bigger share.
Use the right total (e.g. 8 hours of sleep, not 24).

topics.h: Your class has 40 marks scribbled on a page. In two minutes, can you say how many scored above 30? Organise the data and you can!
p: Data are facts or numbers collected for a purpose. Data you collect yourself are primary data; data taken from records or other sources are secondary data.
Raw data are data not yet arranged. Range = highest value − lowest value.
A frequency table shows how often each value (or group of values) occurs. Tally marks help you count.
For large data, use classes like 10–20, 20–30. Class width = upper limit − lower limit; class mark = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2.
In classes such as 10–20 and 20–30, a value of exactly 20 is counted in 20–30 (the lower limit is included).

ex.q: Marks of 12 students (out of 20): 12, 15, 8, 18, 15, 11, 9, 15, 17, 12, 6, 14. Make a frequency table with classes 5–10, 10–15, 15–20.

topics.rl: The Census of India collects data from crores of households and organises it into tables so the government can plan schools, roads and hospitals.

rv.summary: Data can be primary (collected yourself) or secondary. Organise raw data with frequency tables and classes; range = highest − lowest.
focus: Find range, class width and class mark.
Make frequency tables with tallies and classes.
Place boundary values correctly.
remember: Class width = upper − lower; class mark = (lower + upper) ÷ 2.
In 10–20, 20–30, a value of 20 goes in 20–30.
traps: Don't confuse class width with class mark.
Count a boundary value only once, in the upper class.
Total surveyed = sum of frequencies, not the largest one.

topics.h: Add 4,786 and 3,459 by counting dots? You'd still be counting at dinner time! Column addition finishes in seconds.
p: Counting dots works for tiny numbers but becomes impossibly slow as numbers grow; column addition stays fast because the work depends on the number of digits, not the size of the number.
Column addition: line the numbers up by place value, add the units first, write the units digit of the sum and carry any ten to the next column, move left, and write the final carry at the end.
It works because of place value: 10 units make 1 ten, 10 tens make 1 hundred, and so on. Carrying is regrouping.
Adding two 4-digit numbers needs just 4 column steps, while counting dots would need thousands of counts.

ex.q: Add 4786 + 3459 by columns.

topics.rl: Shopkeepers adding a bill in a notebook use the same column method you learnt in primary school.

rv.summary: Column addition lines numbers up by place value, adds from the units leftwards and carries tens. Its work depends on the number of digits, so it is far faster than counting.
focus: Add multi-digit numbers by columns.
Explain carrying as regrouping.
Compare efficiency with counting.
remember: 10 units = 1 ten: that is the carry.
traps: Don't forget to add the carry.
Don't start from the left.
Write the final carry at the end.

topics.h: A recipe for chai, the steps for long division and the instructions inside your phone's map app have something in common: they are all algorithms!
p: An algorithm is a finite list of clear, step-by-step instructions that solves a problem or completes a task.
A good algorithm has an input (what you start with), an output (the result), and steps that are precise, so anyone following them gets the same result.
It must stop after a finite number of steps.
The order of steps matters: 'add 3, then double' is not the same as 'double, then add 3'.
Algorithms can repeat steps (loops) and make choices (if this, then do that).

ex.q: Algorithm: start with a number. If it is even, halve it; if it is odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Stop when you reach 1. Start with 6. How many steps until you reach 1?

topics.rl: Railway ticket booking, ATM cash withdrawal and traffic signals all run on algorithms written by programmers.

rv.summary: An algorithm is a finite list of clear, step-by-step instructions with an input and an output. Steps must be precise, the order matters, and it may repeat or make choices.
focus: Recognise a good algorithm.
Identify inputs and outputs.
Trace an algorithm step by step.
remember: Halve if even, 3n + 1 if odd, from 6: 8 steps to 1.
traps: Vague steps like 'a little' are not allowed.
Count steps (arrows), not numbers in the chain.
Don't mix up input and output.
