topics.h: When you add two numbers, can a carry ever be 2? Try your hardest with 9s: it can't!
p: When adding two numbers, a column sum is at most 9 + 9 + 1 = 19, so the carry is never more than 1. (With three or more numbers, bigger carries are possible.)
If the numbers have different lengths, treat missing digits as 0: 3456 + 78 is 3456 + 0078.
The written method often skips steps like 'write a 0' or 'no carry'; a full algorithm states them clearly.
For decimals, line up the decimal points (fill missing places with 0), add as usual, and put the point in the same column.
topics.rl: Adding ₹149.50 and ₹38.75 at a stationery shop is decimal column addition.

rv.summary: Adding two numbers, a column total is at most 19, so the carry is at most 1. Treat missing digits as 0, and line up decimal points when adding decimals.
focus: Know the largest possible carry.
Add numbers of different lengths.
Add decimals and money.
remember: Two numbers: max column 9 + 9 + 1 = 19; three numbers: carry up to 2.
traps: Line up from the right, not the left.
Line up the decimal points.
Don't forget the carry from paise.

topics.h: Over 2000 years ago Euclid found a way to get the HCF of two huge numbers without listing a single factor. It is still used in every computer today!
p: Division algorithm: for whole numbers a and b > 0, a = b × q + r with 0 ≤ r < b.

Euclid's algorithm for HCF(a, b): divide the larger by the smaller, then replace the pair by (smaller, remainder). Repeat until the remainder is 0; the last non-zero remainder (the last divisor) is the HCF.
LCM(a, b) = a × b ÷ HCF(a, b).
To test if n is prime, you only need to try dividing by primes up to √n.
The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds all primes up to a limit by crossing out multiples of 2, 3, 5, 7, ... Binary search finds an item in a sorted list by halving the search area each time.

ex.q: Use Euclid's algorithm to find HCF(252, 105).
st: The remainder is 0, so the HCF is the last divisor, 21

topics.rl: Online payments are kept safe by codes that use Euclid's algorithm and prime numbers. Searching a contact on your phone uses ideas like binary search.

rv.summary: Famous algorithms: division a = bq + r, Euclid's HCF algorithm, LCM = ab ÷ HCF, trial division up to √n, the Sieve of Eratosthenes and binary search.
focus: Use Euclid's algorithm for HCF.
Find LCM from HCF.
Use the sieve and binary search.
remember: LCM(a, b) = a × b ÷ HCF(a, b).
1 to 100 by halving: at most 7 guesses.
traps: The HCF is the last divisor, not the first remainder.
Test primes only up to √n.
Don't forget to divide by the HCF for the LCM.

topics.h: Before a robot vacuum cleans your room, someone had to think like a computer: break the job into tiny steps, repeat them and make decisions. That is algorithmic thinking!
p: Decomposition: break a big problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve.
Loops repeat a set of steps, either a fixed number of times or while a condition is true.
Conditions (if... else...) let an algorithm choose between different steps.
Flowcharts show algorithms as pictures: ovals for start and stop, rectangles for actions, diamonds for decisions (yes/no questions), and arrows for the order.
Efficiency: different algorithms can solve the same problem in very different numbers of steps. Tracing an algorithm step by step helps you find and fix bugs.

ex.q: Trace this algorithm: set x = 1. While x is less than 50, replace x by 3 × x. Output x.
st: 81 is not less than 50, so stop and output 81

topics.rl: Indian Railways' route planning, Diwali light patterns on a timer and video games all use loops and conditions.

rv.summary: Algorithmic thinking uses decomposition, loops and conditions. Flowcharts show steps with ovals, rectangles and diamonds. Efficient algorithms need fewer steps.
focus: Read and draw flowcharts.
Trace loops and conditions.
Compare the efficiency of methods.
remember: Oval: start/stop; rectangle: action; diamond: decision.
traps: '33 or more' includes 33.
Check the loop condition one more time before stopping.
Nested loops multiply counts, not add.

topics.h: To find all divisors of 36, do you really need to test all 36 numbers? Only up to 6!
p: divisors(n): for each j from 1 to n, check whether j divides n; if yes, add j to a list. Output the list.
The work grows with n: for n = 1000 the simple method checks 1000 numbers.
Divisors come in pairs j and n/j. One of each pair is at most √n, so you only need to check j with j × j ≤ n, and add both j and n/j.

ex.q: Use the pair method to find the divisors of 60.
st: Check j with j² ≤ 60: j = 1 to 7

topics.rl: Packing 60 laddoos into equal boxes? Each divisor of 60 is a possible box size.

rv.summary: divisors(n) checks every j from 1 to n. Since divisors pair as j and n/j, checking up to √n is enough.
focus: List divisors with the simple and pair methods.
Count divisors.
Estimate how work grows with n.
traps: Count a self-paired divisor (like 10 for 100) once.
Include 1 and n.
The simple method's work grows with n, not digits.

topics.h: Write the divisors of 24 and of 36, find what they share, pick the biggest. That's the first gcd algorithm!
p: Step 1: list divisors(m). Step 2: list divisors(n). Step 3: build the list of common divisors (numbers in both lists). Step 4: report the largest.
If the lists are sorted from smallest to largest, the gcd is the last element of the common list.
Naming intermediate results (like Dm, Dn and C) makes an algorithm clear; a list is a simple data structure for storing many values in order.

ex.q: Find gcd(18, 30) with the first algorithm.

topics.rl: Cutting two ribbons of 18 cm and 30 cm into equal pieces of the largest possible length uses the gcd: 6 cm.

rv.summary: First gcd algorithm: list divisors of m and n, find the common ones, and take the largest (the last in a sorted list). Lists and named results make algorithms clear.
focus: Find gcd by listing divisors.
Find common divisors.
Use gcd in real problems.
remember: Sorted common list: gcd is the last element.
Ropes 28 m and 42 m → pieces of 14 m.
traps: The first element is the smallest, not the gcd.
Include only divisors of both numbers.
Don't give the LCM.

topics.t: Working with sorted lists and the LCM
topics.h: Two sorted lists of guests: who is on the first list but not the second? Walk down both lists together!
p: To find elements of sorted list A that are not in sorted list B, walk through both with a pointer each: if the A item is smaller, it is missing from B (record it); if equal, move both; if the B item is smaller, move B's pointer.
Walking down sorted lists once is much faster than checking every element of A against every element of B.
LCM by multiples: list the multiples of the larger number (n, 2n, 3n, ...) and stop at the first one divisible by the smaller number.
Example: LCM(6, 8): multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24; 24 is divisible by 6, so LCM = 24.

ex.q: A = 2, 5, 8, 11, 14 and B = 1, 5, 9, 11, 13. Which elements of A are not in B?
st: Compare 2 with 1: move B. 2 vs 5: 2 smaller, record 2
14 vs 13: move B; B finished, record 14

topics.rl: Buses leaving every 12 and 18 minutes meet again after LCM(12, 18) = 36 minutes.

rv.summary: Walking two sorted lists with pointers finds elements missing from one list quickly. LCM by multiples: list multiples of the larger number until one is divisible by the smaller.
focus: Compare sorted lists with pointers.
Find LCM by listing multiples.
Solve flashing-light style LCM problems.
remember: Diyas every 4 s and 6 s flash together every 12 s.
traps: Don't just multiply the numbers for the LCM.
Move the pointer of the smaller item.
Don't compare every pair.

topics.h: Why list all divisors of both numbers when you could just count down and stop at the first one that works?
p: Improvement 1: check j = 1, 2, ..., min(m, n) only, and keep just the most recent j that divides both. At the end it is the gcd. No lists needed.
Improvement 2: search downwards from min(m, n) and stop at the first j that divides both; that j is the gcd.
Each refinement must still be correct: we must explain why it always gives the gcd (for example, no common divisor can exceed the smaller number).

Efficiency: these methods need up to min(m, n) checks, which grows with the VALUE of the numbers. For a 12-digit number that could be a trillion checks, while Euclid's method grows only with the number of DIGITS.

ex.q: Find gcd(84, 36) by counting down from min(84, 36).

topics.rl: Programmers improve slow apps the same way: first make it work, then make it faster while keeping it correct.

rv.summary: Improved gcd methods check j up to min(m, n), keeping only the latest common divisor, or count down and stop at the first. Each change must be proved correct, and these methods are slow for huge numbers.
focus: Use count-up and count-down gcd methods.
Count the checks needed.
Explain why efficiency depends on value or digits.
remember: No common divisor exceeds min(m, n).
traps: Count the starting number when counting checks.
Speed is no use if the answer can be wrong.
Work growing with value is much slower than with digits.

topics.h: gcd(1000, 3) by subtracting 3 again and again takes over 300 steps. By division it takes just 2!
p: Subtraction method: gcd(m, n) = gcd(m − n, n) for m > n. Swap when m < n. Stop when one number becomes 0, since gcd(m, 0) = m.
When the numbers are very different, subtraction can take very many steps (like 1000 and 3).

Division method (Aryabhata used this repeated division in the kuttaka method of his Aryabhatiya, 499 CE, so it is called Aryabhata’s division algorithm): gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, m mod n), where m mod n is the remainder. Laid out like repeated long division: divide, then divide the divisor by the remainder, and so on, until the remainder is 0.
Why it works: if d divides m and n, it divides m − qn = remainder; and if d divides n and the remainder, it divides qn + remainder = m. So the common divisors (and the gcd) do not change.
The number of division steps grows with the number of digits, so it is very fast: it never needs more than about 5 times the number of digits of the smaller number.

ex.q: Find gcd(1071, 462) by the division method.

topics.rl: Encryption on your phone uses the division gcd algorithm many times a second because it is so fast.

rv.summary: gcd(m, n) = gcd(m − n, n) by subtraction, and gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, m mod n) by Aryabhata's division algorithm. The division method needs few steps, growing with the number of digits.
focus: Use subtraction and division methods for gcd.
Find m mod n.
Explain why the method works.
traps: Stop only when a remainder is 0.
The answer is the last non-zero remainder, not a quotient.
Subtraction can be very slow.

topics.h: The word 'algorithm' comes from a person's name. A Baghdad scholar who wrote about Indian numerals!
p: Al-Khwarizmi (9th century, Baghdad) wrote a book explaining the Indian decimal numerals and methods of calculating with them. Its Latin title began 'Algoritmi ...', and from his name came the word algorithm.
A prime number has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. So 1 is not prime (one divisor) and 4 is not prime (three divisors).
prime(n): compute divisors(n); if the list has exactly 2 elements, n is prime, otherwise it is not.
primedivisors(n): go through divisors(n) and keep only those d for which prime(d) is true. For 60: 2, 3, 5.

ex.q: Use prime(n) to test 91.

topics.rl: Your phone's security uses huge primes found by prime-testing algorithms far faster than listing divisors.

rv.summary: The word algorithm comes from Al-Khwarizmi, who explained Indian decimal numerals. A prime has exactly two divisors; prime(n) checks the length of divisors(n), and primedivisors(n) keeps the prime ones.
focus: Know the history of the word algorithm.
Test primality by counting divisors.
Find prime divisors.
remember: 91 = 7 × 13 is not prime; prime divisors of 60: 2, 3, 5.
traps: 1 is not a prime divisor.
Odd numbers are not automatically prime.
Don't include composite divisors like 9 or 15.

topics.t: Prime factorisation and gcd from factors
topics.h: Every whole number above 1 is built from prime bricks. Record each brick and how many times it's used!
p: Prime factorisation algorithm: start with the smallest prime 2; while it divides n, divide and count; then move to the next prime. Record pairs (prime, power).
Example: 360 → divide by 2 three times (45), by 3 twice (5), by 5 once (1). Pairs: (2, 3), (3, 2), (5, 1), so 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
gcd from factorisations: take each prime common to both numbers with the smaller of its two powers, and multiply.
Example: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5 and 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. Common primes 2 and 3: gcd = 2² × 3¹ = 12.

ex.q: Find gcd(180, 252) from prime factorisations.

topics.rl: Cryptographers depend on the fact that factorising very large numbers is extremely slow, even though multiplying primes is easy.

rv.summary: Prime factorisation divides by each prime as many times as possible and records (prime, power) pairs. The gcd is the product of common primes with their smaller powers.
focus: Find prime factorisations.
Write (prime, power) pairs.
Find gcd from factorisations.
traps: Don't leave composite factors like 14 or 21.
Use the smaller power for gcd (larger is for LCM).
No common prime → gcd 1, not 0.

topics.t: Tiling and the exact meaning of a quadrilateral
topics.h: Floor tiles fit with no gaps and no overlaps. Which four-sided shapes can do that? Every parallelogram, for a start!
p: A tiling covers the plane with copies of a shape with no gaps and no overlaps.
Any parallelogram tiles the plane: two sets of equally spaced parallel lines (like sticks pinned in a grid) make rows of identical parallelograms.
A quadrilateral ABCD is made from four points A, B, C, D (no three on a line) and the four segments AB, BC, CD, DA, where the segments meet only at their ends.
A, B, C, D are vertices; AB, BC, CD, DA are sides; AC and BD are diagonals. AB and BC are adjacent sides; AB and CD are opposite sides; A and C are opposite vertices; ∠A and ∠C are opposite angles.
Name a quadrilateral by going round it in order: ABCD, BCDA or DCBA all name the same one, but ABDC is a different figure.

ex.q: For quadrilateral PQRS, list the diagonals, a pair of opposite sides and the angle opposite ∠Q.
st: Diagonals join opposite vertices: PR and QS
Opposite sides: PQ and RS (also QR and SP)

topics.rl: Brick walls, chessboards and floor tiles are all tilings by parallelograms (rectangles and squares).

rv.summary: A tiling covers the plane with no gaps or overlaps; any parallelogram tiles. A quadrilateral ABCD is four points (no three collinear) joined in order by four sides that meet only at their ends.
focus: Identify sides, diagonals, opposite and adjacent parts.
Name quadrilaterals correctly.
Explain why parallelograms tile.
remember: Diagonals join opposite vertices: AC and BD.
ABCD = BCDA = DCBA, but ABDC is different.
No three points on a line, so there are true corners.
traps: Don't confuse a side with a diagonal.
Not every order of letters names the same figure.
Opposite angles are not adjacent angles.

topics.h: An arrowhead has four sides, but one of its corners points inwards. Is it still a quadrilateral? Yes, a non-convex one!
p: Convex quadrilateral: every interior angle is less than 180° and the two diagonals cross inside it.
Non-convex (concave) quadrilateral: one interior angle is a reflex angle (more than 180°), like an arrowhead; one diagonal lies outside.
The interior angle at a vertex is the angle inside the figure; at the 'dent' of an arrowhead it is reflex. The four interior angles of any simple quadrilateral still add to 360°.

Other four-sided figures: self-intersecting (like a bow-tie, where two sides cross) and non-planar (the four points are not all in one plane, like a bent frame). A Venn diagram of 4-gons puts convex and non-convex quadrilaterals inside the bigger family of 4-gons.

ex.q: An arrowhead quadrilateral has angles 30°, 40° and 30° at three vertices. Find the fourth angle and say what kind it is.

topics.rl: The arrowhead shape is common in road signs and kites; its reflex angle points inwards.

rv.summary: A convex quadrilateral has all angles under 180° and diagonals crossing inside. A non-convex one has exactly one reflex angle. Other 4-gons are self-intersecting (bow-ties) or non-planar.
focus: Classify quadrilaterals as convex or non-convex.
Find a reflex angle from the other three.
Place 4-gons in a Venn diagram.
remember: Interior angles of a simple quadrilateral add to 360°.
Only one angle can be reflex.
traps: An obtuse angle does not make it non-convex.
Subtract from 360°, not 180°.
A non-convex shape is not self-intersecting.

topics.h: Four sticks joined at the ends with pins can wiggle into many shapes. Engineers use this to build machines!
p: A four-bar linkage is a quadrilateral with fixed side lengths but movable joints; its angles change as it moves. It powers windscreen wipers, bicycle pedals with legs, and folding chairs.

Parallelogram linkages keep opposite sides parallel while moving: Watt's parallel motion guided steam-engine pistons; a pantograph copies a drawing larger or smaller; forces combine by the parallelogram rule.
Given 4 points with no three in a line, they can be joined into 3 different 4-gons (the vertex orders ABCD, ABDC, ACBD).

If the 4 points are corners of a convex shape, you get 1 convex quadrilateral and 2 self-intersecting 4-gons. If one point is inside the triangle of the other three, you get 3 non-convex quadrilaterals.

ex.q: Points A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(4, 3), D(0, 3). How many 4-gons can be formed and of which kinds?
st: The points form a rectangle, so they are in convex position
Order ABCD gives the convex rectangle
Orders ABDC and ACBD give bow-ties

topics.rl: Architects and artists once used pantographs to enlarge drawings; today some trains use a pantograph to touch the overhead wire.

rv.summary: A four-bar linkage has fixed bar lengths but moving joints; parallelogram linkages drive pantographs and Watt's parallel motion. Four points can be joined into 3 different 4-gons.
focus: Explain how linkages move.
Count 4-gons on four points.
Use the parallelogram rule for forces.
remember: One point inside the triangle: 3 non-convex quadrilaterals.
Resultant force = diagonal from the common corner.
traps: A linkage is not rigid: angles change.
Don't count all 24 orderings.
An equal-bar linkage stays a rhombus.

topics.h: Kites in the Makar Sankranti sky, carrom boards and window panes are all quadrilaterals, but they belong to different branches of one big family!
p: A quadrilateral has 4 sides, 4 angles, 4 vertices and 2 diagonals. Its interior angles always add up to 360°, because a diagonal splits it into two triangles.
Trapezium: a pair of opposite sides parallel. Parallelogram: both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
Rectangle: a parallelogram with all angles 90°. Rhombus: a parallelogram with all sides equal. Square: both a rectangle and a rhombus.
Kite: two pairs of equal adjacent sides; its diagonals are perpendicular.
So every square is a rectangle and a rhombus, and every rectangle and rhombus is a parallelogram, but not the other way round.

ex.q: The angles of a quadrilateral are x, x + 10°, x + 20° and x + 30°. Find all four angles.

topics.rl: Engineers use parallelogram shapes in car jacks and folding gates, because they can change shape while opposite sides stay parallel.

rv.summary: A quadrilateral's angles add to 360°. Trapeziums, parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses, squares and kites form a family: every square is a rectangle and a rhombus, and these are parallelograms.
focus: Use the angle sum of 360°.
Know the definitions of each quadrilateral.
Place shapes in the family tree.
remember: Kite: two pairs of equal adjacent sides; diagonals perpendicular.
traps: A rhombus need not be a square.
A trapezium is not a parallelogram.

topics.h: Push the top of a folding gate sideways: it leans, but opposite sides stay equal and parallel. That's the parallelogram's superpower!
p: A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles.
In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and opposite angles are equal.
Adjacent angles are supplementary: they add up to 180° (co-interior angles between parallel lines).
The diagonals bisect each other: they cut each other into two equal halves.

A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if any one of these holds: both pairs of opposite sides equal, both pairs of opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other, or one pair of opposite sides is both equal and parallel. In a rectangle the diagonals are also equal; in a rhombus they are also perpendicular.

ex.q: In parallelogram PQRS, ∠P = 65°. Find the other three angles.

topics.rl: Table lamps with folding arms, the scissor lift used by electricians and many bridge frames rely on parallelogram properties.

rv.summary: In a parallelogram, opposite sides and opposite angles are equal, adjacent angles add to 180°, and the diagonals bisect each other.
focus: Find angles and sides of parallelograms.
Use bisecting diagonals.
Know the conditions that prove a parallelogram.
remember: One pair of opposite sides equal AND parallel is enough.
traps: Diagonals are equal only in rectangles.
One pair of equal sides is not enough.
Adjacent angles are supplementary, not equal.

topics.t: Proving a quadrilateral is a parallelogram
topics.h: Measure only the sides, or only the diagonals, and still be sure it's a parallelogram? Yes, with the right converse!
p: If both pairs of opposite sides are equal, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram. Proof: diagonal AC gives △ABC ≅ △CDA (SSS), so alternate angles are equal and the sides are parallel.
If the diagonals bisect each other, it is a parallelogram. Proof: with diagonals meeting at O, △AOB ≅ △COD (SAS, vertically opposite angles), so ∠OAB = ∠OCD and AB ∥ CD; similarly AD ∥ BC.
If one pair of opposite sides is both equal and parallel, it is a parallelogram (△ABC ≅ △CDA by SAS).
Proofs use congruence rules SSS, SAS, ASA and then CPCT (corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal).

ex.q: In quadrilateral PQRS, diagonals meet at O with PO = 5, OR = 5, QO = 7, OS = 7. What is PQRS?
st: O is the midpoint of PR (5 = 5)
O is the midpoint of QS (7 = 7)

topics.rl: A carpenter checking a door frame can measure diagonals: if they bisect each other the frame is a parallelogram.

rv.summary: A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if both pairs of opposite sides are equal (SSS), if its diagonals bisect each other (SAS), or if one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel.
focus: Prove a quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
Choose the right congruence rule.
Use CPCT.
remember: Bisecting diagonals: △AOB ≅ △COD by SAS (vertically opposite angles).
CPCT: corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal.
traps: Check that both diagonals are bisected.
One parallel pair alone is a trapezium.
Use SSS when only sides are known.

topics.t: Rhombus, rectangle and square: special conditions
topics.h: Draw the four angle bisectors of any parallelogram and, like magic, they box in a rectangle!
p: If a diagonal of a parallelogram bisects one of its angles, the parallelogram is a rhombus (the diagonal makes an isosceles triangle, so adjacent sides are equal).
The bisectors of the four angles of a parallelogram form a rectangle: adjacent angles add to 180°, so their halves add to 90°, and each corner of the inner figure is a right angle.

Converses with extra conditions: a parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle; a parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals is a rhombus; a parallelogram with equal and perpendicular diagonals is a square.
Without 'parallelogram' these fail: a kite has perpendicular diagonals but is not a rhombus; an isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals but is not a rectangle.

ex.q: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 110°. The bisectors of ∠A and ∠B meet at P. Find ∠APB.

topics.rl: Window frames and photo frames are checked for squareness by measuring diagonals: equal diagonals of a parallelogram mean a rectangle.

rv.summary: A parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle, with perpendicular diagonals a rhombus, with both a square. A diagonal bisecting an angle makes a rhombus, and angle bisectors form a rectangle.
focus: Identify special parallelograms from diagonals.
Use angle bisectors in parallelograms.
Know when the converses fail.
remember: Bisectors of adjacent angles meet at 90°.
Kite: perpendicular diagonals, not a rhombus; isosceles trapezium: equal diagonals, not a rectangle.
traps: These rules need the shape to be a parallelogram.
Equal diagonals alone don't make a rectangle.
Don't assume a square from one condition.

topics.h: Join the middles of two sides of any triangle and something magical appears: a line exactly parallel to the third side and exactly half as long!
p: Mid-point theorem: the segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and is half of it.
If D and E are mid-points of AB and AC in triangle ABC, then DE ∥ BC and DE = ½ BC.
Converse: a line through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel to another side, bisects the third side.
Joining the mid-points of the three sides makes 4 congruent triangles, each with ¼ of the area of the original.
Joining the mid-points of the sides of ANY quadrilateral, in order, always gives a parallelogram.

ex.q: In triangle ABC, AB = 8 cm, BC = 10 cm and CA = 12 cm. D, E and F are the mid-points of AB, BC and CA. Find the perimeter of triangle DEF.
st: By the mid-point theorem, each side of DEF is half of a side of ABC
DE = ½ CA = 6, EF = ½ AB = 4, FD = ½ BC = 5

topics.rl: Carpenters use the mid-point idea to fix a cross-bar exactly halfway up a triangular roof frame, knowing it will be level and half the width of the base.

rv.summary: The segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half its length. Its converse also holds, and joining mid-points of any quadrilateral gives a parallelogram.
focus: Use DE ∥ BC and DE = ½ BC.
Use the converse to bisect a side.
Find areas and perimeters of mid-point triangles.
remember: Mid-point triangle area = ¼ of the original.
traps: Halve to get DE; double to get BC.
DE is parallel to the third side, not a side it touches.
Area is ¼, not ½.

topics.t: Midpoint theorem: proof, trapeziums and equal parts
topics.h: Split a ladder into equal steps using just parallel lines. The midpoint theorem's big brother does it!
p: Proof of the midpoint theorem by construction: with D, E midpoints of AB, AC, extend DE to F with EF = DE. △ADE ≅ △CFE (SAS), so CF = AD = DB and CF ∥ AB. So DBCF is a parallelogram, giving DE ∥ BC and DF = BC, so DE = ½ BC.
Trapezium mid-segment: the segment joining the midpoints of the non-parallel sides is parallel to the bases and equals half their sum: (a + b)/2.
If three or more parallel lines cut equal parts on one transversal, they cut equal parts on every transversal.
To divide AB in a ratio like 3 : 5, draw a ray from A, mark 8 equal steps, join the 8th mark to B, and draw parallels through the other marks; the 3rd one meets AB at the dividing point.

ex.q: A trapezium has parallel sides 14 cm and 22 cm. Find the length of the segment joining the midpoints of the other two sides.

topics.rl: Tailors dividing cloth into equal strips and architects spacing stairs use the equal-intercept property.

rv.summary: The mid-point theorem is proved by extending DE to F and using SAS. A trapezium's mid-segment is (a + b)/2. Parallel lines that cut equal parts on one transversal cut equal parts on all.
focus: Follow the proof of the mid-point theorem.
Find trapezium mid-segments.
Divide a segment in a given ratio.
traps: Add the bases, don't subtract.
Use the total number of parts (p + q).
The mid-segment is parallel to the bases, not the slanted sides.

topics.h: Balance a cardboard triangle on a pencil tip. The balancing point is where the three medians meet!
p: A median joins a vertex of a triangle to the midpoint of the opposite side. Every triangle has three medians.
The three medians are concurrent: they meet at one point G, the centroid (the balancing point).
Centroid theorem: G divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1 from the vertex, so AG = ⅔ AD and GD = ⅓ AD. (Proof idea: join the midpoints of two sides and use the midpoint theorem.)
Trisecting a segment AD: make AD a median of some triangle (pick B, extend BD to C with DC = BD). The centroid G is at one-third from D; the midpoint of AG gives the other trisection point.

ex.q: Median AD of △ABC is 12 cm. Find AG and GD.

topics.rl: Engineers find the centroid of triangular metal plates so they can be lifted without tilting.

rv.summary: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. The three medians meet at the centroid, which divides each median 2 : 1 from the vertex.
focus: Use the 2 : 1 ratio on medians.
Find the centroid from coordinates.
Trisect a segment using a centroid.
traps: Take ⅔ from the vertex, not ⅓.
A median is not an altitude.
Bisecting twice gives quarters, not thirds.

topics.t: Varignon shapes and tiling with any quadrilateral
topics.h: Even a lopsided, wonky quadrilateral can tile a whole floor. Spin it around its edge midpoints and watch!
p: Varignon parallelogram (midpoints of the sides joined in order): its sides are parallel to the diagonals and half as long.
If the original's diagonals are perpendicular, the Varignon figure is a rectangle; if they are equal, it is a rhombus; if they are equal and perpendicular, a square.

Tiling method 1: rotate a copy of the quadrilateral by 180° about the midpoint of one edge; keep doing this about edge midpoints. The four angles (sum 360°) meet at every vertex, and copies fill the plane.
Tiling method 2: the Varignon parallelograms of copies form a parallelogram grid, which shows how translated copies of the quadrilateral fit together.

ex.q: A quadrilateral has diagonals 10 cm and 14 cm that are perpendicular. Describe its Varignon figure and its perimeter.
st: Sides are half the diagonals: 5 cm and 7 cm
ex.a: A 5 cm by 7 cm rectangle, perimeter 24 cm

topics.rl: Tile designers use 180° rotations about edge midpoints to make floor patterns with irregular shapes.

rv.summary: The Varignon parallelogram has sides parallel to and half the diagonals. Its shape depends on the diagonals. Any quadrilateral tiles using half-turns about edge midpoints.
focus: Find the Varignon figure and its perimeter.
Link diagonals to the Varignon shape.
Explain why any quadrilateral tiles.
remember: Perpendicular diagonals → rectangle; equal → rhombus; both → square.
Varignon area = ½ of the original.
traps: Each side is half a diagonal, not the full diagonal.
Don't mix up the rectangle and rhombus cases.
Use a half-turn (180°), not a quarter turn.

topics.t: Which shapes tile? Pentagons, hats and bow-ties
topics.h: Bathroom tiles are squares, honeycombs are hexagons, but you'll never see a floor of regular pentagons. Why?
p: Any triangle and any quadrilateral (even a non-convex one) can tile the plane.
A regular pentagon cannot: each angle is 108°, and 360 ÷ 108 is not a whole number, so copies cannot fill the space around a point.
Aperiodic tilings cover the plane but never repeat in a regular pattern. In 2023 a single shape nicknamed the 'hat' was found that tiles the plane only aperiodically.
Scissors congruence: a shape can be cut into pieces and rearranged. For example, joining the midpoints of a triangle's sides cuts it into 4 congruent triangles.
In a self-intersecting (bow-tie) 4-gon, the four vertex angles add up to less than 360°: they are 360° − 2θ, where θ is the angle where the sides cross.

ex.q: Can regular hexagons tile the plane? Regular pentagons?
st: Hexagon angle = 120°; 360 ÷ 120 = 3: yes, three meet at a point
So hexagons tile; pentagons do not

topics.rl: Honeybees build hexagonal cells because hexagons tile without gaps and use little wax.

rv.summary: Every triangle and quadrilateral tiles the plane, but regular pentagons (108° angles) do not. The 2023 'hat' tiles only aperiodically. A bow-tie's vertex angles add to 360° − 2θ.
focus: Decide which regular polygons tile.
Know aperiodic tilings.
Use scissors congruence and bow-tie angle sums.
traps: Non-convex quadrilaterals can tile.
Aperiodic does not mean leaving gaps.
A bow-tie's angles do not add to 360°.

topics.h: 2 samosas and 3 jalebis cost ₹110. How much is one samosa? There isn't just one answer, until you get more clues!
p: A linear equation in two variables can be written as ax + by + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a and b are not both zero.
A solution is an ordered pair (x, y) that makes the equation true. Example: (2, 3) is a solution of 2x + y = 7 because 4 + 3 = 7.
A linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions: choose any x, then work out y.
To check a pair, substitute both values and see whether the two sides are equal.
An equation like y = 3 can be written in two variables as 0·x + 1·y − 3 = 0.

ex.q: Find three solutions of x + 2y = 8.

topics.rl: Shopkeepers mixing two kinds of sweets in a ₹500 box face a two-variable equation: many different mixes give the same total.

rv.summary: A linear equation in two variables has the form ax + by + c = 0 (a, b not both 0). A solution is an ordered pair that makes it true, and there are infinitely many.
focus: Check whether a pair is a solution.
Find several solutions.
Write equations from situations.
traps: Keep the order (x, y).
Keep the sign with the coefficient: b = −5.
There are infinitely many solutions, not just whole-number ones.

topics.t: Standard form, scaling and solutions in every quadrant
topics.h: x/2 + y/3 = 1 and 3x + 2y = 6 look different, but they are the very same line!
p: To write an equation in standard form ax + by + c = 0, move every term to one side and clear fractions or decimals by multiplying by a suitable number.
Example: x/2 + y/3 = 1 → multiply by 6: 3x + 2y = 6 → 3x + 2y − 6 = 0, so a = 3, b = 2, c = −6.
Check that an equation really matches a situation by testing a simple case: if a pen costs ₹10 and a pencil ₹5, 'x pens and y pencils cost ₹80' is 10x + 5y = 80, not 10x + 5y = 80xy.
Multiplying an equation by any non-zero k gives the same solutions (the same line): 2x + y = 5 and 6x + 3y = 15 are equivalent.
Solutions can be in any quadrant: for x − y = 2, (5, 3) is in Quadrant I, (−1, −3) in III, and (1, −1) in IV.

ex.q: Write 0.3x − 0.2y = 1.5 in standard form with integer coefficients.

topics.rl: Mobile plans like '₹2 per call and ₹1 per SMS, total bill ₹150' are linear equations in two variables.

rv.summary: Write equations in standard form ax + by + c = 0 by moving terms and clearing fractions. Multiplying by a non-zero k gives the same line. Solutions can lie in any quadrant.
focus: Convert to standard form with integers.
Recognise equivalent equations.
Check that a model matches the situation.
traps: Multiply every term when clearing fractions.
Multiplying by 0 is not allowed.
Match each price with its own item.

topics.h: Plot every solution of x + y = 5 and they line up perfectly, like students at assembly. One equation, one straight line!
p: The graph of a linear equation in two variables is a straight line. Every point on the line is a solution, and every solution is a point on the line.
To draw it, find two or three solutions, plot them and join them with a ruler.
x-intercept: put y = 0. y-intercept: put x = 0. These two points are often the easiest to plot.
x = a is a vertical line through (a, 0); y = b is a horizontal line through (0, b).
y = mx (with no constant term) always passes through the origin (0, 0).

ex.q: Draw the graph of 2x + 3y = 12.
st: Plot the three points and join them: one straight line

topics.rl: A taxi fare chart (fare against distance) or a mobile recharge plan (cost against data) shows up as a straight-line graph.

rv.summary: The graph of a linear equation in two variables is a straight line. Plot two or three solutions; intercepts are easy points. x = a is vertical and y = b is horizontal.
focus: Draw a line from two or three solutions.
Find intercepts.
Recognise vertical, horizontal and origin lines.
remember: x-intercept: put y = 0; y-intercept: put x = 0.
y = mx passes through the origin.
traps: x = 4 is vertical, not horizontal.
Divide by the coefficient when finding intercepts.
Not every line passes through the origin.

topics.h: A wheelchair ramp must rise only 1 cm for every 12 cm along. That 1 : 12 is its slope!
p: Slope (gradient) measures how steep a line is: slope = rise ÷ run = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
On a straight line, the slope is the same whichever two points you use.
Positive slope rises from left to right; negative slope falls; a horizontal line has slope 0; a vertical line has undefined slope (the run is 0).
Real life: ramps, ghats, ski slopes. A wheelchair ramp is recommended to have slope at most 1 : 12, so a 60 cm rise needs at least 7.2 m of run.
Using slope and one point: if the slope is 3 and the line passes through (1, 2), then the point with x = 4 has y = 2 + 3 × 3 = 11.

ex.q: A line through (2, 5) has slope −2. Find y when x = 6.

topics.rl: Government buildings in India add ramps with gentle slopes so that wheelchair users can enter.

rv.summary: Slope = rise ÷ run = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Positive slopes rise, negative fall, horizontal lines have slope 0 and vertical lines have undefined slope.
focus: Find slopes from two points.
Solve ramp and road problems.
Use slope and a point to find another point.
remember: Ramp at most 1 : 12: 60 cm rise needs 7.2 m run.
traps: Don't divide run by rise.
A vertical line's slope is undefined, not 0.
Convert units (km to m) first.

topics.h: Rewrite 2x + 3y = 6 as y = −(2/3)x + 2 and you can read the slope and where it hits the y-axis at a glance!
p: Slope-intercept form: y = mx + d, where m is the slope and d is the y-intercept (the line meets the y-axis at (0, d)).
From ax + by + c = 0 with b ≠ 0: y = −(a/b)x − c/b. So m = −a/b and d = −c/b.
Two different lines with the same slope are parallel: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 4.
Applications: a tank filling at 3 litres per minute holds y = 3x after x minutes (slope 3, intercept 0); Fahrenheit and Celsius are linked by F = (9/5)C + 32 (slope 9/5, intercept 32).

ex.q: Find the slope and y-intercept of 4x − 2y + 6 = 0.

topics.rl: An auto fare chart 'base ₹30 plus ₹15 per km' is y = 15x + 30: slope 15, intercept 30.

rv.summary: In slope-intercept form y = mx + d, m is the slope and d the y-intercept. From ax + by + c = 0, m = −a/b and d = −c/b. Parallel lines have equal slopes.
focus: Find slope and intercept from an equation.
Identify parallel lines.
Interpret m and d in real situations.
traps: Don't forget the minus in −a/b.
Parallel means equal slopes, not equal intercepts.
The rate is the slope, the fixed charge is the intercept.

topics.h: One clue gives infinitely many answers. Add a second clue and, usually, just one answer is left. Two lines, one meeting point!
p: Two linear equations in the same two variables form a pair. A solution of the pair must satisfy both equations.
Graphically, the solution is the point where the two lines meet.
Lines that cross give exactly one solution. Parallel lines give no solution. Lines that lie on top of each other (the same line) give infinitely many solutions.
Substitution method: make one variable the subject in one equation and put it into the other.
Elimination method: add or subtract the equations (after multiplying if needed) to remove one variable.

ex.q: Solve x + y = 10 and x − y = 2.
st: Put x = 6 in x + y = 10: y = 4

topics.rl: Comparing two mobile plans, or finding prices from two shopping bills, is solving a pair of linear equations.

rv.summary: A pair of linear equations is solved by finding the point on both lines. Crossing lines give one solution, parallel lines none, the same line infinitely many. Use substitution or elimination.
focus: Solve pairs by substitution and elimination.
Find the number of solutions.
Read solutions from graphs.
remember: Same slope, different intercept → parallel → no solution.
Multiple of the same equation → infinitely many.
traps: Not every pair of lines crosses.
Different-looking equations can be the same line.
Give the value the question asks for.

topics.t: Shape puzzles and the comparison method
topics.h: Two apples and a banana weigh 500 g; one apple and a banana weigh 350 g. Take one picture from the other and an apple pops out!
p: Shape-value puzzles: pictures like 🍎🍎🍌 = 500 and 🍎🍌 = 350 are pairs of equations in disguise. Comparing them shows one 🍎 = 150, then 🍌 = 200.
Comparison method: make the same variable the subject in both equations, then set the two expressions equal.
Example: y = 2x + 1 and y = 7 − x give 2x + 1 = 7 − x, so 3x = 6, x = 2 and y = 5.
Always check the solution in both original equations.

ex.q: Solve by comparison: x + y = 9 and x − y = 3.
st: From both: y = 9 − x and y = x − 3

topics.rl: Kids' puzzles on social media like 'burger + burger + fries = 30' are simultaneous equations in disguise.

rv.summary: Shape-value puzzles are pairs of equations in disguise. The comparison method makes the same variable the subject in both equations and sets them equal.
focus: Solve shape and price puzzles.
Use the comparison method.
Check solutions in both equations.
traps: Set the expressions equal; don't add them.
Don't stop after finding one value.
Check in both equations.

topics.t: How many solutions? The ratio test
topics.h: Without solving, can you tell if two lines cross, never meet, or are the same line? Compare the coefficient ratios!
p: For a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0:
If a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂, the lines cross: exactly one solution.
If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂, the lines are the same (coincident): infinitely many solutions. While solving, you get 0 = 0.
If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂, the lines are parallel: no solution. While solving, you get a false statement like 0 = 5.

To build a second equation for 2x + 3y = 6: for crossing lines change the ratio of x and y (x − y = 1); for parallel lines keep 2 : 3 but change the constant (4x + 6y = 5); for the same line multiply everything (4x + 6y = 12).

ex.q: Decide the number of solutions of 3x − 2y = 5 and 6x − 4y = 9.

topics.rl: Two trains on parallel tracks never meet; two roads that cross meet at exactly one junction.

rv.summary: Compare ratios a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂, c₁/c₂: unequal first two → one solution; all equal → same line; first two equal but not the third → parallel. 0 = 0 means infinitely many; 0 = 5 means none.
focus: Use the ratio test.
Interpret 0 = 0 and false statements.
Build equations with a chosen number of solutions.
traps: 0 = 0 does not mean x = y = 0.
Check all three ratios.
Scale both sides to get the same line.

topics.h: Ages, coins, incomes, ticket prices: two clues give two equations, and two equations crack the case!
p: Name the two unknowns clearly (for example x = price of a pen, y = price of a pencil).
Turn each clue into one equation, then solve the pair by substitution, elimination or comparison.
Two-digit numbers: 10t + u; reversing gives 10u + t. Fractions: write as x/y and turn each clue into an equation.
Income and expenditure in a ratio: incomes 3k and 4k; savings = income − expenditure.
Check the answer against the story: ages must be positive, coins must be whole numbers.

ex.q: Find a fraction x/y that becomes 1/2 when 1 is added to its numerator, and 1/3 when 1 is subtracted from its denominator.

topics.rl: Planning a school picnic budget with buses and vans of different capacities is a two-variable problem.

rv.summary: For word problems, name the two unknowns, turn each clue into an equation, solve the pair and check the answer fits the story.
focus: Solve number, age, coin and digit problems.
Solve fraction and fare problems.
Check answers make sense.
remember: Fraction x/y: +1 on top → 1/2, −1 below → 1/3 gives 1/4.
traps: Don't give the reversed number.
Don't mix up which unknown stands for the ₹10 notes and which for the ₹50 notes.
Coins and people must be whole numbers.

topics.h: Over 1100 years ago, Mahaviracharya asked: what is the price of one citron and one wood-apple? Pairs of equations are that old!
p: Mahaviracharya (9th century) posed: 9 citrons and 7 wood-apples cost 107; 7 citrons and 9 wood-apples cost 101. Adding: 16(x + y) = 208, so x + y = 13; subtracting: 2(x − y) = 6, so x − y = 3. Citron 8, wood-apple 5.
Babylonian tablets, the Chinese 'Nine Chapters' (with a method like elimination) and Indian texts all solved such problems long ago.
Graphical method for word problems: write both equations, draw both lines carefully on graph paper, and read the meeting point. Then check it in both equations.
Comparing plans: two phone plans y = 200 + 2x and y = 50 + 5x meet where 200 + 2x = 50 + 5x, at x = 50. Below 50 units the second is cheaper; above 50, the first.

ex.q: Gym Plan A costs ₹500 to join plus ₹300 a month; Plan B costs ₹1100 to join plus ₹200 a month. After how many months do they cost the same?

topics.rl: Before buying a two-wheeler or a phone plan, families compare costs over time, exactly like reading where two lines meet.

rv.summary: Pairs of equations have a long history: Mahaviracharya's citron problem, the Chinese Nine Chapters and Babylonian tablets. Graphs help compare plans by finding where cost lines meet.
focus: Solve historical problems by adding and subtracting.
Compare plans with equations and graphs.
Check graph readings by substitution.
traps: Don't trust a graph reading without checking.
The cheaper plan depends on usage.
Parallel cost lines never meet.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.t: Surface versus space: cuboids in layers
topics.h: A 1 × 1 × 8 stick of clay and a 2 × 2 × 2 cube use the same clay. Which needs more wrapping paper?
p: Every solid has a surface (measured as area, in square units) and takes up space (volume, in cubic units).
Volume as layers: stack thin layers each with the base area; volume = base area × height. For a cuboid that is l × w × h.
The same volume can have different surface areas: 1 × 1 × 8 and 2 × 2 × 2 both have volume 8, but surface areas 34 and 24. Compact shapes lose less heat and need less packaging.
If the three face areas of a cuboid are A₁ = lw, A₂ = wh, A₃ = hl, then A₁ × A₂ × A₃ = (lwh)², so V = √(A₁A₂A₃).

ex.q: A cuboid's faces have areas 12 cm², 15 cm² and 20 cm². Find its volume.

topics.rl: Laddoo boxes and milk cartons are shaped to hold a lot with as little cardboard as possible.

rv.summary: Every solid has a surface (area, square units) and takes up space (volume, cubic units). Volume = base area × height. Equal volumes can have very different surface areas.
focus: Find volume as base area × height.
Compare surface areas for equal volumes.
Find volume from three face areas.
traps: Don't mix up cm² and cm³.
Equal volume does not mean equal surface area.
Take the square root of the product of face areas.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.t: Surface area of cuboids, cubes and cylinders
topics.h: How much paper do you need to gift-wrap a box of sweets for Diwali? That is a surface area question!
p: Surface area is the total area of all the outer faces of a solid, measured in square units.
Cuboid (l × b × h): total surface area = 2(lb + bh + hl). The four walls of a room (lateral surface) = 2(l + b) × h.
Cube of edge a: total surface area = 6a²; lateral surface area = 4a².
Cylinder of radius r and height h: curved surface area = 2πrh; total surface area = 2πr(r + h).
Open shapes (a box without a lid, a pipe without ends) need only the faces that are really there.

ex.q: A closed cylindrical tin has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. How much metal sheet is needed to make it? (Use π = 22/7.)

topics.rl: Painters charge by the square metre of wall, and tin factories order metal sheets by the surface area of the cans they make.

rv.summary: Surface area is the total outer area. Cuboid 2(lb + bh + hl), cube 6a², cylinder curved 2πrh and total 2πr(r + h). Open shapes need only the faces present.
focus: Find surface areas of cuboids, cubes and cylinders.
Find lateral and curved areas.
Handle open boxes and pipes.
remember: Cylinder r = 7, h = 10: CSA 440 cm², TSA 748 cm².
Doubling a cube's edge makes its area 4 times.
traps: Don't give volume instead of area.
Leave out faces that are not there (lid, ends).
Area scales by 4, not 2 or 8, when the edge doubles.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.t: Packing, painted cubes and integer boxes
topics.h: Dip a 4 × 4 × 4 cube of small cubes in paint. How many small cubes have no paint at all? Only the hidden heart!
p: Packing: the number of small boxes a × b × c that fit (in the same orientation) in a box L × W × H is (L ÷ a) × (W ÷ b) × (H ÷ c), using whole numbers only.
Painted n × n × n cube cut into unit cubes: 3 faces painted: 8 (corners); 2 faces: 12(n − 2) (edges); 1 face: 6(n − 2)² (face centres); 0 faces: (n − 2)³ (inside).
Cuboids with whole-number edges and surface area S: solve lw + wh + hl = S/2. For S = 22 there are exactly two: 1 × 1 × 5 and 1 × 2 × 3.

ex.q: A 5 × 5 × 5 painted cube is cut into unit cubes. Count the cubes with 2 faces painted and with none.

topics.rl: Warehouse managers plan how many cartons fit on a truck using this packing calculation.

rv.summary: Count packed boxes by dividing each dimension. A painted n-cube cut into unit cubes has 8 with 3 faces, 12(n − 2) with 2, 6(n − 2)² with 1 and (n − 2)³ with none.
focus: Count boxes that fit in a carton.
Count painted unit cubes.
Find whole-number cuboids with a given surface area.
traps: Use whole numbers along each edge, not volume ÷ volume.
Use n − 2, not n.
Double lw + wh + hl for surface area.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.t: Cylinders: discs, ratios and percentage changes
topics.h: Stack khakhras one on top of another and you've built a cylinder!
p: A right circular cylinder has two equal circular bases, every cross-section parallel to the base is the same circle, and its axis is perpendicular to the base.
Think of a cylinder as a stack of thin discs (like khakhras or coins): each has area πr², and the stack has height h, so V = πr²h.
Ratios: if the radius is multiplied by k, volume is multiplied by k² (height fixed); if the height is multiplied by k, volume is multiplied by k.
Percentage change: radius up 10% (× 1.1) makes volume × 1.21, a 21% increase. Curved surface area 2πrh grows by the same factor as r × h.

ex.q: Cylinder A has radius 3 cm and height 8 cm; cylinder B has radius 6 cm and height 4 cm. Compare their volumes.
ex.a: B has twice the volume of A

topics.rl: A stack of ₹10 coins is a cylinder; doubling the stack doubles the volume, but a coin twice as wide holds four times the metal.

rv.summary: A cylinder is a stack of discs, so V = πr²h. Volume scales with r² and with h, so a 10% larger radius gives 21% more volume.
focus: Find cylinder volumes.
Compare cylinders with ratios.
Find percentage changes in volume.
remember: r = 3, h = 8 vs r = 6, h = 4: volumes 72π and 144π.
traps: Volume depends on r², not r.
Don't double a percentage change.
A wider glass does not always hold more.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.t: Volume of cylinders, cones and spheres
topics.h: Fill a cone with water three times and pour it into a cylinder of the same base and height: it fills up exactly. Maths predicted it!
p: Volume is the space a solid takes up, measured in cubic units. 1000 cm³ = 1 litre, and 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
Cuboid: V = l × b × h. Cube: V = a³.
Cylinder: V = πr²h (base area × height).
Cone: V = ⅓πr²h, exactly one third of a cylinder with the same base and height.
Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³. Hemisphere: V = (2/3)πr³. When a solid is melted and recast, its volume stays the same.

ex.q: A cone-shaped heap of wheat has radius 7 m and height 3 m. Find its volume. (Use π = 22/7.)

topics.rl: Water tankers, LPG cylinders, ice-cream cones and gol gappas all have volumes that companies calculate with these formulas.

rv.summary: Volume is the space a solid fills. Cylinder πr²h, cone ⅓πr²h, sphere (4/3)πr³, hemisphere (2/3)πr³. 1000 cm³ = 1 litre and recasting keeps volume the same.
focus: Find volumes of cylinders, cones and spheres.
Convert cm³ and m³ to litres.
Solve recasting problems.
remember: Cone = ⅓ of the cylinder with the same base and height.
traps: Don't forget the ⅓ for a cone.
A hemisphere is half a sphere.
1 m³ is 1000 litres, not 100.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.t: Cones: how they form and where we meet them
topics.h: Spin a set square around one of its short edges really fast: the blur you see is a cone!
p: A right circular cone is formed by rotating a right triangle about one of its legs: that leg becomes the height h, the other leg the radius r, and the hypotenuse the slant height l.
Rotating the same triangle about the other leg gives a different cone (radius and height swap).
Problems: a birthday cap needs paper = curved surface πrl; a conical tent needs canvas πrl and holds air ⅓πr²h; a tarpaulin to cover a heap uses πrl.
A conical cup filled to half its depth holds only 1/8 of its full volume, because the water forms a smaller cone with half the radius and half the height: (½)² × ½ = 1/8.

ex.q: A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the volume of the cone made by rotating it about the 8 cm leg. (π = 3.14)

topics.rl: Ice-cream cones, traffic cones, mehndi cones and tent tops are all cones.

rv.summary: Rotating a right triangle about a leg gives a cone: that leg is the height, the other the radius, the hypotenuse the slant height. Caps and tents use πrl; air inside uses ⅓πr²h.
focus: Find the cone made by rotating a triangle.
Solve cap, tent and tarpaulin problems.
Use the 1/8 rule for half-depth.
remember: Rotating about the hypotenuse → two cones.
traps: The axis leg is the height, not the radius.
Use slant height for πrl.
Half the depth is not half the volume.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.t: Surface area of cones and spheres
topics.h: A birthday cap, an ice-cream cone and a cricket ball: two of these are cones and one is a sphere. How much material covers each?
p: A right circular cone has radius r, height h and slant height l, where l = √(r² + h²).
Curved surface area of a cone = πrl; total surface area = πr(l + r).
Surface area of a sphere of radius r = 4πr².
A hemisphere has curved surface area 2πr² and, with its flat circular face, total surface area 3πr².
If the radius of a sphere doubles, its surface area becomes 4 times as big.

ex.q: A conical birthday cap has radius 7 cm and height 24 cm. How much paper is needed for it? (Use π = 22/7.)

topics.rl: Tent-makers measure canvas for conical tents with πrl, and football manufacturers need 4πr² of leather for each ball.

rv.summary: A cone has slant height l = √(r² + h²), curved area πrl and total area πr(l + r). A sphere has area 4πr²; a hemisphere has curved area 2πr² and total 3πr².
focus: Find slant heights.
Find curved and total surface areas.
Choose curved or total area from the context.
remember: Sphere r = 7: 616 cm²; hemisphere TSA 462 cm².
A cap has no base: only πrl.
traps: Don't add r and h for the slant height.
Sphere area is 4πr², not πr².
Include the flat face for a solid hemisphere.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.h: The great pyramids of Egypt and the sharp peak of a temple tower share one formula!
p: A pyramid has a polygon base and triangular faces that meet at a point called the apex. Egyptian pyramids are square pyramids; mountain peaks and some temple roofs look pyramidal.
Volume of any pyramid = ⅓ × base area × height (height measured straight up from base to apex).
Surface area = base area + areas of all the triangular faces.
A cone is like a pyramid with a circular base: V = ⅓ × πr² × h follows the same rule.

ex.q: A square pyramid has base side 6 m, height 4 m and slant height (of each triangular face) 5 m. Find its volume and total surface area.

topics.rl: Glass pyramids above museums and paper lampshades use pyramid surface area for material and volume for the space inside.

rv.summary: A pyramid has a polygon base and triangular faces meeting at the apex. Volume = ⅓ × base area × height; surface area = base + all triangular faces.
focus: Find volumes of pyramids.
Find surface areas of square pyramids.
Link pyramids and cones.
remember: Base 6, height 4, slant 5: V = 48 m³, TSA = 96 m².
Pyramid = ⅓ of a prism with the same base and height.
Number of triangular faces = number of base sides.
traps: Don't forget the ⅓.
Use base area, not base side.
Include the base in total surface area.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.h: Archimedes was so proud of this that he wanted it carved on his tomb: a sphere inside a cylinder!
p: A sphere is the set of all points in space at the same distance r from a centre.
Surface area = 4πr². Archimedes showed this equals the curved surface area of the cylinder that just encloses the sphere (radius r, height 2r): 2πr × 2r = 4πr².
Volume = (4/3)πr³, which is exactly 2/3 of the enclosing cylinder's volume πr² × 2r = 2πr³.

Hands-on: wind a string tightly over half a ball (a hemisphere), then use the same length of string to fill circles of the ball's radius. A whole ball needs string to fill exactly 4 such circles, so its surface is 4πr².

ex.q: A ball has radius 7 cm. Find its surface area and volume. (π = 22/7)

topics.rl: Cricket balls, footballs and laddoos are close to spheres; makers use 4πr² for leather and (4/3)πr³ for filling.

rv.summary: A sphere's surface 4πr² equals the curved surface of its enclosing cylinder, and its volume (4/3)πr³ is 2/3 of that cylinder's volume, as Archimedes found.
focus: Find surface area and volume of spheres.
Use Archimedes' sphere–cylinder results.
Explain the string activity.
remember: Sphere = ⅔ of the cylinder's volume.
traps: Use the radius, not the diameter.
Cylinder height is 2r, not r.
Sphere is ⅔ of the cylinder, not ⅓.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.t: Maps, growing balls and hemisphere problems
topics.h: On many world maps Greenland looks as big as Africa. In reality Africa is about 14 times bigger!
p: A cylindrical map projection wraps a cylinder around the globe and transfers the surface onto it. Near the equator it is fairly accurate, but near the poles the map gets badly distorted (on the common Mercator map, regions near the poles look much bigger than they really are).
If a sphere's radius is multiplied by k, its surface area is multiplied by k² and its volume by k³. A 10% larger radius gives 21% more area and 33.1% more volume.

Hemisphere problems: a dome's curved surface is 2πr² (for painting); a solid hemisphere's total surface is 3πr²; a hemispherical shell with outer radius R and inner radius r has volume (2/3)π(R³ − r³).

ex.q: A hemispherical dome of radius 7 m is painted at ₹12 per m². Find the cost. (π = 22/7)

topics.rl: Temple and mosque domes, gol gumbaz and planetarium roofs are hemispheres; painters estimate cost from 2πr².

rv.summary: Cylindrical map projections distort areas near the poles. Scaling a sphere's radius by k multiplies area by k² and volume by k³. Hemisphere problems use 2πr², 3πr² and (2/3)π(R³ − r³).
focus: Apply k² and k³ to spheres.
Solve dome and shell problems.
Explain map distortion.
remember: Dome r = 7 at ₹12 per m²: 308 m², ₹3696.
traps: Use k² for area and k³ for volume.
Cube the radii before subtracting.
Use 2πr² for an open dome, 3πr² for a solid hemisphere.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.h: How many golgappas does India eat in a day? Nobody counts, but you can make a smart guess!
p: Everyday objects match solids: a gas cylinder (cylinder), a laddoo (sphere), a matchbox (cuboid), an ice-cream cone (cone plus hemisphere). Use the matching formula to estimate volumes.
Units: 1 litre = 1000 cm³, 1 m³ = 1000 litres, 1 m² = 10,000 cm².
Guesstimation: make clear, reasonable assumptions, round numbers, and combine them to get a sensible estimate (often just to the nearest power of 10).
Different assumptions give different answers: the number of tennis balls in a room depends on the room size and how tightly they pack. State your assumptions.
Projects: water you drink in a lifetime (≈ 2 L a day × 365 × 70 years ≈ 51,000 L), ink in a pen, volume of your house.

ex.q: Estimate the litres of water a person drinks in 70 years at 2 L a day.
st: About 51 m³, enough to fill a small swimming pool

topics.rl: Engineers planning a city's water supply start with exactly such guesstimates.

rv.summary: Everyday objects match solids, so their volumes can be estimated. Guesstimates state clear assumptions, round numbers and combine them; different assumptions can give different sensible answers.
focus: Match objects to solids and estimate volumes.
Convert between units.
Make and explain guesstimates.
remember: 1 litre = 1000 cm³; 1 m³ = 1000 L; 1 m² = 10,000 cm².
2 L a day for 70 years ≈ 51,000 L.
traps: Use 10,000 for m² to cm², not 100.
Convert m³ to litres.
Estimation is not random guessing.

topics.ch: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume
topics.t: The Earth-string puzzle and cube formulas
topics.h: Tie a string around the Earth's equator, then add just 1 metre. Could a cat crawl under it? Surprisingly, yes!
p: Earth-string puzzle: circumference C = 2πR. Adding 1 m makes C + 1 = 2π(R + gap), so gap = 1/(2π) ≈ 0.16 m, about 16 cm.
The gap does not depend on R at all: the same 16 cm for a football, the Earth or the Sun.
For a cube of edge a: V = a³ and S = 6a². Since a = V^(1/3), S = 6V^(2/3).
Example: V = 64 cm³ gives a = 4 and S = 6 × 16 = 96 cm². Doubling the volume does not double the surface; it multiplies it by 2^(2/3) ≈ 1.59.

ex.q: A string is wrapped tightly around a football (radius 11 cm). It is lengthened by 1 m. How big is the gap now?
st: About 16 cm, the same as for the Earth

topics.rl: Puzzles like this show why we trust algebra over gut feeling.

rv.summary: Adding 1 m to a string round any sphere lifts it by 1/(2π) ≈ 16 cm, whatever the size. For a cube, S = 6V^(2/3).
focus: Solve the Earth-string puzzle.
Move between a cube's volume and surface area.
Use scaling for cubes.
traps: The gap does not depend on the radius.
Area does not change like volume.

qa.q: What is the main job of a coordinate system?
qa.a: To fix exact locations using numbers
qa.e: A coordinate system is a framework of numbers that pins down exactly where something is.

qa.q: Which ancient feature shows early grid-based thinking in India?
qa.a: Streets of Mohenjo-daro laid out in a grid
qa.e: Planned cities of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation had straight streets crossing at right angles, like grid lines.

qa.q: Indian astronomers used which city as a reference line for longitude?
qa.e: Ujjayini (Ujjain) was the standard reference for longitude in Indian astronomy, much as Greenwich is today.

qa.q: Whose rules for zero and negative numbers made it possible to label points on both sides of an origin?
qa.e: Brahmagupta gave arithmetic rules for zero and negative numbers, which coordinates on the left and below the origin depend on.

qa.q: Which scholar is known for recording latitudes and longitudes of many places?
qa.e: Al-Biruni studied geography and gave coordinates of cities, and also estimated the size of the Earth.

qa.q: Omar Khayyam's contribution relevant to coordinates was that he:
qa.a: linked algebra with geometry by solving equations with curves
qa.e: He solved cubic equations using geometric curves, an early bridge between algebra and geometry.

qa.q: Descartes' key idea was that a point on a flat surface can be described by:
qa.e: Two numbers, one along each axis, fix any point on a plane. This is the Cartesian system.

qa.q: Aryabhata described the positions of what using coordinate-like measures?
qa.e: Aryabhata worked out positions of planets and stars in the sky, a celestial use of coordinates.

qa.q: On a map with scale 1 cm = 1 foot, a bed is 6.5 cm long. How long is the real bed, in feet?
qa.e: Each centimetre on paper stands for 1 foot, so 6.5 cm means 6.5 feet.

qa.q: A table is 4 feet long. On a map with scale 1 cm = 2 feet, how long should it be drawn?
qa.e: Divide the real length by 2 because every 2 feet becomes 1 cm.

qa.q: Why can a window not be marked on a floor map of a room?
qa.a: It is above floor level, so it has no position on the floor
qa.e: A floor map records what stands on the floor. A window is in the wall, higher up.

qa.q: In a tactile floor map made with pins and threads, what could the threads best show?
qa.a: The walls and edges of objects
qa.e: Threads stretched between pins make lines you can feel, like walls and table edges.

qa.q: Who is a tactile map most useful for?
qa.a: A person who cannot see and reads by touch
qa.e: Tactile means 'by touch'. Raised pins and threads let a visually impaired person feel the layout.

qa.q: A room is 15 feet by 10 feet. With scale 1 cm = 1 foot, what is the area of the room on paper?
qa.e: The map is 15 cm by 10 cm, so its area is 15 × 10.

qa.q: Simran's map has scale 1 cm = 3 feet. The door on her map is 1.2 cm wide. How wide is the real door, in feet?
qa.e: Multiply the paper length by 3 to get real feet.

qa.q: Which item belongs on a floor map of a classroom?
qa.e: The desk stands on the floor, so its outline can be marked. The others are above the floor.

qa.q: In the point (−6, 2), what is the abscissa?
qa.e: The abscissa is the x-coordinate, the first number of the ordered pair.

qa.q: What is the ordinate of the point (5, −9)?
qa.e: The ordinate is the y-coordinate, the second number of the pair.

qa.q: Which point lies on the y-axis?
qa.e: Points on the y-axis have x-coordinate 0, so (0, 7) is on the y-axis, 7 units above the origin.

qa.q: Where do the x-axis and the y-axis meet?
qa.e: The two axes cross at the origin, where both coordinates are zero.

qa.q: Arjun stands at the origin, walks 3 units left and then 5 units up. What are his coordinates now?
qa.e: Left makes x negative, so x = −3. Up makes y positive, so y = 5. He is at (−3, 5).

qa.q: Point A is at (4, 0). How far is A from the origin?
qa.e: A is on the x-axis, 4 steps to the right of the origin.

qa.q: Which statement about the point (2, 9) is correct?
qa.a: It is 2 units from the y-axis and 9 units from the x-axis
qa.e: The x-coordinate 2 tells how far the point is from the y-axis; the y-coordinate 9 tells how far it is from the x-axis.

qa.q: How far is the point (−5, 3) from the y-axis?
qa.e: Distance from the y-axis is the size of the x-coordinate. A distance is never negative, so it is 5 units.

qa.q: In which quadrant does (−5, 8) lie?
qa.e: x is negative and y is positive: (−, +) is Quadrant II, the top-left part.

qa.q: A point has a negative x-coordinate and a negative y-coordinate. Which quadrant is it in?
qa.e: (−, −) means left of the y-axis and below the x-axis: the bottom-left part, Quadrant III.

qa.q: Which point is in Quadrant IV?
qa.e: Quadrant IV has positive x and negative y. Only (3, −2) has the sign pattern (+, −).

qa.q: Where does the point (0, −6) lie?
qa.a: On the y-axis, in no quadrant
qa.e: Its x-coordinate is 0, so it sits on the y-axis. Points on the axes are not in any quadrant.

qa.q: Find the distance between A(2, 1) and B(8, 9).
qa.e: Across 6 and up 8 form the legs of a right triangle; the distance is the hypotenuse.

qa.q: How far is the point (−5, −12) from the origin?
qa.e: Use √(x² + y²). Squaring removes the negative signs.

qa.q: On a town map (1 unit = 1 km), Harpreet's house is at (−3, 4) and her school is at (5, 4). What is the straight distance between them?
qa.e: Both points have y = 4, so the line joining them is horizontal. Subtract the x-coordinates.

qa.q: The point (a, 3) lies in Quadrant II. Which value can a be?
qa.e: Quadrant II needs a negative x-coordinate. Only −4 is negative. (a = 0 would put the point on the y-axis.)

qa.q: To plot (−4, 6), which move do you make first from the origin?
qa.e: The x-coordinate comes first. It is −4, so move 4 units to the left, then 6 units up.

qa.q: Which point lies on the same horizontal line as (3, −2)?
qa.e: A horizontal line keeps the y-coordinate the same. (−5, −2) has y = −2, just like (3, −2).

qa.q: Kabir plots P(1, 2) and Q(1, 8). What is the length of PQ?
qa.e: P and Q have the same x-coordinate, so PQ is vertical. Its length is the difference of the y-coordinates.

qa.q: Riya draws a rectangle with corners (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 4) and (0, 4). What is its area?
qa.e: The length along the x-axis is 6 and the height along the y-axis is 4, so the area is 6 × 4.

qa.q: Three corners of a square are (1, 1), (5, 1) and (5, 5). What is the fourth corner?
qa.e: The side from (1, 1) to (5, 1) has length 4. The missing corner is 4 units above (1, 1), at (1, 5).

qa.q: Meena reads a point on a graph: it is 3 units below the x-axis and 7 units to the left of the y-axis. Which point is it?
qa.e: 7 units left of the y-axis gives x = −7; 3 units below the x-axis gives y = −3.

qa.q: On graph paper Joseph uses the scale 1 cm = 2 units. How far along the x-axis must he move to plot (10, 0)?
qa.e: Each centimetre stands for 2 units, so 10 units need 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.

qa.q: Points A(−3, 2) and B(4, 2) are plotted. What is the length of AB?
qa.e: Same y-coordinate, so AB is horizontal. Length = 4 − (−3) = 7 units.

qa.q: In a room plan, a door runs along the x-axis from (2, 0) to (5.5, 0), in feet. How wide is the door, in feet?
qa.e: Both ends are on the x-axis, so the width is the difference of the x-coordinates.

qa.q: A wheelchair needs at least 2.8 ft of clear width. A door goes from (4, 0) to (6.5, 0) in feet. Will the wheelchair pass?
qa.a: No, the door is only 2.5 ft wide
qa.e: Width = 6.5 − 4 = 2.5 ft, which is less than 2.8 ft.

qa.q: A 3 ft door is hinged at (0, 0) and swings into the room. A table leg is at (2, 2). Will the door hit it?
qa.a: Yes, the leg is about 2.83 ft from the hinge, inside the 3 ft swing
qa.e: The door sweeps a quarter circle of radius 3. The leg's distance from the hinge is √(4 + 4) = √8 ≈ 2.83 ft, which is less than 3.

qa.q: Kavya's room is 16 ft by 12 ft, with one corner at the origin. Where is the centre of the room?
qa.e: The centre is at half the length and half the breadth.

qa.q: A 6 ft × 4 ft carpet is centred at (8, 6). What is the x-coordinate of its left edge?
qa.e: Half of the 6 ft length is 3, so the left edge is 3 ft left of the centre.

qa.q: A wardrobe has corners (0, 2), (2, 2), (2, 8) and (0, 8) in feet. How much wall space along the y-axis does it use, in feet?
qa.e: Along the y-axis it runs from y = 2 to y = 8.

qa.q: What shape do (0, 0), (8, 0), (6, 4) and (2, 4) make?
qa.e: The bottom (length 8) and top (length 4) are both horizontal, so they are parallel; the slanted sides are not parallel.

qa.q: The corners of a bathroom in a plan are (10, 0), (14, 0), (14, 5) and (10, 5). What is its floor area?
qa.e: It is a rectangle 4 ft by 5 ft.

qa.q: Find the length of side PQ of triangle P(−2, 1), Q(4, 9), R(4, 1).
qa.e: Across 6 and up 8, so PQ is the hypotenuse of a 6-8 right triangle.

qa.q: In triangle P(−2, 1), Q(4, 9), R(4, 1), which side is parallel to the y-axis?
qa.e: Q and R both have x = 4, so QR is vertical, parallel to the y-axis.

qa.q: What is the mirror image of (−5, 3) in the y-axis?
qa.e: Reflecting in the y-axis changes only the sign of the x-coordinate.

qa.q: A triangle with sides 5, 6 and 7 units is reflected in the x-axis. What is the length of the longest side of the image?
qa.e: A reflection does not change any length.

qa.q: Neha wants a right triangle with legs 5 and 12 using the corner (0, 0). Which pair of other corners works?
qa.e: (5, 0) is on the x-axis and (0, 12) on the y-axis, giving legs 5 and 12 meeting at a right angle at the origin.

qa.q: What is the hypotenuse of the right triangle with corners (0, 0), (5, 0) and (0, 12)?
qa.e: Use Pythagoras on the legs 5 and 12.

qa.q: Triangle A(1, 2), B(6, 2), C(1, 7). At which vertex is the right angle?
qa.e: AB is horizontal (same y) and AC is vertical (same x). They meet at A.

qa.q: The point (2, −6) is reflected in the y-axis and then in the x-axis. Where does it end up?
qa.e: First (2, −6) → (−2, −6), then (−2, −6) → (−2, 6). Both signs change.

qa.q: Points (−5, 2), (−5, 1), (−5, 0), (−5, −1) go down a line. In which quadrant is the next point (−5, −2)?
qa.e: x stays −5 (negative) and y is now −2 (negative): (−, −) is Quadrant III.

qa.q: Which point lies on the same vertical line as (6, −3)?
qa.e: A vertical line keeps the x-coordinate fixed. Only (6, 10) has x = 6.

qa.q: The line y = −4 is drawn. Which quadrants does it pass through?
qa.e: y = −4 is a horizontal line below the x-axis, running through the bottom-left and bottom-right quadrants.

qa.q: For points A, B, C, AB = 7, BC = 5 and AC = 12. What can you say?
qa.a: A, B and C are collinear
qa.e: AB + BC = 7 + 5 = 12 = AC, so B lies on the segment AC.

qa.q: Are P(0, 0), Q(3, 4) and R(9, 12) collinear? Use distances.
Points A(0, 0), B(4, 3) and C(4, 0). AB = 5, BC = 3, AC = 4. Are they collinear?
qa.a: No, 3 + 4 = 7 is more than the longest side 5
qa.e: For collinear points the two shorter distances must add to exactly the longest. Here 3 + 4 = 7 ≠ 5, so they form a triangle.

qa.q: Rohit draws a grid with no negative numbers to map his school. What must he do?
qa.a: Put the origin at a corner so everything is to its right and above
qa.e: Without negatives, nothing can lie left of or below the origin, so it must be at the bottom-left corner.

qa.q: What is a limitation of a coordinate system without negative numbers?
qa.a: Places left of or below the origin cannot be named
qa.e: Negative coordinates are needed for points on the other side of each axis.

qa.q: Is the point (5, 12) inside, on or outside the circle of radius 13 centred at the origin?
Where is (−6, 7) compared with the circle x² + y² = 81 (radius 9)?
qa.e: 36 + 49 = 85, which is more than 81.

qa.q: A screen is 100 pixels wide and 60 tall, with corners (0, 0) and (100, 60). Does a circle of radius 35 centred at (50, 30) fit?
qa.a: No, it pokes out at the top and bottom
qa.e: The centre is only 30 from the top and bottom edges, which is less than the radius 35. It is 50 from the side edges, so the sides are fine.

qa.q: Two circles have centres (0, 0) and (6, 8), with radii 4 and 5. Do they meet?
qa.a: No, the centres are 10 apart and 4 + 5 = 9
qa.e: Distance between centres = √(36 + 64) = 10, which is more than the sum of radii 9.

qa.q: Show that P(0, 0), Q(3, 0), R(3, 3), S(0, 3) is a square. What is its area?
qa.e: All four sides are 3 and both diagonals are √18, so it is a square of side 3.

qa.q: Points (0, 0), (2, 1), (1, 3), (−1, 2): each side is √5 and both diagonals are √10. What is the area of this square?
qa.e: Area of a square = side² = (√5)² = 5.

qa.q: In a city grid, Shreya is at the corner of Street 3 and Avenue 5, written (3, 5). She walks 4 streets east and 2 avenues south. Where is she?
qa.e: East increases the street number by 4; south decreases the avenue number by 2.

qa.q: A triangle has base A(−3, 0), B(3, 0). Which third vertex makes the two slanting sides equal (an isosceles triangle)?
qa.e: A point on the y-axis is equally far from (−3, 0) and (3, 0), so the two sides from the apex are equal.

qa.q: What is the midpoint of A(−4, 6) and B(8, 2)?
qa.e: Average the x-coordinates and average the y-coordinates.

qa.q: Is M(3, 5) the midpoint of P(1, 2) and Q(5, 9)?
M(2, −1) is the midpoint of AB and A is (−3, 4). What is the x-coordinate of B?
M(2, −1) is the midpoint of AB and A is (−3, 4). What is the y-coordinate of B?
Which point divides the segment from (0, 0) to (12, 6) at one-third of the way from the origin?
qa.e: One-third of the way means one-third of each change: 12/3 = 4 and 6/3 = 2.

qa.q: Find the second point of trisection (two-thirds of the way) from A(−3, 1) to B(6, 7).
qa.e: The change is 9 in x and 6 in y; two-thirds of that is 6 and 4. Add to A.

qa.q: The midpoints of the sides of a triangle are D(3, 4), E(5, 2) and F(1, 1). The vertex between midpoints D and E (opposite F) is D + E − F. What is it?
Gurpreet's home is at (−2, 8) and Asha's at (6, 0). Where is the halfway meeting point?
What is the degree of 3x⁴ − 7x² + x − 10?
qa.e: The highest power of x is 4.

qa.q: What is the degree of the polynomial 12?
qa.e: 12 = 12x⁰, so the highest power of x is 0.

qa.q: Which is a quadratic polynomial?
qa.e: A quadratic has degree 2. In 5 − x² the highest power is 2.

qa.q: How many terms are there in 8y³ − y + 2?
qa.e: The terms are 8y³, −y and 2.

qa.q: Which expression is NOT a polynomial in one variable?
qa.e: x² + y has two different variables, x and y.

qa.q: Why is the degree of 9 equal to 0?
qa.e: Any non-zero constant can be written with x⁰, so the highest power is 0.

qa.q: In 2x − 7x³ + 4, which term decides the degree?
qa.e: −7x³ has the highest power, 3, so the polynomial is cubic.

qa.q: Which is a cubic polynomial?
qa.e: x − x³ has highest power 3.

qa.q: What is the coefficient of x² in 7x³ − 4x + 9?
qa.e: There is no x² term, so its coefficient is 0.

qa.q: What is the coefficient of x in 5 − x + 2x²?
qa.e: The term −x means −1 × x.

qa.q: What is the constant term of 3x² − 8x − 11?
qa.e: The term without x is −11; the sign belongs to it.

qa.q: If p(x) = x² − 4x + 3, find p(−1).
If q(x) = 3x² − 2, find q(−3).
qa.e: Square first: (−3)² = 9, then 3 × 9 − 2.

qa.q: A ball's height after t seconds is h(t) = 20t − 5t² metres. What is its height at t = 2?
Which is a polynomial of degree 3 with constant term −2?
qa.e: Its highest power is 3 and its constant is −2.

qa.q: If p(x) = 2x + 7, find p(−4) + p(4).
qa.e: p(−4) = −1 and p(4) = 15, so the sum is 14.

qa.q: Which of these is a linear polynomial?
qa.e: 4x − 1 has the form ax + b with highest power of x equal to 1.

qa.q: If p(x) = 3x − 7, find p(4).
qa.e: Replace x by 4 and simplify.

qa.q: What is the degree of the polynomial 6 − 2x?
qa.e: The highest power of x is x¹, so the degree is 1.

qa.q: Aisha's phone plan costs ₹99 fixed plus ₹2 per GB of data. Which polynomial gives the cost for x GB?
qa.e: The ₹2 is paid for each GB, so it multiplies x. The ₹99 is paid once, so it is the constant.

qa.q: For p(x) = 5x + 2, find p(−3).
At a sports shop the price of x cricket balls is p(x) = 150x rupees. What is p(4) − p(3)?
qa.e: One extra ball adds the coefficient of x, ₹150, to the price.

qa.q: Which expression is NOT a linear polynomial?
qa.e: x(x + 1) = x² + x has degree 2, so it is not linear. x/3 + 1 is linear because x/3 = (1/3)x.

qa.q: If p(x) = ax + 4 and p(2) = 10, what is a?
qa.e: Put x = 2: 2a + 4 = 10, so 2a = 6 and a = 3.

qa.q: What is the zero of p(x) = x − 6?
qa.e: x − 6 = 0 gives x = 6. Check: 6 − 6 = 0.

qa.q: Find the zero of 4x + 20.
Where does the graph of y = 2x − 10 cross the x-axis?
qa.e: On the x-axis y = 0, so 2x − 10 = 0 and x = 5. The crossing point is (5, 0).

qa.q: How many zeros does a linear polynomial ax + b (with a ≠ 0) have?
qa.e: A non-horizontal straight line crosses the x-axis exactly once, at x = −b/a.

qa.q: Is x = 3 a zero of p(x) = 3x − 9?
qa.e: p(3) = 3 × 3 − 9 = 0, so 3 is a zero.

qa.q: Arjun's lemonade stall makes a profit of p(x) = 5x − 150 rupees when he sells x glasses. How many glasses must he sell to break even (zero profit)?
qa.e: Break even means p(x) = 0: 5x = 150, so x = 30.

qa.q: The zero of 3x + k is 2. What is k?
qa.e: Since 2 is a zero, 3 × 2 + k = 0, so k = −6.

qa.q: What is the zero of p(x) = 2x + 3?
